item.title: [投资TALK君] ✨【投资TALK君1493期】鹰还是鸽？走入沃什的内心世界！✨20260916#CPI #nvda #美股 #投资 #英伟达 #ai #特斯拉
item.dc:creator: 投资TALK君
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：这次加息其实是一场"信号被过滤"的实验

小陶反复强调"凯文沃什一直在给指引，只是市场没有接收到"——这句话背后藏着一个远比"鹰派/鸽派"更值得警惕的现象：市场并不是被信息不足打败的，而是被自己的叙事偏见打败的。

从 6 月到 9 月，两年期美债收益率一直在替沃什"做事情"，债券市场其实早已完成定价。但股票市场的参与者却死死抱住"沃什是川普选上来的人，不可能加息"这一先验假设——即使债券市场用真金白银给出反证，他们仍然把它当噪音过滤掉。

这几乎是香农信息论的一个反面案例：信号本身清晰、重复、冗余度极高（6 月讲、7 月讲、8 月 Jackson Hole 再讲），但接收端的"贝叶斯先验"太强，导致真实信息被系统性地丢弃。今天市场大跌收盘、盘后反弹 0.6-0.7%，正是这种"叙事被现实撞碎"后的迟到修正。

二、跨领域连接：沃什在建立的是"央行界的纳什均衡"

小陶用了一个非常关键的词：Follow through。这个词在网球和高尔夫里叫"随挥动作"，在心理学里叫"承诺一致性"，但在央行学里——它其实是信用货币化。

沃什这次真正在做的事情，不是加不加息，而是让"说到"和"做到"之间的因果链条被市场看见并验证。一旦这个链条被建立，一件反常的事情就发生了：市场现在的定价比 SEP 点阵图还要鹰派 0.6 个百分点（相当于两次以上的加息）。

这不是市场不信他，而是市场"过度相信"他——由此进入一个博弈论意义上的新均衡：沃什现在可以用更少的实际动作，去撬动更大的预期调整。这就像日本剑道里的"气"——真正的高手拔剑之前，对手已经跪下。未来沃什可能不需要真的加息，只需要暗示，市场就会自动完成收紧。这也解释了为什么他这么在意"过去 120 天一直在思考"这句话——他在为未来的每一次"仅凭嘴巴调节"打信用地基。

三、最容易被忽略的伏笔：油价被纳入决策函数，是一次静默的范式转变

传统上美联储盯的是核心通胀——刻意剔除食品和能源，因为这两者太受供给冲击影响。但沃什这次两次提到"地缘政治—油价"影响了加息决定，这几乎是打破了 Bernanke 以来 20 年的央行正统。

这里面藏着一个让人后背发凉的反馈回路：

地缘政治紧张 → 油价上涨 → 美联储加息 → 美元走强 → 新兴市场压力 → 地缘政治更紧张

这是一个正反馈系统（褒义上的"共振腔"，贬义上的"死亡螺旋"），美联储把自己主动接入了这个回路。历史上格林斯潘和伯南克都极力避免这种耦合，因为一旦耦合，货币政策就从"独立变量"变成了"内生变量"，Fed 会失去自己在通胀周期中的高地。

沃什这么做，可能不是失误，而是主动重新定义了央行的坐标系。他给的信号是：这一届美联储不是象牙塔里的模型派，而是拿着新闻头条做决策的现实派。这也意味着——下一次油价如果因为中东局势急跌，市场应该立刻重新定价 12 月不加息的可能性。小陶讲这是"意外"，但我认为这可能是这次会议最深远的、被所有人低估的一个变化。

四、附赠一个隐藏结构：估值悖论正在把美股推向一次"分子分母之争"

小陶最后提到：PE 18.9 倍绝对不是泡沫，但 E（盈利）本身可能是泡沫。这句话如果展开，就是整个 AI 资本开支叙事的核心风险——大科技公司之间互相买卡、互相签云合同、互相计入收入的"循环资金"（circular funding）正在制造一种统计上真实、经济上可疑的盈利增长。

如果 2026 年财报季 AI 相关的 revenue 增速开始与 capex 增速脱钩，那么现在这个"低 PE"就会瞬间被 revalue 成"高 PE"，而这一切与沃什加不加息无关——它是货币政策管不到的、发生在会计层面上的风险。这可能才是未来 6 个月真正的定价错误来源。

📝 转录文本

开场：这次会议真正的价值

今天美联储的会议到底是鹰还是鸽？凯文沃什的讲话到底是鹰还是鸽？我觉得比起找到这一个答案，这一次的美联储会议我认为是一个非常好的机会，我们可以去了解凯文沃什这一个为人，包括他的一个做事方法，还有他的一个判断标准。所以今天我希望大家可以跟着我这期视频，我们一起进入凯文沃什的世界。

啊，欢迎大家来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小陶。应大家在 X 上的这个需求，虽然我今天已经做过直播，在 APP 上面已经做过直播，虽然现在的时间也已经不早了，但是还是决定为大家来做一期视频，但是这期视频我尽量保持的时间稍微短一些，但是我还是想帮大家一起去过一下这一次的一个美联储会议。

一、客观数据：SEP 与加息决定

好，我们先来看一下，先来看一些数据，先从一个比较客观的视角去看一下这一次的美联储会议。首先是公告本身，公告是对于 SEP，然后还有美联储这一次决定，从加息或者不加息这个决定去看，市场原本在会议之前的预期是完全正确的。

那所以到现在为止，我相信应该不会有人在预期今年年底的时候还会降息吧，对吧？即使在其实在这一次美联储会议之前，市场有不少的声音认为、仍然认为啊，今年美联储会降息，就或者说这么觉得是——很，很，还有另外一部分的声音认为凯文沃什是川普选上来的，所以川普选上来的人就不可能加息。那这一部分人我相信在这一次加息完之后已经没有了，已经不存在。

二、SEP 相对市场其实是鸽派

所以我们来看一下 SEP，这一次的 SEP 其实和市场的这个预期做对比的话是鸽派的。鸽派在哪呢？我们从核心 PCE 这个角度去看，和 6 月份所做的这个预期做对比的话，核心 PCE 26 年年底只上升了 0.1%，而 27 年对于通胀的这个预期完全没有任何的改变。

在 Federal Funds Rate、在隔夜利率这一块，或者美联储的联邦利率、基准利率这一块，在 26 年是上升了一次加息，从 3.8 上升到了 4.1，而整个 27 年上升了 0.5 个基点或者两次加息。但是我们把 26 年和 27 年去做对比的话，27 年在 26 年的基础上不会有任何的加息。

那看到这一次 SEP，有人会问：那这一次的 SEP 和 6 月份做对比的话是鹰派的呀？的确和 6 月份做对比的话是鹰派的。但是你要知道市场现在定价了多少。我们到底是鹰派还是鸽派，我们是和现在债券市场做的这个定价去做这个对比，而不是和上一次的 SEP 做对比。和上一次已经没有任何的意义了，因为从 6 月份到 9 月份到现在为止，过去的三个月市场是有波动的，市场是有这个定价在那边。

三、点阵图解读

从点阵图这一个角度去看，对于今年加息次数的这个预期非常的一致，多数的人都认为——多数的美联储成员都认为今年还会有一次加息。那至于这一次加息会在什么时候，稍后我会和大家分享一下我自己的一些看法。我认为 10 月份加息的概率非常的低，12 月份加息的概率几乎是 100% 会确定会加息，或者这个加息的概率会非常的高，不能说 100%，不能那么的绝对嘛。

2027 年你可以看到，在上一次 SEP 里边的话，2027 年的预测是非常的分散。那么我在昨天视频里面有聊过，非常分散的一个点阵图是没有任何参考意义。但是这一次 2027 年的点阵图其实已经非常集中了。那非常集中的一个结果就是有 6 位美联储成员认为 27 年不会加息，3 个人认为会降息两次，有 1 个人认为会降息四次（那这个人的观点是没有任何的参考价值，不用去看），然后有 8 个人认为 27 年还会加息一次。

但是，即使有 8 个人认为 27 年还会加息一次的这个基础上，和现在市场的预期去做对比的话，现在市场的预期接下去还会有 3.2 次的加息（算上 12 月份的加息），那市场预计 27 年有 2.2 次。啊，所以即使美联储的成员认为 27 年还会有一次加息的这个概率在那边，和现在市场预期 27 年还会有 2.2 次这个加息去做对比，仍然这个点阵图是鸽派的。

四、从债券期货市场看真实定价

有些人问我，那我怎么知道市场到底定价了多少次加息？其实从债券市场——债券的一个期货市场是可以看到市场的这个定价和预期的。9 月 15 日，也就是在这一次会议之前，昨天的一个收盘可以看到市场预计或者定价了 27 年最高隔夜利率会达到 4.6%。那 4.6% 从现在的这个基础就是会上升，差不多加息 3.8 次。

从债券期货市场，无论是周二的收盘还是周三的收盘去看，债券市场对于加息次数的这个定价，都比 SEP 要鹰派。所以点阵图本身和市场的预期去做对比的话，是一个鸽派的一个点阵图。那加息是符合市场预期的这个结果。

五、记者会第一点：Jackson Hole 就已给过指引

然后我们来看一下这一次的记者招待会里面的 Q&A。总体来说，这一次的美联储会议，我前面说的，我说你去探究它是一个鹰派的加息、还是鸽派的加息，我觉得意义可能已经不是那么的大。更加重要的意义是，我们通过这一次美联储会议去进入或者去了解凯文沃什这个人。

那这一次会议之后，我认为我对于他的了解有了非常深入、有了非常深刻的这个了解。我认为这一次的会议是成功的，而且也大大增加了市场对于凯文沃什或者这一届的美联储的一个信心和信任在背后。这也是为什么现在市场那个定价反而比——就对于加息这个定价反而比美联储 SEP 里面所给的这个指引更加的鹰派。

然后我们来看一下凯文沃什讲话第一点：他说到 "Jackson Hole 会议的时候，我说过让我现在去说市场是紧缩的，我会受到非常大的这个挑战，所以今天我加息了。" 这一句话给我的一个感觉就是，他想要表达：其实在 Jackson Hole 会议 8 月份的时候，我就已经给过市场这个指引了。

他在今天的一个讲话里面，他有很多次都引用了他在 6 月份讲过的话、他在 8 月份所讲过的话。他想表达什么？他想表达"我其实并没有不给市场指引，我一直在给市场指引，只是市场没有接收到我的信号"。

六、回顾 6 月到 9 月：信号一以贯之

从某种程度，我们现在回过头去看，我认为随着这一次 9 月份的一个加息完之后，我们回过头去看 6 月份的市场、6 月份美联储会议、7 月份美联储会议、8 月份 Jackson Hole 会议、9 月份这一次加息——全部可以串起来。

我稍微带大家回顾一下。6 月份那一次会议之后，我当时的观点，我说凯文沃什非常的鹰派。但是当时底下的留言有——我记得印象非常深刻的一个留言是——"但是市场不认同你的看法，特别是股市不认同你的看法，因为那一天股市上涨了"。

其实我今天这期视频一开始我想讲的是：我们要去判断凯文沃什的讲话或者美联储到底是鹰派还是鸽派，千万不要拿当天市场的一个走势去做这个判断。OK，你拿当天市场的一个走势，周三市场最后的确是收跌的。那，如果你从开会之前到开会之后的话，市场的确是下跌的，然后你的理解就是"OK 市场下跌，所以美联储是鹰派的"。但是你怎么去解释现在的盘后是上涨了？现在盘后上涨了 0.6% 、0.7% 吧，指数上涨 0.6、0.7。那到底是鹰派的还是鸽派的？

啊，所以美联储鹰派还是鸽派，对于市场的这个影响，它是可持续的。千万不要从结果去出发，去倒推美联储是鹰派的还是鸽派的。

6 月份的鹰派信号

所以 6 月份他讲了什么？对吧，6 月份他讲"我一定要压制通胀"，啊，"我对于压制通胀的这个决心，我们整个美联储对于压制通胀的这个决心非常的一致"。其实他那一天讲完话之后，我说他是鹰派的，然后那一天其实债券市场就已经在开始帮他做事情了，债券市场就已经开始在帮他定价加息了。

只是当时市场说你不会加息的，当时市场说——哎，啊不，或者一部分的参与者认为他是（凯文沃什是川普选上来的，所以）"在川普中期选举前，他怎么可能逆着川普的话或者逆着川普的意思去进行加息"，没有人认为。即使债券市场已经定价加息，但是很多人仍然认为不会加息。这其实是我非常疑惑的一个点。包括在两三周之前，我发了一张图，我说两年期的美债收率引领着加息这个周期，很多人仍然认为——就仍然认为这张图是不可靠的，或者仍然认为还会有降息的这个概率在那边。其实我非常地不理解，对吧。

所以 6 月份的时候，他讲完话之后，鹰派的发言，债券市场两年期的美债收率马上帮他开始定价加息。

7 月份的"我们不是来惊吓市场"

然后 7 月份，当时 7 月份的一个背景是什么？在进入 7 月份会议之前，市场认为 7 月份加息的概率是 35%。我说当时有一个不对称的风险，不对称的风险是凯文沃什有可能在 7 月份加息。然后在那次会议的时候，他的确没有加息。

他会议里面的第一句话说："我们不是来惊吓这个市场。" 当时我说从预期这个角度去看的话，这句话本身是给了市场一定的确定性——就在正常情况下，我不会来惊讶这个市场、不会来惊吓这个市场。什么意思？当你市场有大概率的情况下定价我不会加息，那我就不会加息。所以在这一次会议之前，市场预期 90% 以上的概率认为它会加息，那就它就会加息，因为它在 7 月份会议的时候已经告诉市场了——你市场怎么定价，我就怎么去做。

8 月份 Jackson Hole 的铺垫

然后到了 8 月份的那一次 Jackson Hole 会议，他说道："现在的是，如果让我说现在市场是紧缩的话，我会受到非常大的这个挑战。" 意思就是说，我认为当下的一个市场金融环境是不紧缩的，是在一个宽松的一个状态之下。其实就是为了 9 月份的这个加息去做一个铺垫。

所以它从 6 月份开始就已经在向市场去透露要加息的这个决心和信心了，或者他的一个想法在背后了。啊，所以这一点，他是故意让市场知道，我在 8 月份的时候就已经给你们提示了。

七、记者会第二点：过去 120 天一直在思考

第二点，今天的这个决定是我过去 120 天里边一直在思考的。这句话再次验证了这一次加息、9 月份的这个加息，我在 120 天之前——110 天、120 天之前，我就在想了。那时候什么时候？6 月份，他刚刚上位的时候。

所以，他想说的是这两句——我说这，把这两句话放在一起的话，有可能是在为加息做解释。但是他给我的一个感觉就是加息这一个决定，或者加息的这个种子，早就在 6 月份的时候就已经铺下去了。所以我们并不应该无视他在 6 月份当时的一个发言。

所以当时 6 月份市场的这个定价是正确的，他讲完话之后，两年期美债收益率开始去定价，马上又开始进行加息，市场的定价就是正确。那所以这也解释了、或者这也合理地解释了为什么 6 月份当时的发言是鹰派的，因为市场开始定价这个加息嘛。其实也是因为凯文沃什所透露出来的这些信息，或者说前瞻性的指引——他给了前瞻性的这个指引了，但并不是没有给。

八、记者会第三点：判断标准是"趋势"而非"单点"

然后第三点，这一点我认为非常的重要，就是接下去他判断的一个标准是什么。他说"市场关注单一数据是非常危险的行为，随着时间的这个推移，市场会慢慢的理解这一届美联储是怎么做决定的"。

他说的非常的明确，他说"我看的是一个趋势，我并非只看这一个单一的数据点"。因为问题问的是——市场当时非常关注 8 月份的通胀数据，认为 8 月份的通胀数据好你就不会加息、8 月份的通胀数据不好你就会加息，但是凯文沃什说：其实 8 月份的通胀数据，在他眼里并不是一个决定性的因素。

那也正是因为他说我通常是看数据的，那你想一下，接下去 10 月份和 12 月份——12 月份他应该还能够看到 9 月份、10 月份、11 月份的通胀，我不知道他看不看得到，就起码能够看到两组到三组的数据。但是刚刚过去的这一个月的数据，通胀并不好。你要看到这个趋势的话，起码是两个月的数据。那所以除非 9 月份和 10 月份的通胀数据非常的好，环比增速在 0.1% 或者 0.1 以下，那有可能 12 月份不加息，不然的话在 12 月份之前，他是看不到通胀数据放缓的这个趋势的。趋势不是一组数据、不是单点的数据，是几组数据连在一起，起码要两三组数据连在一起。

九、10 月低概率、12 月高概率

啊，所以我认为 9 月份加息的概率非常的大，且非常的确定。那为什么不会在 10 月份加息？也是因为经过这一次加息完之后，我会发——我发现或者我认为凯文沃什是一个说到做到的人。什么叫说到做到？那就是他以前也说过，他说在中期或者有些政治事件之前，美联储不宜去做一些决定。

那如果他还是按照原来自己这个原则的话，在 10 月 28 日下一次美联储会议的时候，最正确的一个决定是不去做任何加息或者不加息的这个决定，不去影响到中期选举。啊，所以我认为虽然现在市场是定价了 10 月份有 50% 的概率会加息，但是我认为 10 月份加息的概率不高、比较的低，而 12 月份加息这个概率非常的高。好吗？

十、记者会第四点：十年期利率上涨的三个原因

然后第四点，市场问他"十年期的利率为何上涨"，他说——

第一点，因为经济非常的强。

第二点，资金的竞争，就是大科技这一块资本的一个开支。资本开支来自于哪？很多的钱是来自于融资，融资的这个钱主要来自于比如说举债。举债会影响到——就市场里面钱就这么点，钱非常的稀有。钱，当钱非常稀有的时候，你的钱的一个成本、借钱的这个成本就上升；借钱的成本上升，利率就上升。那一部分企业债券的这个利率的上升，也导致了国债利率的这个上升。没有非常直接的这个影响，但也部分也会影响到。

第三个就是地缘政治。地缘政治这一块非常的有意思，他两次聊到了地缘政治影响到了 10 年期利率的这个上涨，且地缘政治影响到他们这一次做加息这个决定。也就是说，油价的这个上涨是影响到了他们的决定了。这一点非常的有意思。但是起码他也给了这个标准了——就是如果接下去油价出现下跌的话，我们有可能会考虑不加息。

十一、Follow through：说到做到的信用

所以通过这一次的会议，我认为我对他已经有了一个比较完善的一个了解了。就从 6 月份到 7 月份到 8 月份的讲话，到这一次的一个会议的一个讲话，整个过程我认为他是基本上是说到做到了。而且他说了市场开始定价，定价完之后他就 follow，呃——我在过去几次会议里面，我一直用的一个词是什么？Follow through。

什么叫 Follow through？就是你用嘴去调节市场这个预期可以，但是市场已经帮你去做这件事情，你就必须要跟着市场去做。不然的话你不去做的话，你就会在市场这块失去你的这个信用，那未来你再用这张嘴去调节市场预期的话，你就做不到了。啊，所以这就叫 follow through——就你说到要做到，你说到市场帮你去定价，你就要做到。

所以他整个这一个一套逻辑，他已经走下来，他说到了，市场也定价了，他也做到了。啊，所以他算是一个说到做到的一个美联储主席，所以他也获得了市场的这个信任。

十二、美联储内部的共识

包括这一次，我想一下，从 12 月——上年 12 月份是鲍威尔最后一次会议的一个决定，他是决定要降息，但是上年的 12 月份就已经有人 dissent、就已经有人不同意他上次一个降息。从上一次利率会议到现在为止，几乎每一次的一个美联储会议都有人不同意最后一个决定。

这一次终于所有的美联储成员，大家的一个意见是一致的，大家统一的都认为这一次应该加息。那所以美联储的内部好不容易现在也有了一个共识。这个共识其实还比较重要，因为对于凯文沃什来说，在美联储的内部获取这一个信任也非常的重要。

所以这一次我认为：一，获取了市场的这个信任；第二点，获取了美联储内部的这个信任；第三点，给了市场非常重要的——他的一个判断标准到底是什么。

十三、总结沃什的画像

啊，所以我这边做的总结第一点就是：他其实一直认为经济是太强了，通胀是不可接受的，所以加息在他的一个视角里面其实早就该做了。7 月份的时候他可能就应该想做了，然后他说 7 月份的时候"我们再给市场一些时间，我们再去观察一下、再给我们自己观察一下"。但是其实他在 7 月份的时候，就已经认为当时通胀的一个趋势是他不能接受的。那所以当凯文沃什上来的时候，他就是属于鹰派的那一类。但起码暂时来说，他是属于鹰派的那一类，对吗？

然后第二点就是他注重的是一个趋势，而并非单一的这个数据。那也就是加息可能是连贯的。所以我像我前面说到，我认为 10 月底的这个会议——因为在中期选举之前，所以根据他以前的这个讲话，加息的概率是比较低的，而 12 月份加息的这个概率是比较的高或者比较的确定。

十四、市场反馈：比美联储还鹰派

那最后这边就是今天市场的这个反馈。两年期美债收入上涨了 7 个基点，市场明显比美联储——整个美联储比他更加的鹰派。某种程度也是市场对于凯文沃什给予的信心，或者认为他能够去压制通胀。

那所以接下去我认为，因为两年期美债收入的一个上涨，短期来说长债收益率也出现了上涨，但上涨不是非常的明显。但是你随着时间的这个推移，我认为长债这一块的一个通胀预期、break even 是会下降的。整体来说，名义利率会不会下降还要取决于另外一个点：就是贝森特会不会行动。在中期选举之前，如果贝森特也行动的话，我认为名义利率是会下降的、长债这一块的名义利率。

啊，两年期上涨了 7 个基点，那就是定价了接下去还会有 3.2 次这个加息——就是你如果加息完 3.2 次的话，联储利率要去到 4.7% 了，但是在点阵图里面是多少？4.1。就是现在明显市场是比美联储点阵图里面还要鹰了多少？0.6 个百分点。0.6 个百分点是两次加息以上了。那所以我认为当下市场的一个现状就是：市场对于加息周期的这个次数是过于悲观了，那反映在期货市场里面。

十五、恐慌情绪：油价 + 参与度双低

第二个，市场现在对于油价非常担心。油价现在在多少？105、1.6 左右。呃，对于油价非常的担心，对于战争非常担心。然后再是一些数据，CNN 的恐慌贪婪指数里面的广度和深度都在一个极度恐慌。然后你再去看市场的一个参与度，现在又是在一个恐慌的阶段。

那所以从一个相对比较短期的一个角度去看，那么我这是我是写在下午 4 点半的时候，我说我从一个短期的一个角度去看，在财报之前，在这个位置或者这个位置以下，我认为都是买点。因为现在市场的一个 setup 就是在一个恐慌的阶段，而且市场对于加息又担心、对于油价又担心，参与度又在一个低位，所以现在市场就是处在一个恐慌的阶段。

参与度这边：标普 500，20 日均线跌到了 18，50 日均线也跌到了 31；罗素 2000，20、25，350 日的话跌到了 32%；纳指也是一样的，20 日均线跌到了 25%，50 日均线跌到了 32%，200 日均线都跌了 38%。就有超过 50% 以上的公司、60% 的公司、纳指都是跌于 200 日均线以上。200 日均线通常是一个长期的一个牛熊分界线。啊，所以从纳指的一个参与度可以看到，现在市场的情绪面是非常的低、参与度非常的低。

十六、估值不是泡沫，争论点在盈利能力

从估值这个角度去看，标普 500 的估值，4OP 跌到了 18.9 倍，跌到了今年 3 月份的水平。在上年 2025 年 3 月份是在 18 倍，那在 21 年年底到 22 年那一波加息周期的一个起点是在 21.5 倍。所以现在的估值——OK，很多人认为"啊，我们要重复 2022 年的这种跌幅"，也可以，你可以这么去认为。但是整个市场的一个 setup 是不一样的。从估值这个角度就不一样，现在的估值比 22 年年初的时候还要低。

那所以美股，你无论去看标普 500 也好、纳指也好、半导体板块也好，都是一样，现在估值就是在一个相对的低位。所以整体现在美股是没有估值这个泡沫，就是这是一个事实，是绝对没有估值这个泡沫在那边，PE 是没有泡沫的。

现在市场的一个争论点是在这个 earnings、盈利能力是不是有一个泡沫。因为如果盈利能力被高估的话，你简单来说，现在估值虽然看起来非常的低，但其实估值比较的高，因为你的盈利能力有泡沫。啊，所以现在市场的一个争论点不是在估值有没有泡沫——估值绝对没有泡沫——而是盈利能力是不是有泡沫。

那盈利能力是不是有泡沫，这就是一个见仁见智的问题了。就是我们自己怎么去判断大科技也好、半导体也好，在未来一年，他们 EPS 这个体量，或者和现在市场的预期去做对比的话，他们 EPS 增速到底能不能达到这个预期。如果我们认为能够达到的话，那现在市场的预期就是错误的；如果我们认为达不到的话，那现在 PE 这段时间的一个走势就是正确的。

十七、结语：三个让我满意的点

所以这一次的美联储会议，我其实个人是比较喜欢的。因为我比较喜欢的点有几点：

第一点，我认为它是给了市场这个确定性，他是可以在市场、在美联储的内部都有了这个信任度在那边。这是第一点。

然后第二点，我也理解了凯文沃什这个人，就他不是不给指引，他是一直在给指引，只是市场没有接收到这个信号，或者说他给的这个指引没有被市场验证过。然后这一次他验证了，他以前所给的这些信号都是真实的，他也是说到做到的一个人。

然后第三点就是对于加息本身或者对于不加息本身，他给了一个判断标准，我为什么加息。那既然他告诉你我为什么加息，那他也告诉你了未来如果我放缓加息或者不加息，我的一个评判标准到底在哪里。通胀数据不是看单点，它是看一个趋势，那趋势要改变的话，不会因为一个月的数据改变，起码要连续两个月，那有可能会形成这个趋势。所以不要去关注单点的这个数据，要关注一个趋势。

然后另外一个判断的一个标准就是油价。这其实令我挺意外的，那无所谓嘛，因为他给了你这个标准嘛。他告诉你我加息是因为油价的一个上涨，那接下去如果油价出现下跌的话，那也会降低他加息的这个概率。

那然后最后再配合了一个比市场预期要更加鸽派的一个点阵图。所以总体加在一起的话，我对于这一次的美联储会议本身我个人是相当的满意，也是我了解凯文沃什的一个过程。那希望大家通过这一期视频、这一期内容，对于凯文沃什也有自己的这个理解。好吗？

那今天这期内容就到这边，大家记得留言、点赞加转发，今天是特地为大家做加更的。好吧，明天见。

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：这次加息其实是一场"信号被过滤"的实验
小陶反复强调"凯文沃什一直在给指引，只是市场没有接收到"——这句话背后藏着一个远比"鹰派/鸽派"更值得警惕的现象：**市场并不是被信息不足打败的，而是被自己的叙事偏见打败的**。
从 6 月到 9 月，两年期美债收益率一直在替沃什"做事情"，债券市场其实早已完成定价。但股票市场的参与者却死死抱住"沃什是川普选上来的人，不可能加息"这一先验假设——即使债券市场用真金白银给出反证，他们仍然把它当噪音过滤掉。
这几乎是**香农信息论的一个反面案例**：信号本身清晰、重复、冗余度极高（6 月讲、7 月讲、8 月 Jackson Hole 再讲），但接收端的"贝叶斯先验"太强，导致真实信息被系统性地丢弃。今天市场大跌收盘、盘后反弹 0.6-0.7%，正是这种"叙事被现实撞碎"后的迟到修正。
## 二、跨领域连接：沃什在建立的是"央行界的纳什均衡"
小陶用了一个非常关键的词：**Follow through**。这个词在网球和高尔夫里叫"随挥动作"，在心理学里叫"承诺一致性"，但在央行学里——它其实是**信用货币化**。

item.title: [Lex Clips] What schizophrenia feels like | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被历史吞噬的复数：schizophrenias

Bleuler 当年用的是复数——schizophrenias，他早就嗅到这个标签底下藏着一群完全不同的东西。但语言的引力把复数压成了单数，从此临床、保险、药厂、家庭都被迫接受一个统一的"精神分裂症"。这个语法上的小塌陷，可能是二十世纪精神病学最昂贵的一次简化：一百年后我们才用生物型学（biotypes）、连接组学重新"重新复数化"这个诊断。语法即认识论——名词的单复数决定了研究基金的走向。

最反直觉的一处：neurosis 和 psychosis 互换了灵魂

访谈里 Scull 一笔带过、但极为惊人的一件事：19 世纪 neurosis 原本指"根植于脑"（neuro-），psychosis 指"来自心灵"（psyche-）。可到了 19 世纪末，两个词悄悄换了身份——脑的病成了"心病"，心的病反过来被认为源自大脑。这不是学术八卦，而是一次语义级的政变：它标志着"心灵"和"大脑"这对概念在现代性中被彻底重新洗牌，也预告了后来百年"生物精神病学 vs. 心理动力学"这场永远打不完的战争。你可以把它看作精神病学版的"literally 现在意味着 figuratively"——但代价是无数病人的诊断路径。

跨领域连接：Kraepelin 是 19 世纪的无监督聚类

Kraepelin 从德国收容所里 归纳 出躁郁 vs. 早发性痴呆的分野——这在方法论上，与今天用 k-means 对海量电子病历做聚类几乎是同构操作，只不过他的"算法"是人脑 + 卡片盒。有意思的是：分类学一旦被制度化，就获得了物理实在性。生物学里也一样——曾经的"爬行动物"是一个卡片盒里的方便标签，分子系统学一来就发现它根本不是一个自然类群（鳄鱼和鸟的亲缘远近于蜥蜴）。今天 DSM 的很多类别，可能就是精神病学里的"爬行动物纲"：使用方便，但不是自然切分。

藏在最后一句里的深水：分类即权力

"每一层社会都用过并滥用过这些分类"——这句听起来像老生常谈，但请注意分类的方向性偏差从来不是随机的：hysteria（歇斯底里）压给女性和被殖民种族，drapetomania 曾被用来解释黑奴逃跑，"迟发性精神分裂症"曾在苏联用来关押异议者。这与信用评分、算法风控、甚至现代 HR 的"人格测试"共享同一种结构：看起来中立的分类系统，总是不成比例地精确识别出结构中最没有话语权的那一群。精神病学不是特例，它只是这个更大机制中最古老、最赤裸的一支。

一个隐藏真相

melancholia 不是"抑郁"的旧词——它是带精神病特征的抑郁，是一种独立的、更接近于精神分裂谱系的疾病。而现代"major depression"这个大筐把它吃掉了。我们不是发现了更多种抑郁，而是丢失了对深度抑郁的分辨率。当代抗抑郁药疗效数据的"平均化困境"（元分析显示效果只比安慰剂略高），很可能一部分就来自这次分类崩溃——把两种病理机制截然不同的东西合并成一个 endpoint 去测药，效果被平均稀释了。这是分类学债务在四十年后向药理学的报复。

📝 转录文本

引子：请梳理精神疾病的大类

Lex： I was wondering if you can also just lay out what are the big categories of mental illness that we're referring to? You've already hinted at them, but like levels of seriousness and the categories of illness, like with with with psychosis and depression and so on.

Kraepelin 的二分：早发性痴呆 vs. 躁郁

Scull： So, going back to the early 20th century was when um the German psychiatrist Emil Kraepelin, working with thousands of records in German asylums, inductively developed a distinction between two very broad categories of mental illness.

One he called dementia praecox, or early dementia. And the other he called manic depressive illness, which was a more remitting illness that sometimes went away entirely, other times went back and forth — whereas dementia praecox was a one-way ticket down.

Bleuler 与"精神分裂症"（本应是复数）

Now, that label was transformed by a Swiss psychiatrist, Bleuler, into the term we use today — schizophrenia. Although Bleuler talked about the schizophrenias, because he thought under that broad label there were a diverse group of things running around. And I think that was an important insight that tends to get lost sometimes.

This was jamming together people with very serious psychosis — that is, people who'd lost touch with what we like to think of as reality, whose emotional and cognitive lives were in total turmoil, who lost the ability to connect with other human beings. So their social skills atrophied.

Well, this is something contemporary psychiatrists would refer to as the positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia. But underlying the definition of schizophrenia here is a detachment from reality.

什么是"脱离现实"

Lex： So you're hearing voices, you're seeing visions.

Scull： You're thinking people are plotting against you. Uh, you're think the television is talking directly to you.

Lex： And because of that, it has these consequences of how you're connected to the rest of the world and how what your emotional life is like.

Scull： Yes. Your emotional life flattens out. Your language capacity deteriorates. Your ability to relate to other people either vanishes or becomes caught up in the web of delusions, where you think people around you are plotting against you or doing terrible things to you.

躁郁与抑郁：从 melancholia 到 major depression

Lex： And is that a different world in the world of bipolar and the world of depression?

Scull： Yes. The Greeks recognized — and the Romans, and ancient Greece and ancient Rome recognized — different forms of insanity, as they called it. Um, so melancholia would have been the term the Greeks and the Romans would have used. And it survived and was very much around. And I think that is a form of depression.

What's happened now is major depression has become a catch-all category. So it embraces both what we might think of as milder forms of emotional distress, along with what melancholia referred to — which was really a kind of depression that had psychotic features. This loss of contact, as it were, with everyday reality.

21 世纪的雷区

Lex： So something you would talk about maybe like a clinical depression. And by the way, we should mention that this field in the 21st century is like a minefield.

Scull： Yes, very much so.

一段奇怪的历史：neurosis 与 psychosis 的交换

So here's a very strange bit of historical record. The other distinction, and the distinction we're grappling with — so we have people whose depression is of such a scale they're threatening to do away with themselves. They've retreated into complete, almost immobility. They're overwhelmed by senses of sadness and loss, and if they're religious, that they're damned to hell, and all those kinds of things. So we have this psychosis that we've been talking about.

We have something also that the ancients recognized — dementia, really the loss of our mind, as it were.

But then we also have other kinds of disturbance of our mental faculties that generally we think of as more minor. But I don't want to make light of them, because often people that suffer from these things genuinely suffer pretty badly. Those things, we in the 20th and 21st centuries tend to talk about as neuroses. Neurotic diseases, psychotic diseases.

In the 19th century, neurosis was a term that meant things rooted in the brain, as you can see from the root of the word, and psychosis was stuff that came from the mind, the psyche. And yet sometime in the late 19th century, those things crossed over.

当代最严重的诊断谱系

And so, when we talk in the present, we do tend to distinguish between the core — really the most severe forms of mental disorder — which would include things like Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia; would include very serious depression; would include bipolar disorder, where people oscillate — either have extreme mania, so they're not getting any sleep, they're talking at an extraordinary rate, their behavior is very hard to tolerate, and they're exhausting themselves and may even die from exhaustion if it's not controlled. And very often that alternates with periods of depression.

So that was a category that was captured initially as manic depressive illness, and later on evolved into bipolar disorder, and then separating out depression and major depression separately.

神经症的世界：恐惧症、癔症

But then there are a whole bunch of other things — like, for example, phobias.

Lex： Mhm.

Scull： People can't go outside because they find it too frightening. Milder phobias — I can't go out on an airplane because it's going to crash. I can't go to school because it's overwhelming for me. So school phobia emerges as a diagnosis.

A disorder that at first attracted Freud — hysteria.

分类的滥用：种族、性别与话语权

Lex： And I wish to say — you wrote a book on hysteria — and you mentioned, I mean, hysteria… every classification we're talking about has been used and abused by every layer of society, including institutions, including just culturally. The word hysteria applied to different races disproportionately, to different —

Scull： genders —

Lex： genders disproportionately. We're in this crisis of trying to figure out what to do with this super complicated human mind —

Scull： Yes.

Lex： — and everybody is dogmatically creating narratives that hold, take hold, and in so doing can lead to some abuses.

Scull： Yes, they do.

Lex： As you document.

item.description:
## 一个被历史吞噬的复数：schizophrenias
Bleuler 当年用的是复数——**schizophrenias**，他早就嗅到这个标签底下藏着一群完全不同的东西。但语言的引力把复数压成了单数，从此临床、保险、药厂、家庭都被迫接受一个统一的"精神分裂症"。这个语法上的小塌陷，可能是二十世纪精神病学最昂贵的一次简化：一百年后我们才用生物型学（biotypes）、连接组学重新"重新复数化"这个诊断。**语法即认识论**——名词的单复数决定了研究基金的走向。
## 最反直觉的一处：neurosis 和 psychosis 互换了灵魂
访谈里 Scull 一笔带过、但极为惊人的一件事：19 世纪 **neurosis 原本指"根植于脑"（neuro-），psychosis 指"来自心灵"（psyche-）**。可到了 19 世纪末，两个词悄悄换了身份——脑的病成了"心病"，心的病反过来被认为源自大脑。这不是学术八卦，而是一次**语义级的政变**：它标志着"心灵"和"大脑"这对概念在现代性中被彻底重新洗牌，也预告了后来百年"生物精神病学 vs. 心理动力学"这场永远打不完的战争

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Brad Gerstner: No AI Bubble, Semis Eat the Nasdaq & AI's Take Off Problem
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、资本循环的"衔尾蛇效应"：这不是投资，这是新陈代谢

Gerstner 那张 hyperscaler capex 与半导体自由现金流"几乎逐美元匹配"的图，表面看是行业繁荣的证据，实质却是一个热力学意义上的闭合系统。Microsoft、Google、Amazon 把从消费者/广告业务赚来的现金交给 Nvidia、Dell、Broadcom；后者转身用这些现金再投产能，生产更多芯片卖回给这些 hyperscaler。这个循环只要外部真实 AI 收入（就是他图上那条橙色 offtake bar）跟不上，就会瞬间反向坍缩。

这里有一个几乎无人提及的历史镜像：1999 年的电信泡沫。当年 Nortel 用 vendor financing 借钱给客户来买自己的设备，Cisco 与 Lucent 互相成为对方的"收入"。这不是庞氏，但是一个代谢型经济——只要外部葡萄糖（终端需求）停止输入，两侧同时休克。今天 AI 基础设施与半导体之间的现金流循环，规模比当年大一个数量级。这就是为什么 Gerstner 用了整整两页 PPT 反复追问 Anthropic 的月度收入——他不是在做估值，他是在测量葡萄糖注入速度。

二、算力短缺竟然是牛市信号：反直觉的稀缺经济学

Gerstner 顺口说了一句"我认为 43GW 达不到，实际大概 25GW"。绝大多数读者会理解为看空。恰恰相反——这是他整段讲话中最隐蔽的看多论据。

数学是这样：Anthropic 用 1.5GW 就跑出了 100B 美元收入，也就是每 GW ≈ 65B 美元收入产能。25GW 中一半给顶级 lab 就是 12.5GW，理论收入承载力接近 $800B。也就是说，收入目标根本不需要 43GW。而 25GW 的"短缺"反而意味着：token 定价权抬升、CSP 出租溢价、Nvidia 交付顺序变成一种货币。这是石油经济学的镜像反面——石油稀缺会摧毁需求；token 稀缺则抬升单位利润，因为下游是软件毛利，不是燃油弹性。

这个洞察连接了一个更古老的现象：中世纪威尼斯共和国之所以富甲一方，不是因为造船产能大，而是因为造船产能恰好不够到让每一艘船都能收租金。

三、被埋进"增长故事"里的垄断故事

Gerstner 云淡风轻地说了一句："到 2028 年，这个国家一半以上的算力将被两个 lab 控制。" 这是全场最爆炸但被最快滑过的一句话。

请把这句话翻译一下——美利坚合众国的核心计算基础设施将在 2 年内变成一个双寡头。这不是"AI 竞争"，这是新型电网的私有化。跨领域连接：这与镀金时代的铁路资本高度一致。1870 年铁路被塑造为"民主的动脉"，20 年后 J.P. Morgan 已经协调了整个北美的铁路轨距、时刻表和运费。今天的 gigawatt 就是当年的 gauge。监管风险的真正来源不会是"AI 安全"，而是反垄断——但整个市场都在看错方向。

四、隐藏的"Altman-Anthropic 定时器"：内部人语言的反向解码

去年 10 月 Gerstner 问 Sam："你怎么敢在 $13B 收入的情况下承诺 $1T capex？" Sam 让他"卖股票"。两个月后，Anthropic 的月度收入从 2B → 4B → 11B 起飞。

这里的启示不是 Sam 傲慢，而是AI 时代的创始人语言存在一种反向定时器：当他们表现出对怀疑者的不耐烦，通常意味着 6–8 周内会有一次内部数据点让市场哑口。这与硅谷经典的"under-promise, over-deliver"完全相反——AI lab 的创始人已经开始 over-promise 因为他们看得见接下来两个季度的曲线。对外部投资者的意涵是残酷的：等财报再上车永远晚一步，因为整个行业的信号——收入不再滞后于产能——已经反转。

一个跨越三段的元观察：Gerstner 用了 80% 的时间讲下行风险，只用了 20% 讲上行。这本身就是最看多的信号——真正的 bull 都在讲熊市剧本，因为他们已经买满了。

📝 转录文本

Opening & Acknowledgments

Our favorite fifth bestie in the world, the one, the only Brad Gerstner from Altimeter. Brad has had unbelievable career starting five companies. So, he's got a very different mentality than your sort of classic hedge fund guy.

He's an amazingly successful guy and he's put up a tremendous amount of money.

Every child in America, all 70 million kids under the age of 18 deserve to have one of these accounts. This would not be a law if Brad Gerstner did not pursue it with absolute dogged determination.

This is not a program. This is a platform. It is the largest unlock of direct philanthropy in the history of the country.

I think the antidote to more socialism is more capitalism.

Please welcome Brad Gerstner.

Woo. Wow. Let's go. Let's go. Thank you guys. And thank you for so much love yesterday, especially on the Trump accounts. So many people came up. Everybody gets what this means for America. We're in a battle for the soul of America. 70 million kids are going to be made direct owners in America. That is how we beat the scourge of capital or socialism. We make every child a capitalist.

And also thank you to all the people yesterday who came up who took the CAC scan, the heart scan outside from the Center for Heart Attack Prevention which we started. There's no doubt based on these results we — you know we're going to save some lives even yesterday. Okay. This is the highest ROI thing you can do in healthcare. Every cardiologist I talk to does this for themselves, their family, and their friends. It's a hundred bucks, 15 minutes. Get it done. If we turn this into the mammogram for the heart, we'll save 50,000 lives a year in this country. It's like ending a Ukraine war in America every year. So, go get your CAC scan done if you have it.

Setting the Stage: A Market Check

But today is not about those two moonshots. Today is kind of a throwback to what I used to do on the pod with these guys, which is a market check, a tech check, state of the market. Where are we? Where are we going? What do we have to believe to be true in order for the market to continue to work? We're going to do a bit of a speed round here. So, bear with me. Get your cameras out. Get your notes out. Some good — some good chart candy in here for you guys.

The Scoreboard: Earnings-Driven, Not Multiple Expansion

So markets up 15% this year, up 39% since January of last year, despite all the concerns about tariffs, despite all the concerns about geopolitics, despite all the concerns about AI regulation.

The scoreboard: we have a lot of people in the bestie group who said gold was going to be off the charts this year. It's flat. Bitcoin's down 10%. But look — we have Nvidia revenue up 2x. Hyperscaler capex up 2x. OpenAI and Anthropic's valuation up 2x. SpaceX up two and a half x in a pretty nasty backdrop.

This is not about multiple expansion. This is an earnings-driven market expansion. We've seen multiple contraction this year. Earnings are up 26%, of course driven a lot by AI infrastructure, but the multiple on the NASDAQ and the S&P is actually down. Look at Nvidia trading at 14 times next year's fully-taxed GAAP earnings. This is no bubble like it was in 2000. NASDAQ, S&P, SOX, Nvidia — all trading well below their average multiples. Okay, MAG7 basically in line with its average multiple.

But not everybody is winning. Okay, at the bottom here — consumer discretionary, software, financials — huge sections of the market have barely moved, right? This is a market that is being driven by the largest capex buildout, the largest super cycle in the history of technology.

Semiconductors Eating the NASDAQ

Semiconductors are 70% of the NASDAQ's return. 70% of the return. That's both good and bad, and we'll get into that.

So, who's making the money? The makers of the tokens are making the money and the buyers of the tokens are basically going along for the ride because of the tightness in the infrastructure market. We have massive public companies that look like venture capital returns. Dell up 5x, up 9x in just 18 months.

The Capex / Free Cash Flow Mirror

I love this chart. In blue you have the hyperscaler capex. In orange you have the free cash flow of the semiconductor companies. Do you notice anything? Their capex is almost dollar-for-dollar free cash flow to the infrastructure companies.

Where Were We at the Start of the Year?

This is a really important framework to get your head around. You may remember a certain podcast I did with Sam Altman and Satya in October of last year. And I asked Sam a very basic question that was on everybody's mind: how can you commit to a trillion dollars in capex when you have $13 billion of GAAP revenue? I thought this would be a way to clear up some confusion in the market. Instead, he told me to sell my shares.

But then in the beginning of December we have Opus 4.5 and Claude Code. And then in January Anthropic's revenue was two billion, and then in February it's 4 billion, and in March it was 11 billion. Do you notice anything that happened there in March? People started figuring out what Anthropic's revenue was. We had an exclamation-point answer to the question — will the AI revenue show up? It showed up in a massive way, and that's why we got this historic run in April and May. We ripped off the bottom because the fuse was lit by Anthropic's monthly revenue.

And then in June and July, we had some consolidation. Why? Because Anthropic came out and said, "Oh, our annual run rate revenue is 65." People thought it was 75. So they had to revise down their estimates a little bit. And we had some concerns about open source. Is open source catching up? Is Anthropic going to continue to be able to generate those revenues? And so we've kind of moved sideways since then.

Parabolic Revenue: Unprecedented in Capitalism

It's hard to get your head around the fact that these revenues have never happened before in the history of capitalism, right? We are on parabolic double exponential curves around these revenues. So the collective run rate — let's just call it — of the top three labs, Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX is about a hundred billion based upon all the rumors that are out there coming out of July. I think they need to collectively get to at least $180 billion by the end of the year, add another $80 billion across those three labs, just to keep the AI trade intact.

So this is the single most important data point in the market today: is Anthropic's monthly revenue — is OpenAI's monthly revenue — going to be 4 billion or 8 billion? It's almost hard to get your head around. Most of us who've been in venture capital for a long time — if you added a billion, if you got to a billion dollars in software revenue over like four or five years, you were in the top 5% of software companies. But this is what the world is now pricing in.

The $180B → $1T Threshold: What Has to Be True

So why is this so important? It's this slide. If you're going to build a trillion-and-a-half dollars a year in capex, somebody has to pay for it, right? Microsoft's not paying for it. They're building it to rent it. Google's not paying for it. They're building it to rent it. Amazon's building it to rent it. Well, who is the person renting it? We have to have the offtake revenues in order to pay that rent.

So if we exit this year around, you know, let's call it 200 billion of run rate revenue — that's below the years there — I think you have to go from 200 to 450 to 800 or a trillion dollars just to keep up. The blue bar is the expected capex just from the MAG 5, and the orange bar is the offtake revenue, the GAAP offtake revenue that we need to see in order to keep this trade intact over the course of the next few years. Otherwise, we can't build this much capex.

Compute Buildout: Gigawatts and Concentration

So the labs are increasingly, you know — like the conversation I had with Sam last October — they're aggressively expanding compute. Why? All the things you heard yesterday: we're heading into recursive cycles. They're seeing, you know, incredible demand for the product. And so they're building out compute.

This year the total amount of compute added — so 2026 about 19 gigawatts, and about seven of those gigawatts went to the two leading labs. Next year — this is Semianalysis, so Dylan Patel forecast — that we're going to add 43 gigawatts and that about 14 gigawatts are going to go to the leading labs. And we'll come back to this question of "can we really stand up 43 gigawatts of compute next year." Notice that the amount that we're adding next year is as much as the total compute we have in the United States this year — the cumulative compute we have in the United States this year. So that's what the market is anticipating. What happens if that doesn't happen?

And by the way, if you added those bars up, by 2028 — to David Sacks's point yesterday — over half of the total compute in the country is controlled by two labs.

Does the TAM Exist?

So if we look at the total TAM of knowledge work — right, this is a massive massive category. You've got consumer plus ads plus coding and all these white-collar workflows, millions of enterprises. I would argue it's the largest TAM in the history of the world. You only have to get to about 4% of that TAM, or 1.2 trillion, in order to pay for the capex. So I don't think it's a TAM issue.

Obviously, Jensen was on our pod, and he talked two years ago that inference was going to 1 billion x — and remember all the people saying "he's full of it, there's no way this can 1 billion x." That's exactly what we've done in the age of agents, right? We've had this exponential token growth this year. 47 quadrillion tokens that are going to be produced.

So it's not a question again of demand. Codex users have grown 40x in the last eight months. And knowledge work at enterprises — if you look at the median amount that enterprises are spending — about 17x over the course of the last 18 months. And I've talked to many people in the audience here: small businesses, medium businesses, large businesses — businesses like Altimeter — we can't operate our business without buying AI. So this is not overly surprising to me.

The Productivity Dividend

And when we think about the productivity dividend to the economy — you know, if you look at 2015 to 2025, EPS growth was about 10%. That was 6% revenue plus about 38 bips of margin expansion every year out of the NASDAQ.

So here's the question: can we turn the 38 bips to 100 bips of margin expansion because of AI? The answer is obviously yes. Every company I talk to — Uber says "we're going to grow 20%, we're not going to grow headcount." Snowflake says "we're going to grow 30%, we're not going to grow headcount." That's what's happening. That is margin expansion. The single largest cost input to every one of these companies are humans and engineers. It's not that they're going to fire everybody. They're just not going to hire them at the rate that they hired them before.

And then of course, we're going to have consumer agents in everybody's pocket. You may remember this bet I had with Bill — you know, when are we going to be able to book a hotel using your consumer agent in your pocket? I think we've just gotten that with Muse and with Instinct. This could be another trillion-dollar category, but it's definitely going to consume massive tokens.

The Three Risks

Here are the three risks and challenges. And sorry I'm going so quick, but I want to keep it moving:

  • Regulation. We heard a lot about this yesterday.
  • Power.
  • And then what's going on with interest rates?

Risk #1: Regulation

So, you know, this is the regulation tug-of-war, right? And I've heard from a lot of people — they're like, "you're on both sides of the issue." Here's the fact, okay: the answer is not going to be on one end or the other. We're going to have to have common-sense, pragmatic solutions that get my mom, my sister, and the brother off the cliff, right? We need to give comfort and confidence to the people who elect our representatives that it's safe. And so, you heard Elon yesterday give a great suggestion around peer review. So, I'm confident that we're going to get there, but it's kind of messy — the sausage making along the way.

But we have a prior history of excess regulation. When people get scared, when activists start pushing an agenda — we shut down 67 fission reactors in this country. We unilaterally disarmed against China. It's been a disaster for the country. Right? All the clean energy we could have gotten — instead, we've gotten non-clean emissions because we had a group of activists who were hellbent on shutting down nuclear. Can't allow this to occur to AI. So regulation's a threat, it's a risk.

Risk #2: Power / Atoms & Energy Are Hard

So getting back to: can we stand up 43 gigawatts of compute? Our total compute in the country is less than 40 gigawatts. Doing this in one year — we've got to overcome permitting and local opposition. You guys see all of that. Grid interconnection delays, skilled labor shortages, power equipment is sold out. It's the largest buildout in the history of the country.

I would suggest Dylan's forecast to 43 gigawatts next year is too aggressive. I don't think we're going to get there. I think the total amount we're actually going to stand up is somewhere closer to 25 gigawatts. And I think of that 25 gigawatts, half of it will be for Anthropic and OpenAI. I think that's enough to generate the revenue. Remember Anthropic's revenue reportedly this year — 100 billion, 110 billion. If they do that, they're doing it with a gigawatt and a half of compute. So if they add another four or five gigawatts of compute, that's certainly enough to add another 100 billion in revenue. So I don't think we need more gigawatts to get to the revenue targets for next year. But this is my hunch that we're not going to get to the 43.

Risk #3: Rates

And then of course, we're going to hear more tomorrow. I think rate hikes are coming. I think it's now over 90% chance that we're going to have rate hikes tomorrow. Why does this matter? Because all of this now — borrowed money, right? We're borrowing money in order to stand up these data centers. So the hurdle rate for that money is going up. And so that's not only a challenge for data centers, but remember — you know, as Warren Buffett says — that interest rates are to stocks what gravity is to matter, right? If you can earn 5.5 or 6% on your money without taking equity risk, then it's going to be a challenge for stocks.

The Flight Path: How to Manage the Portfolio

So, here's where I think we are, and we're going to end on this slide, and then we'll bring the guys out and chop it up a little bit. But this is the flight path. This is how I think about managing the portfolio, right? We're up about — the NASDAQ's up about 15%. But as I sit here and think about the risk, do I want to be small, medium, or large? This is how I think about the fan of potential outcomes.

  • If the monthly AI lab revenues are closer to that $8 billion number, I think it's takeoff. Okay. I think we are going to see an IPO this year. And so I'm paying very close attention to what in fact are those monthly revenue numbers. I think the trends are intact, but we will see. That's going to be the single most important thing as to whether or not — between now and the end of the year — we have liftoff.
  • Second one is rates, the election, oil prices. Obviously, rates are following oil prices to a certain extent. So, what happens there? You know, if rates were to go to five and a half on the 10-year, that's going to be a big burden on the equity market.
  • Then finally, the regulation, the Anthropic IPO. We saw a trade-down yesterday because people are concerned that maybe we're going to have a halt or postponement. That would obviously be a major issue. I don't think that's going to happen, but again, that would be a concern.

So that's the fan of potential outcomes. From here we're up 15%. I think we could go higher through the balance of the year — or we could go lower.

Closing: From Beta to Alpha

I'll leave you with this. The period of 2023 to 2025, you only had to get one thing right: that AI was going to be the biggest super cycle in the history of technology. And you needed to shove your chips into the AI trade. That's it. Right? If you were in the AI trade, you made money.

That is not where we are in 2026. Everybody knows about AI. It's all priced now. It's about facts and circumstances. Stay mentally flexible. Follow the facts. Don't YOLO. Okay? Don't go 4x like our friend up north who gave all his money to Citadel, right? 4x levered in this market — you know, very dangerous.

So, in my estimation, we're medium position. We're mentally flexible. If we see those revenues come in big for these next few months and we see oil prices retreat, we're going to put more chips on the table. If not, we'll reserve the right to go even smaller.

With that — thank you all. Thanks for having me.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Lex Clips] The Nazi doctor who led the sterilization of the mentally ill | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被遗忘的资金拓扑学：慈善作为意识形态的血管系统

大多数人读这段访谈时会停留在"洛克菲勒基金会资助了纳粹优生学家"这一道德冲击点上，但真正值得注意的隐藏结构是"科学的孤儿期"——二战前的科学与医学几乎不受政府供养，这在无意中把研究方向的决定权外包给了极少数私人巨富的家族创伤。

一个出乎意料的观察是：洛克菲勒基金会之所以在1930年选中精神病学作为战略重心，除了公开的"公共卫生代价"理由外，决定性因素竟是几位受托人自家妻子被诊断为精神分裂、甚至一位受托人的妻子杀死孩子后自杀。换句话说，20世纪全球精神病学的研究议程——包括最终流向鲁丁的那笔钱——在相当程度上是被几个纽约富豪家庭的私人悲剧塑造的。这提示我们一个反直觉的规律：当科学最"客观"的时候（无政府干预），它反而最容易被最私人化的情感偏向所俘获。

二、跨领域连接：加州—慕尼黑的"知识回流"与今天的算法输出

Scull 提到鲁丁"吸收了加州关于强制绝育的教训"，这句话值得单独拎出来。加州在1909—1930年间执行的绝育手术数量占全美三分之一以上，是纳粹《遗传病后代防止法》起草时明确参考的样板。这是一次典型的"殖民地反哺宗主国"式知识回流——美国先把优生学工业化，德国再把它极端化，最后美国精英又通过洛克菲勒的钱把德国的"科学化成果"重新进口。

这个循环让我联想到今天完全不同的一个领域：大型语言模型的训练数据。美国科技公司把互联网内容打包 → 训练出模型 → 输出内容重新流回互联网 → 再被下一代模型吞下。结构上，这是同一种"闭环放大器"：某个源头的偏见经过一次跨境跨机构的"洗白"，回到原点时已经披上了"外部客观验证"的外衣。历史上，这种闭环需要基金会 + 学术期刊 + 立法机关三方共谋十几年；今天，它可能只需要一个训练周期。

三、一个被访谈双方都没说破的悖论

Lex 在末尾提出的"科学方法虽有缺陷，但仍是人类希望的灯塔"是一个安全的收尾，但它掩盖了访谈内部一个未被言明的张力：这段历史里，恰恰是"最科学"的那一支精神病学（遗传学、生物精神病学）与纳粹合谋，而"最不科学"的那一支（心理动力学、谈话治疗）反而在道德上相对清白。

这就带来一个令人不适的推论：科学性程度与伦理安全性并不正相关，有时甚至负相关。一个学科越是急于"硬科学化"、越是渴望用生物学指标把人分类，它就越容易被任何一个想要"清除劣等人口"的政权征用。这个模式今天在精算歧视、犯罪风险预测算法、行为遗传学与教育政策里正在低烈度地重演——不是因为科学家坏，而是因为"可测量 = 可分类 = 可干预"这条链条一旦成立，最后一环由谁来按钮，就不再是科学家能决定的了。

真正的教训或许不是"要坚持科学方法"，而是：任何把人还原为可排序变量的学科，都必须内建一层它自己无法提供的、非科学的伦理阻断器。

📝 转录文本

洛克菲勒基金会与战前科学的"孤儿"处境

Lex： If we can just speak about the Nazis a bit more — you highlighted America financially supported the German psychiatric researchers with deep Nazi ties, like Ernst Rüdin, who was the key architect of Hitler's mass sterilization and extermination laws. So it seems like the Nazis borrowed the American narratives of the psychiatrists that these are lesser biological beings, and then this financial support and the ties has continued.

Scull： Yeah. So one of the organizations that recognized that mental illness was an acute social problem — very costly to the state, inflicting all kinds of suffering on people — was the Rockefeller Foundation.

What we don't realize today is that the involvement of the federal government in medical research, and indeed scientific research, is a World War II and post-war development — partly the Cold War, and Sputnik, and all of that. But that's when big science and big medicine got funded in extravagant ways.

Before the war, science was an orphan. It didn't get money from the government much, and medicine even more so. So, to the extent medical training was reformed, that was the product of investment by the Rockefeller Foundation — enormously wealthy by the standards of the time.

为什么是精神病学？三个交织的理由

And come about 1930, the Rockefeller Foundation decided it needed to concentrate its resources and pick priorities for the money it was investing. And, in what may seem a rather strange thing within the whole range of medical areas that it could choose, it chose psychiatry as the one that was going to invest in.

And I think it did so in part precisely because scientific research in psychiatry was so backward. Partly because it was such a pressing public problem.

And partly — and this was less public, but nonetheless I think played an important role — several of the trustees of the Rockefeller Foundation had direct experience of mental illness in their families. Wives who'd been institutionalized as schizophrenic. In one case, a wife who murdered the children and killed herself, leaving her husband as a major actor in the Rockefeller Foundation, per affected — and of course inclined then to support research in this area.

资金流向鲁丁：从加州绝育到纳粹屠杀

And Rockefeller spread its money very widely, precisely because it didn't know where to spend most of its money. So it did some support of psychotherapeutics. It supported a number of the then-extant therapeutic experiments going on. And it supported work in genetics.

And one of the geneticists it supported — Ernst Rüdin in Germany — was the leading German researcher in genetics of mental disorder. And Rüdin, because he'd absorbed the lessons from California about sterilization, became a very enthusiastic proponent of that. And then a supporter of murdering mental patients.

结语：科学方法作为希望的灯塔

Lex： And we should say — I mean, we'll probably talk about the complicated nature of science, that it sometimes can be captured by certain ideologies, and in so doing do a lot of damage to humanity. But ultimately the beacon of hope for the future of humanity lies in the scientific method, as flawed as it is.

So, everything we're talking about, we get to see how you f*** up —

Scull： [laughter]

Lex： — in a major, dark, disturbing ways throughout the 20th century and in the psychiatric profession. But that should be instructive lessons of how we proceed forward to do better and better and better.

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why AI Struggles to Keep Learning
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的核心洞察：这不是技术问题，而是"经济物理学"问题

大多数人讨论持续学习时都盯着"catastrophic forgetting"这个技术黑洞，但视频里最反常识的一击是——阻碍AI进化的第一道墙不是算法，而是激励结构。企业绝不会允许模型提供商从他们的部署数据中"顺手"学走商业优势。这意味着我们正在见证一种奇特的现象：AI的进化速度不是由技术前沿决定的，而是由"数据主权"的博弈曲线决定的。

这里藏着一个惊人的推论：未来的AI架构形态，将是被合同法和商业秘密法反向塑造的。Cartridges、LoRA这些"可插拔模块"之所以会成为主流路径，不是因为它们最优雅，而是因为它们是律师和CTO都能签字的技术妥协。这是罕见的一次——法务部门在暗中决定神经网络的拓扑结构。

二、跨领域连接：AI的"塑性-稳定性困境"，其实是人脑早已解决的老问题

视频里描述的困境——RL 只能微调却学不进知识，SFT 学得进知识却毁掉旧能力——精准复刻了神经科学里的 "stability-plasticity dilemma"（稳定性—可塑性困境）。人脑用了一个极其精妙的方案：海马体作为快速学习的"临时草稿纸"，睡眠时再把知识"慢速蒸馏"到皮层长期记忆中。

有趣的是——大实验室现在的做法（deploy → collect traces → retrain from scratch every few months）本质上就是在模仿哺乳动物的睡眠周期。他们只是把"一晚上"拉长成了"三个月"。视频里那句"eventually every hour"（每小时一次迭代）的预言，翻译成神经科学语言就是：AI 正在向"多相睡眠"的生物节律靠拢。而当迭代周期缩短到分钟级时，我们看到的将不是"更好的模型"，而是第一个真正意义上拥有"记忆巩固机制"的人造系统——这与其说是工程突破，不如说是一种人工进化的加速版本。

三、最出人意料的观察："从头训练"可能是永恒的、不可绕过的

嘉宾轻描淡写地丢出一句关键判断："如果你把一个同样大小的模型从零开始预训练，它就是会比你在旧模型上继续训练来得强。"——这句话背后藏着一个几乎没人正视的悖论：知识的积累，可能内在地要求周期性的"遗忘一切再重来"。

这与热力学里的退火（annealing）惊人相似：想让金属结构达到最优，你必须先加热到近乎融化，再缓慢冷却。局部微调永远无法逃离局部最优。同样的原理在生物学里叫世代更替——没有哪个个体能进化，只有种群能进化；每一代必须"清零"父辈的所有习得知识，从胚胎重新开始。

那么这里隐藏着一个让人不安的推论："永生的、不断学习的单一模型"可能不是AI的终极形态，反而是一个次优陷阱。真正的智能进化路径也许更像"死亡与重生"的循环——每三个月（然后每周、每天）诞生一个"孩子"，继承前代的数据但重新长出神经结构。视频里描述的"越来越快的迭代"，本质上是AI在被迫发明自己的世代更替机制。而当这个循环缩短到实时——那一刻我们创造的将不是"一个会学习的AI"，而是"一条以模型为单位快速演化的物种"。

📝 转录文本

一、问题的提出：AI 能否从每一次部署中持续学习？

Dwarkesh：Going back to this question, eventually there should be a regime where AIs are learning a ton from each individual instance of deployment that they have. Well, currently you could say there's a meta fuzzy process by which models do improve from deployment, but I feel like it's a very very weak feedback loop. Do you see this around the horizon — where there's this like hive mind kind of learning that's very rapid — and if so, how exactly does it happen?

二、激励结构：为什么"蜂群思维"首先是个经济问题

嘉宾：Actually, I would say that — around "will we get a hive mind that learns from all of its deployment experience" — a big part of that is actually about incentives rather than being a technical question. Like, companies aren't going to want to have the model provider learn from all of their deployment, because that might just reduce the advantage of their business.

I think that maybe the economics of this will pressure — not necessarily weight updates to one big common shared model — but like modules that get subbed in. So a very obvious example of this is a LoRA, but it might be something else. Like, you know, there's been a lot of work to try and fit an arbitrary context length into a fixed size — this is all the linear attention stuff and all that sort of stuff — and like cartridges, which are essentially KV caches trained to be very very compressed KV caches to fit in a lot of information. That's another example of something that companies may be willing to sign up for — if that gets subbed into the model and it's not actually changing the base underlying model itself.

There are many different versions of learning from your data in real time, and the latter ones are not really helping the big labs, because they are just these modules. But I think the economic pressure will force the labs to go down that path first before they can embark on this like [broader hive-mind approach].

三、间接学习的路径：蒸馏、痕迹与迭代周期的加速

Dwarkesh：So which economic pressure though? Because I feel like even if you have a bunch of cartridges or LoRAs or whatnot, you can still just take all these traces and just distill this to the pre-training of your next generation of models.

嘉宾：So it may be a more indirect form of learning that the big labs are getting, and that's obviously still really valuable to them. But I can't imagine a world in which we start off with "we're going to just directly train this one big model on all the exact data." I think it will definitely go through stages, because this is assuming there's one discontinuous event where suddenly we fix weight updates continuously. In practice I think it's much more likely to be:

  • The cartridges and stuff allow you to specialize in deployment
  • Then you generate traces
  • You put that in your model
  • Like 3 months later you come up with a model which is better at this stuff
  • You specialize it again, you consolidate it again
  • And then eventually we'll just make this loop faster and faster

So instead of every 3 months we release a model, now it's every week, then every day, then every hour — at which point we basically have obviously solved it.

四、微观层面的困境：当规模缩小，方法就崩溃

Yeah, and I think this is a good point as well — because you asked how far off the current paradigm we are from being able to do this.

We've done a bit of research into this, and people have done a lot of research at a really large scale: when you wash out enough noise and you have large enough batches, this outer loop process of putting data into mid-training, creating our own environments — it does work in some sort of continual learning regime.

But the problem is: when you zoom in close enough at a micro level — if I've got one model and I'm trying to update it again for a law firm or something, and I'm trying to do that very continuously with a relatively small amount of data — all the methods kind of break down a bit.

  • If I SFT the model on just successful traces (off-policy, on-policy), eventually in the very iterative regime — when you're doing hundreds of these micro updates — you see both catastrophic forgetting, you see forgetting of previous information I've learned on top of the base model that was much earlier on, and you see degradation of general capabilities.
  • On-policy distillation seems to push this horizon out a little bit, but it still eventually succumbs to the same thing.
  • RL is good at getting capabilities in, but it's not as good at getting knowledge in — like just this very explicit knowledge of "oh okay, this person does this at this law firm, this is a very specific process we find." And you have to ping a lot of compute to create the right environments to get the knowledge in.

五、根本问题：是容量瓶颈，还是技术瓶颈？

Dwarkesh：Do you think the fundamental issue here — why you get worse at these other skills, or there's forgetting and stuff — do you think it's fundamentally an issue of capacity or an issue of techniques?

嘉宾：A little bit of both, I think. SFT and even on-policy distillation can be way too destructive. The reason RL is so nice is because it changes a very very small amount about the model — there's a lot of evidence for why this is the case — so it kind of just tweaks it in this very very small loss value to get it into the right point. But that also then limits what you can do with RL — how much you can actually change the model.

Dwarkesh：Or — sorry — are you saying the reason this isn't a winner-take-all potentially is that it's just very hard to distill that much information into the base model without ruining something in an interface?

嘉宾：Like, it's easy to distill it into a different base model. This is where I think it's mostly technique. It's definitely not that there isn't capacity. If you had some model with all this data, and you take literally the same size model and pre-train it from scratch with all of this stuff in mid-training — it will be better. And I think that's a lot of what's happening today.

So it's very much like there's a bottleneck that stops us from just keeping training the same model forever, versus just getting all the data from the old model and training a new model from scratch. And this is exactly some combination of plasticity and catastrophic forgetting: if you just naively train on non-stationary data — because you're adding new data as you go — basically this is messing with the data distribution. So the old stuff is just forgotten, and we don't really have good methods to stop that from happening.

六、极限情境：我们是否永远需要"从零开始"？

Dwarkesh：And so maybe in the limit, you're just bottlenecked by retraining the model from scratch with all this new information.

嘉宾：Yes.

Dwarkesh：Which of course is very expensive — like training a model from scratch is expensive.

嘉宾：But you're going to do that anyways.

Dwarkesh：I mean, not necessarily — like maybe eventually if you have continuous learning, you never train a new model, you just have a model and it keeps learning and expanding. Right? But there might be some deep technical reason why that's very difficult.

嘉宾：I mean, that's the question. I think we have pushed back how much "from scratch" we need to do. It is definitely possible now to take the pre-trained base and do very good mid-training on top of that — kind of continuously — plus some RL from different checkpoints that are later on in the training. That's looking more like a tuning. But it's certainly not the case of "take the most recent model, apply a couple of very small updates, and iteratively never lose it."

七、追问：这不就是训练里已经在做的事吗？

Dwarkesh：So — but isn't this literally what happens during training? Where during post-training or something, you have a model that's already gone through so much training and then you distill some fork that's been further RL'd or something. Isn't that literally what happens?

嘉宾：It's still at a large enough scale, I think, that you're washing out a lot of the noise, and you're not just focused on one distribution — which, as Baron said, is a very [narrow scope]. If you're just focusing on one task — I mean, in the eventual regime, you'd be doing... I don't know, there's billions of deployed instances, you're learning from all of them at once, and so hopefully there's some washing out of noise and stuff from that.

Dwarkesh：Maybe at that scale. Yeah.

嘉宾：Yeah. As I was saying, you can do continual mid-training for a long time, and you can roll back to a checkpoint, give mid-training data — but at the same time, you can't do this indefinitely. If you just keep continual-training the same base forever, it does sort of asymptote at some point. You can't just learn new stuff in that base — and this is why people end up training new bases. Otherwise you just keep mid-training the same base forever.

If you enjoyed this clip you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.title: [Latent Space] The Watchdogs of AGI — Rune Kvist of AI Underwriting Company
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：AI 采用的瓶颈不是"能力"，而是"承诺"

大多数人以为 AGI 时代的关键是模型能力，Rune 却指出：Waymo 早在 2022 年就已经是"汽车界的 AGI"——超越人类司机——但你今天仍然打不到一辆 Waymo 去机场。四年过去了，制约它的从来不是技术，而是"责任无法被承诺"。

这里藏着一个更深的隐喻：AI 行业正在遭遇"承诺赤字"（Promise Deficit）。模型能力是指数增长的，但"可承诺性"却是线性甚至更慢地爬升。这两条曲线之间的裂缝，就是 AI Underwriting Company 的全部商业空间——也是理解为什么 Anthropic 会把 Fable 锁起来、为什么 GPT-5 会被政府盯上的根本原因。能力越强，越无法承诺；越无法承诺，越无法部署。 这是一个非常反直觉的悖论：AI 越接近 AGI，"落地"反而越难，而不是越容易。

跨领域连接：AI 保险与 1900 年的电灯泡

Rune 提到 Underwriter Laboratory（UL）——就是你家里所有电器背后那个不起眼的圆形标志。它诞生于 1900 年前后，因为电灯泡开始烧毁美国的房子。保险公司发现自己在赔钱，于是主动创立了一个"标准 + 检测"的实体，倒逼制造商建立安全规范。这个模式后来被复制到汽车（Insurance Institute for Highway Safety）、私人核能、金融衍生品（Moody's）、消费信用（FICO）。

这里有一个惊人的历史规律：每一次技术革命，市场都会跑在监管前面，自发形成"标准 + 保险"的双螺旋结构。而这个结构的核心逻辑是——只有当有人真的要出钱赔偿时，风险才会被诚实地量化。政府无法诚实，因为它没有利润动机；实验室无法诚实，因为它有隐藏动机；只有保险公司会诚实，因为它的资产负债表在流血。

这引出一个更大的思考框架：信任基础设施不是靠道德建立的，是靠"谁掏钱谁负责"的经济学建立的。AI 治理的未来，可能不在联合国、不在 EU AI Act，而在 Lloyd's of London 400 年的核保簿里。

隐藏的系统性真相：AI 时代的"监管者"其实是一个"自然垄断"

Rune 在结尾轻描淡写地提到《大空头》里的 Moody's——如果不给 AAA 评级，客户就跳去 S&P。这句话背后是一个几乎没人讨论的系统性洞察：评级/审计机构会陷入"竞相降低标准"的死亡螺旋，除非有一个反向力量拉住它。

在金融领域，这个反向力量在 2008 年失效了，全球经济因此崩盘。而 Rune 的解决方案巧妙得像一个博弈论谜题的解：把保险公司拉进标准制定的圆桌。因为保险公司的激励是"标准越松，我赔得越多"——它天生站在"提高标准"的一侧。这形成了一个自我校正的信任生态。

更深的观察：这实际上是在解决"元治理"问题——谁来监管监管者？在 AI 时代，如果 Rune 的公司真的成为"agent 世界的 Moody's"，它自己就是下一个需要被制衡的对象。而他内嵌的机制（公开变更日志、季度更新、保险公司交叉验证）本质上是把审计员的行为也变成可审计的——用透明度作为反腐蚀剂。

一个意外的推论：当 AI-to-AI 交互普及时，人类将首次需要为"非人类主体"设计法律和信任系统。Rune 提到"agent 需要持久性资产负债表才能建立信任"——这暗示了未来 agent 可能需要自己的"信用评分"、自己的"保险单"，甚至自己的"法人资格"。我们正在无意识地为一个后人类经济体（post-human economy）铺设法律地基。

Now why standards and insurance? Uh if you trace this problem back through history, every technology wave has had some version of this problem.

  • 1900：electricity comes out. Franklin, houses burn down, lots of people die.
  • 1930s：cars are a big deal, kill lots of people.
  • 1950s：private nuclear energy is a big deal, poses big risks.

In each of those instances, the market runs ahead of regulation to create confidence infrastructure because that's required to make go decision. They're required for adoption and the market fundamentally wants adoption. And in all of those instances, common blueprint emerges between standards and insurance.

The reason it's these two components is standards kind of provide the rules of the road and they also specify like what are the tests that need to be run so we can get a sense of how high the risk is. Taking the case of cars, it's like a car crash. Great. Everyone, they inform your insurance pricing today. They inform your purchasing decisions, etc. That's basically the risk framework.

The insurers are important because they pick up the bill.
