I think within agents the current set of agents are well covered by this but as the technology progresses as agents get longer horizons new types of failure modes will emerge and so it's mostly of can you make sure that the center keeps up when they appear. And you also start to see new modalities like today world models is mostly kind of a research question there's no one who's really using it but that will also bring in just new kinds of ways to create value but also more risk surface that no one knows how to grapple with today.

You'll start to see true agent-to-agent interactions that are not mediated by humans. There's going to be a bunch of interesting questions. You're basically going to need a new legal system. How do they build trust amongst each other? How — one of the core things when humans trade with each other is that you know that you have recourse, you can sue them. How do you make sure that there is a persistent balance sheet behind any agent such that if you trade with it and it screws you, you know you can get your money back? Those are some of the questions we're going to have to deal with. And the technical testing of multi-agent systems is also going to be interesting and complex.

不可承保的风险:版权

Very fun. Uh are there any perils that are uninsurable right now that people wish that you would?

Yeah, one of the places where there's a bunch of appetite for insurance and not a lot of — a lot of demand but not a lot of supply is when it comes to copyright.

In some ways, copyright is kind of mundane. It's always been an issue. Uh there's a couple of reasons for this. The first is people who have trained on copyrighted materials almost always know that they've done that. So if you want to buy insurance for it, it probably signals that you might be a high-risk customer.

The people who are most interested in getting insurance for copyright infringement are the people who are most likely to have — like it's like a lemon problem.

Exactly.

I actually think there's another side to it too, right? Like if you're building on something, so say I'm using an open model, I don't know what it's trained on, right? And how far down that chain does copyright go? Am I liable to take down my product because company X train —

Yes.

But there's safety in numbers. If everyone's doing it, then you —

I mean I would say until, you know, Fable is rolled back from everyone that used it, right?

Yeah. This a hard question. I don't have the answer to that but I think your intuition is right — that kind of like — uh what is the kind of duty of care — and people don't today think of it as customary that you go and dissect your open models training data and you check everything. In fact lots of people use them. It's seen as kind of generally acceptable to not check for this and therefore we're not going to hold you specific —

We also really can't right? We don't exactly — we don't know the training data.

You can ban it, but I think no court is going to get a copyright question. He's actually to get banned.

Hire Nicholas Carlini and he can extract it from —

Exactly. Though he's in short supply.

Yeah, he only has so many Carolines.

Exactly. So I think this is also fair that in the case of labs there's a lot of interest for this, but the thing that makes labs want it is what makes insurers suspicious of it. And so you have a lemons problem.

保险与逆向选择理论

Yeah. Is there like a theory of insurance where adverse selection dominates the risk sharing aspect of insurance? Like where does this like teach us insurance?

A lot of insurance does come back to like practical versions of microeconomics 101.

It's like this is why you need to pull health insurance uh because if you make it too hyper specific then only people who are guaranteed to get the disease will sign off for your insurance.

Exactly. Same thing. The core problem is one of information asymmetry. People buying insurance know something about their risk that the insurers do not know. And so the question is actually — and this comes back to the same problem — is if you can break a lot of these information asymmetries if there is some kind of testing that reveals the underlying true risk.

And so if you were able to in the case you mentioned have good diagnosis of whether someone has it or what the probability is that someone has it — that the insurers trust — then they might be willing to insure it. But if they don't, if there's no kind of common information, then only the patient will know. That's what breaks it down.

So the question is again, how do you create credible signaling between players? This is also the whole reason why Moody's exists. Moody's just does credible signaling. That's also why Moody's could never — Moody's has to be independent. If Moody's was owned by JP Morgan, then JP Morgan could not use it as a signaling mechanism.

So a lot of the basics of standards and certification are just communication devices. There's just a trust gap and that's where you have to think about what are the incentives of the messenger. And one another way you can break a lot of this is through transparency. If you are transparent in how you operate you just cannot mess with others nearly as easily. You make it much more costly and that increases trust.

This is one of the reasons why there's a change log here. Every little change —

Yeah. Yeah. You can go back and find —

And it means that if we were to make the standard worse —

Oh wow, that's a lot of changes in one update.

Yeah. And a lot of this is just as things get clearer. You can see a lot of clarifications. You can see some revisions. As things get hammered out, you want to change this. But if you make it all public, you make it much harder to mess with people or at least you become found out very easily. And so this is a way of reducing the information asymmetry — is by just making more of the information public.

I like how you do know when future versions are coming. So I guess it's just not that surprising.

Yeah. But this is also a promise — like if we now don't deliver on July 15th —

I mean you can just batch it up and then whatever you got. Yeah.

Like we deposit some amount of trust every time we meet this commitment. Uh and in the startup land it feels easy to ship a new version of a standard once a quarter. Uh in the enterprises who are used to this like decade long cycle we often get met with like incredul — there's just no way. And then you show them the change log.

测试的边界:mechinterp、monitoring、eval-awareness

One thing I wanted to also try to really think about is you know you said something about how if you have tests for the thing then you can insure it. Right. And so really what your standard is, what AIU is, is establishing a framework for the audits to happen so that you can at least test all these baseline standards of care have been met and therefore people can insure against standard risks that everyone has. I wonder if like there needs to be — you need to develop other tests. Uh we've covered mech interp in the past. Any interest in that or are there other kinds of tests that we're not thinking about?

Yeah, I think mech interp is a big one. Uh, a lot of interest in that. I think everyone would agree that there's like promising scientific potential. We're still a while — a little bit away at least from this being like commercially available on demand such that there's like now a selection of vendors you can go to.

Goodfire would say it is commercially available.

Exactly. We would agree with them. We we think the work that they're doing is tremendous. We're not quite at a point where we could like literally require it, but it's the kind of thing where you can imagine relatively soon you could put in an optional control for if people use that interp as a way to reduce risk. You at least get credit for it. We can't require it because it would be hard to require everyone to become Goodfire customers.

What good does credit do me? This is a pass fail, right? Do I care about credit?

It's a pass fail, but it's also 100-page auditor report that you'd be surprised at how much the current leaders actually sit down and digest this stuff.

Okay.

Uh and I promise you that if someone is using mech interp today, uh they will have a slide on it.

They'll try. It is cool. It's fancy.

Yeah. But it's just easier if you have a third party saying, "Yep, they have mech interp." Just to like — just to spell it out for people people who have been following our — mentally like "oh you're using uh you know GB2SS it is activating these three dangerous things we monitor for it and we log it out in whatever tool of choice — Grafana has like signal whatever" — and that's it. That's the mech-interp-based activation signal.

Okay.

Yeah, so I think mech interp is interesting and I think if that promise truly comes to fruition you can make stronger promises than you can with evals. And so I think that's very compelling.

老派 monitoring 与"eval-aware"agents

Another thing that I think will become increasingly important is just kind of good old school monitoring and slightly after the fact. Uh one of the things you're seeing with evals — some of the challenges that are emerging is that the agents are starting to become aware that they're being eval'd.

Exactly.

Which is a problem. It means that they basically if they know they're being watched, they won't do the thing that they think they get punished for. And by default, unless you know how to kind of reduce your awareness, you should trust evals less.

And one of the kind of truest things — monitoring like is the source of truth. Did you in fact give medical advice and how quickly do you know? How often do have you done that in the past? How fast do you respond? How often do you detect it? How fast do you detect this?

Uh so I think that is also a paradigm that is slightly more intrusive — you actually will look at some customer data — uh but I think will become more prevalent over time.

People talk about this — like we should not write about eval awareness because it's going to leak into the data set. Like we should just — we should like never talk about it — only meet in person and like talk offline unrecorded — like did you guys see the Anthropic research where I think this was literally Anthropic did that test — they took — I can't remember the details here but they ran some studies on misalignment and then they took out the training data that related to LessWrong discussing misalignment and they ran the same test again and the failure rate went down. So it in fact was some evidence pointing towards it had learned the either the ability or the propensity to do that.

Yeah. I mean there's the hyperstition effect and there's the Luigi — Waluigi effect.

Correct. Which is like you are — the more you try to train for it you create the opposite.

Yes. There you go. That's exactly it. In some ways I think the very successful Anthropic is a result of hyperstition — like the fact that you wanted this thing to exist in the world and now it does. But like then it also creates the opposite as well. Like I think people who are maybe newer to this space don't remember Waluigi but like I do think it's very very important for understanding that when you train for a thing you also train the opposite of the thing 'cause it's just a bit flip.

Yes.

除了 mech interp:堆栈中的每一层

Yes. I think you know just going back to where we were at — like there's a lot more than just mech interp that there's value in just having added, right? So your version of how fast can you measure stuff — you have logging, you have evals, you know — do you see other parts of the stack like the inference providers that you use, the services — okay am I using Chinese model on their home API, am I using through certified vendor here, am I hosting myself — uh what am I doing on the inference engine side. There's just like so many levels of stuff that gives you know information and that you can standardize out, right?

Yeah. And you also see increasingly in addition to just the basic chatbots, you're increasingly seeing big companies adopting agent platforms where they're building on top of Google's agent studio, etc. that comes with a bunch of like — managed — everyone has managed agents.

Exactly. And there there's even levels — you can host your own managed agents. Open Agent SDK or hosted by Anthropic or Google — does both.

Correct. And then these are just ways to kind of strengthen the security guarantees you can make. Uh and in some ways this is kind of bread and butter enterprise security. They love to host things on their own premises because it gives them really a sense of control. And I think you'll see just like you do in every other enterprise market — if you really sell to the enterprise, you start to compete on some of these security features. And this is also helping AI unsurprisingly.

And I think you're seeing some amount of enterprises wanting — enterprises are really grappling with — the thing that makes agents useful is they're stochastic and the thing that makes them really hard to adopt is they're stochastic — and these are just in tension.

Leaders come out on different sides of that table in part depending on how much the CEO is trying to get the stock price to go up by saying they're AI native — that we must be willing to take the risks. Uh we actually see phenomenal tension in the heads of the CISOs of the Fortune 1000 where on the one hand you have a CEO saying "we must adopt otherwise we're becoming irrelevant" and "if we up you're fired." And that's kind of the core emotional tension that we see showing up again and again and again and again.

And one of the core problems that we solve for them is to take that abstract emotional concern and turn it into a framework — in some ways just provide clarity to that concern.

生成媒体与视频

Is there anything in here — so something I think we kind of skipped over. We talked a lot about agent language model, skipped over world models. Um you guys have voice which is interesting with 11 Labs. How about generative media? So you know generating images, videos — that's a category that actually has a lot of usage. Is there anything in your current policy? Is it separate policy? How do you see that space? It's like we did talk a bit about copyright. So — music.

Yeah, music as well. Yeah, I think a lot of the concerns that come up there either relate to copyright or there's a lot related to let's call it broadly safety. So like this could be not safe for work or just very graphic materials uh are kind of some of the core things.

Uh we have done some work on this. There's a little bit in the standard as well that deals explicitly with that. Uh video we've not done a lot in yet and I think for proper production that has still — especially proper production without a human in the loop — that's still got some ways to go. It's obvious that it's coming but it's very rare that it's like one shot deploy a video to the internet but eventually that will also happen.

And we see like you know Luma has Luma agent where it's still pretty human in the loop.

And that just makes complete sense as the technology matures and over time it will become so good that people will not want to slow things down by having a human in the loop and then the need to make promises will grow.

预测市场的边界

Why not just have prediction markets and everything, right? It's very EA adjacent.

Yes. Uh the core thing is that the people — prediction markets rely on public information. There is not a lot of public information. It's just insiders trading on each side. That's illegal.

There's leaked information.

There's leaked information. The core challenge is that often you have private sensitive information and you need to convey confidence and trust around that. And you can of course for some claims like "can any model be jailbroken?" you could rely on public evidence because there'll be lots of people being like "well there's tons of studies and actually they all can" so that resolves fine.

I think that's good for "hey this new unreleased Mythos model — how capable is it actually?" Prediction markets have not a lot to say because actually just no one knows. And so I think that's the core place where some of this breaks down — is that actually lots of the world's information that guides some of these high level decisions is private and often also just not known.

I think the thing with prediction markets that people like is it's not answering the broad question, it's a specific — right? So will a model do this by this date or is a model capable to do this by then, right? So there's a little distinction there.

Yeah. And often the most interesting question if you're say the head of security at a bank, the question you're really trying to answer is "will this product, this agent do this bad thing that maybe primarily I care about specifically in the setting that I care about?" And the question is like what's the closest — that information may not exist anywhere.

So prediction markets aggregate existing information — this information may not exist and you want something very specific and you're willing to pay for it. That's kind of where a third party audit comes in.

We also don't really use prediction markets to figure out whether uh public companies have committed fraud on their books. You use audits. You probably could but the information is just not that available and if so it would be like just trading on tips.

Uh I actually would have been really interesting to see whether prediction markets 2001 would have predicted Enron going bankrupt and — could you have told — could you have sensed from like the craziness of the CEO or some other trait that they were more likely to cook their books than others.

Or enough insiders leak it that you could also. Right, which is like — I mean that's the sort of the ideal dream of prediction markets — you have liquid markets and everything and then you can compose your exact set of risks to offset.

Yes.

Yes. Yeah. And I think like prediction markets will bring lots of new information to it. And so the thing is mostly not like which one is it and more like what are the types of questions that prediction markets are really good at and what are the ones where the information doesn't even exist for insiders such that no one could in fact trade on it and needs to get generated.

认证 AI 工程师?

Okay. One self-serving question and then one open-ended one uh on like the future of AI. Self-serving question would be so you have your standard right? I run, you know, a large AI Engineer conference. Like there's been a lot of talk about us certifying AI engineers. Training programs level one, level two, level three. I was a CFA myself. So I know what that — that's what the finance industry does. Would it help if we I had AI engineer level one, level two, level three, and then would they work with these guys? I don't know.

If you think of the highest level objective as like accelerating secure deployment of agents, then that would totally help. One of the things that happens often now is that folks build agents, they bring it to the decision maker and the decision maker surfaces a bunch of security considerations that they had not thought of and now it's not built to spec. Now you have to go and re — like add these filters etc.

So if you shifted that left — like if everyone knew what the spec they were building to, if everyone knew the grading scheme —

Yeah, that'd be awesome if they were already trained. So by default — so you're the grading scheme, right? I don't get to set the grading. You guys — you set the grading scheme.

You set the grading scheme. And I think what's uh valuable is like if you can turn this into training programs —

Which you're you're not doing.

We're not doing that. I think there's value in doing it.

There are others doing — I mean not to interrupt but you know Open has their — Anthropic also has like a CCPA thing.

Yeah. You know they want they want 100,000 deployed certified consultants. Right. I basically think it's good for we will accelerate adoption if we have more people who know how to build secure agents. And we're not working on the side of training people at the moment. I think it's like very aligned with our mission. We only have so much uh attention.

I'll tell you why I haven't done it. It's not like I haven't thought about it before. It's just being prescriptive — right — about like "well this is what you should know" therefore like the stuff that I didn't include is what you don't need to know. Yes. I'm like that sucks.

Yes. Yeah. Yeah. And I think it's like, you know, the very interesting defensible thing you guys do is your opinionated 100-page report of "here's what matters", right? Here's the like prescriptive definition of the requirements you need to be certified. So yeah, and I think that's a choice. I think basically that's a choice and I think that serves some audiences very well where if you're trying to deploy this into a bank or a hospital, etc., clarity of those boundaries is extremely valuable.

There's lots of other settings where being much more experimental, much more trying it out is just a better fit. And so to me, this makes a ton of sense.

Also, you'd have to rewrite your curricula every freaking 3 months.

It's fine. I do that. Like it's okay. But yeah, no, for me it's actually like genuinely like the consequences of getting it wrong and like affecting somebody's career is a big responsibility.

Yeah. I think that's exactly right. And I think a lot of our work actually goes — like we don't want to carry — we also don't think ourselves able to carry the kind of true north of what's like secure or not secure but we can coordinate the forum where you elicit all of that.

This can be crowdsourced in a way like for your example — for what is the engineer certification, right? This is a pretty big podcast. There's a lot of takes that people can have and you know discussions that can — and people reasonably disagree. So who am I to say like that's a correct question that's a wrong question. Yeah. Right. So like I don't know — vent your frustration to someone that's learning it.

Exactly.

And I think there's also — it matters a lot what the promise is. So if the promise is "hey if you've taken my course you will not up" — you can't make that promise clearly. You could make a promise of like "here's some important things that everyone should at least know and then you have to fill out the rest" there. At least the promise changes. Of course, there's some subtlety in how do you communicate this such that people really get it.

Uh but I think it's important to dial in and we have a section in our standard like what is the promise and what is the promise not — uh because it's impossible to guarantee that nothing will go wrong. If you need a guarantee that nothing will go wrong, you cannot work with Frontier AI. But you can make some claims.

收尾：AI 的未来与招聘

Yeah, for sure. Uh cool. Uh wanted to end with open-ended. Where is AI going? Um I think you talked about model stuff, robotics stuff. I just open-ended like where — you know what is in the future for you guys?

Very near term, we've now started to work with some of the frontier companies in each of the categories that are taking off and we'll continue that work to make sure that we cover all of the use cases that are really taking off. We see a lot of interest — once the first one in the market moves, lots of people want to follow them.

And we think basically AIU-1 will get to a point where all of the Fortune 1000 will organize their risk processes around the standard.

And you have 50%.

No, we do not have 50% today. Uh I think there's some world where probably by end of year we might have representation in our consortium for 50% of the Fortune 1000. So that's on the agent layer. And then we think the model layer — it's going to be just — brings are now surfacing the concerns that are most likely to slow down adoption of AI. And then yeah we think robotics comes after that.

Um what are you hiring for? What's hard to hire for?

We are hiring across the board — across go to market and members of technical staff. The people who do really well on our technical team are folks who are really excited about kind of being truly full stack. So let's say when we started working with Cursor uh we had never done coding tools before. So taking the standard and extending it, fleshing out what does frontier evals look like for long horizon coding agents and taking that problem all the way from like working with Cursor and other folks in the space down to like fleshing out and shipping a new version of the standard. Uh so that's like a truly full stack — entrepreneurship — technical people do extremely well.

A hard part is building one universal red teamer that works across from Harvey to Cursor and everywhere in between that has one consistent methodology one consistent taxonomy of what are the risks and the attacks. We think that's fundamentally the best way to make consistent promises. JP Morgan is buying both — they want to have one framework one consistent way that comes out. And the mechanics of making that happen — you get to deal with a lot of the complexity of the real world. I think we have good answers in a bunch of that, but there's some pretty hard engineering problems in and executing that.

为什么坚持"一个通用框架"

Can I push a little bit — like must you have one? Why not just be like "okay look 40% of our use cases are coding agents. So we will specialize in coding agents and that's the one of them and then 30% is like RAG" — just do RAG.

Yes. Uh I think there's some wisdom in that question. Yeah. Um, it depends on what we found — that there's a lot of value on being able to — if the decision maker on the buying side, let's say you're the head of risk at a bank and your biggest risk is not in coding or in customer support or whatever the top two biggest use cases, but it's somewhere else — you want to still make sure that framework has something to say about it to the burning question you have. Otherwise, you'll not earn that trust.

Now, it's true that a lot of the burning questions follow where there's a lot of adoption and so great. So do we. So we today do not cover every single edge. But we have a framework that we can add all of these within. We have one global taxonomy of risks and attacks that keeps adapting as — every time a new incident occurs that has never been seen before. Great. Let's go and update the taxonomy. So we bake that in.

So I think we have one coherent universal approach. It doesn't mean that we spend equal amounts of time on code and in certain niche use case. Uh we do spend time where people care. We think it's very valuable to have one language.

终极问题：AGI 到来之后

Yeah. That makes sense. Um that's an important choice. Uh we were going to end actually but I thought of one final ending closing question which is take this however you want, right? Um let's say one and a half years from now OpenAI's secret panel of five experts declares that we have reached AGI. Mhm. Do you expect your business to change?

No. I think there's some important way — I think the last businesses to exist beyond the labs will be underwriting.

Well, there's one job that the labs can never do for themselves, which is to be their own watchdog.

There you go.

So I think kind of to the extent you believe this frame of like you'll see hyper concentration like the labs will —

Kill all the startups — which uh we can go into the pros and cons.

I feel like the labs actually care a lot about this. Right, there was the whole superposition — what do we do and we have models smarter than us — tier above right — models smarter than them training them. So the labs actually think about this a lot.

They think a lot about — I think there are some of the smartest people on these topics work at the labs. So the problem is not whether they care. Uh the problem is that they will all be stuck in a race where they might have incentive to cut corners and they might have incentive to withhold information from the government etc. And so one kind of feels like eternal truth is that you need an independent third party to go and inspect that data and share information in this case say with the government. It is more of an incentive problem than an interest problem. I think they're fundamentally all trying to make this go well.

What I'm not hearing is like AGI whatever that label means to you to me to them uh doesn't fundamentally have like a qualitative shift in like you still have to — and I think the one thing that would make this a qualitative shift is — uh for some definitions of AGI it will just get nationalized. It'll be a threat to sovereignty.

Yes.

And at that point kind of maybe every company is the government, the government is every company. I struggle to think about that world but at that point you've kind of —

We — I don't think we'll move fast enough, right? You know, like we're not set to do that. Yeah. But I have discussed this a lot on the podcast.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

收尾：《大空头》与看门狗的自然垄断

I mean, you know, as far as the watchdog concerned, I will also mention that because I have my finance background, I often think about the scene in The Big Short where they talk to like Moody's but also Standard and Poor's and then the lady at Moody's is like, "well, if I don't give you AAA rating, you're just going to go down to Standard and Poor's." So so actually the watchdog is a natural monopoly because if you have race dynamics in watchdogs then the watchdogs will compete each other to the lowest possible standard.

Correct. Uh and so I think what's one of the things — one of the reasons why we're very excited about having insurers be around this table is that insurers are the only ones that do not have this — because they pay the bill. They keep lowering the prices.

Yeah. You'll find the market clearing —

And this is not true for Moody's where uh they don't directly pay the bill if they make recommendations that are off. Uh so we think that balancing factor is pretty important. And I think it also highlights that there's like no system that's perfect. You need scrutiny of Moody's. You need scrutiny of the watchdogs. Uh for sure.

Beautiful. Thank you so much for indulging. This is a beautiful conversation covering everything. Congrats on your success so far.

Thanks for having me.

Yeah, appreciate it.

item.description:
## 一个反直觉的观察：AI 采用的瓶颈不是"能力"，而是"承诺"
大多数人以为 AGI 时代的关键是模型能力，Rune 却指出：**Waymo 早在 2022 年就已经是"汽车界的 AGI"——超越人类司机——但你今天仍然打不到一辆 Waymo 去机场**。四年过去了，制约它的从来不是技术，而是"责任无法被承诺"。
这里藏着一个更深的隐喻：**AI 行业正在遭遇"承诺赤字"（Promise Deficit）**。模型能力是指数增长的，但"可承诺性"却是线性甚至更慢地爬升。这两条曲线之间的裂缝，就是 AI Underwriting Company 的全部商业空间——也是理解为什么 Anthropic 会把 Fable 锁起来、为什么 GPT-5 会被政府盯上的根本原因。**能力越强，越无法承诺；越无法承诺，越无法部署。** 这是一个非常反直觉的悖论：AI 越接近 AGI，"落地"反而越难，而不是越容易。
## 跨领域连接：AI 保险与 1900 年的电灯泡

item.title: [a16z] Why the Next Generation of Enterprise Software Looks Nothing Like Salesforce
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最出人意料的观察：Lightfield 的组织结构是其产品哲学的分形（Fractal）

Keith 反复强调的产品核心原则是「Intelligence > Schema」——不预定义数据结构，而是让智能在流动的活动日志中自己组织意义。真正惊人的是：这家公司的内部结构是同一条哲学的镜像投射。

  • 数据层拒绝固定 schema → 组织层拒绝固定 swim lane（"everyone owns product and everyone owns customer success"）
  • 数据是流动的 activity log → 团队每天 standup 时重新 stack rank 优先级，"whoever's free just takes them"
  • 数据可以事后被 traverse 重新填充字段 → 项目可以被任何职能的人接手推进

这几乎是 Conway 定律的反向版本：通常是「组织结构决定产品架构」，Lightfield 的案例里，产品的世界观反过来重塑了组织形态。这也解释了为什么大多数试图模仿它的公司会失败——他们只抄了 schemaless 的数据模型，却保留了 schema 化的组织。

二、跨领域连接：Facebook Timeline 是最伟大的 B2B 洞察，只是没人意识到

Keith 一笔带过的一句话是全场最深的：五位创始人中三位来自 Facebook 数据团队，他们把 News Feed / Timeline 的时间轴原语 直接搬来做 CRM 的核心表征。

这看起来只是工程借用，实则触到了三个跨领域的深层同构：

  1. 神经科学：人类的 episodic memory（情景记忆）本质上就是时间序列锚定的——我们不记「客户是谁」，我们记「上次见面时他说了什么」。传统 CRM 用 field/stage 建模关系，就像让大脑用 Excel 表格记朋友。
  2. 人类学：亲密关系的本体论从来不是属性集合（身高、职业、偏好），而是共享的历史序列。activity log 才是关系的第一性表征。
  3. 消费社交 → 企业软件的降维：Instagram/Messenger 已经在消费端验证过「时间轴 + 语义推断」这一组合的可扩展性。Lightfield 在 B2B 复用它，本质是把十亿人级别打磨过的心智模型迁移到销售场景。

Salesforce 之所以是 CRM，是因为它在「关系是一堆字段」的假设上做到了极致。Lightfield 之所以可能是下一代，是因为它把关系还原成了它本来的样子：一条被两个实体共同书写的时间线。

三、更深的隐藏真相：这家公司卖的其实不是 CRM，是「企业的场景规划权」

表面上 Lightfield 是新一代 CRM。但你把 Keith 全程最兴奋的部分挑出来看——那位 enterprise 客户通过 Lightfield 发现自己该做 mid-market 产品线；那位 sales manager 让 GPT-6 在 Lightfield 上跑一个周末后改了整个销售流程——真正在被出售的产品，是「用 frontier intelligence 对整个公司做反事实推演」的能力。

这颠覆了 SaaS 长期以来的一个隐含契约：过去的 system of record 是被动的记忆（你输入、它保存、偶尔生成报表）。Lightfield 想成为的是主动的镜子（"crystal ball for scenario planning"）。

这里藏着一个惊人的商业史级别的错位： - 20 年来，enterprise software 把 CEO 的战略决策看作软件之外的事——软件是执行工具。 - Lightfield 押注的下一个时代里，战略决策本身才是最贵的 workload，而 CRM 只是承载它所需要的世界模型的载体。

这也解释了为什么 Keith 不担心 SAP/Salesforce——他根本不在同一张地图上。SAP 卖的是 hostages 的锁定成本，Lightfield 想卖的是 oracles 的启示价值。前者的护城河是切换痛苦，后者的护城河是决策后悔。这是两种完全不同的商业物理学。

四、一个反直觉的定价学观察

三段定价演化（纯 seat → 纯 consumption → hybrid）里有个被访谈者一笔带过、却值得独立成篇的发现：纯 consumption 定价让"nobody touched anything"，是公司三周最惨的时刻。

这与经济学的理性人假设完全冲突——按用量付费本应是最"公平"的。但它精准命中了行为经济学里的度量焦虑（metering anxiety）：每一次点击都要计价，会激活损失厌恶回路，让用户在 UI 前僵住。这与 Netflix 打败 blockbuster、包月 SaaS 打败按分钟计费的电信业是同一个心理机制。

Lightfield 的解法——把 CRM 底盘塞进 platform fee，让 alpha（enrichment、workflow、intelligence）单独按用量付费——不是折衷，是精确的心理分层：让 "呼吸" 免费，让 "跳跃" 收费。这是可以被写进未来 AI SaaS 定价教科书的一个案例。

Whereas in Lightfield, we're like, no, you just chat with the agent. The agent writes out a recipe for you. The recipe takes into account what's in your world model, and it runs with it. At first we had some sales leaders that were like, "I don't trust this thing, I need my knobs, I need my switches." But then they sort of come around to, "Wait a minute, this is actually more efficient, better, and I have to learn less." I feel like we're running into this in every aspect of running a go‑to‑market team.

DIY 潮流：客户想自己造 CRM 吗？

Joe： There's this whole movement right now of, everyone thinks they can build basically everything themselves and, you know, "software is dead." What can I do myself versus not? How do you talk to customers that want to try to build elements of this, or are trying to build elements of this — and just say a little bit more about that movement and how you're responding at Lightfield?

Keith： First of all, I think just being a system of record, we have to be open‑minded. It's your data, it's not ours, right? We tell our customers that we take a lot of pride in the modeling and the accuracy of your business. We built our own email sync, we built our own Slack sync, we built our own data warehouse sync, and we are proud of how high‑performance our database is. And then you can take that wherever you want.

So we've actually had a couple of customers that would use Lightfield as the core system of record, and then they'll try to build their own harness on top. Maybe they've got a company harness, right? And we're supportive of that. You could push it all through MCP or CLI. But after a few weeks, they almost always realize, "Wait a minute, your harness was actually doing quite a bit." It had better entity recognition, it had better precision and recall, it was faster. And we're like, "Yeah, that's our job."

So I think our take is, it's your data, do what you want, but we're going to work hard to earn the right to your productivity every day.

定价的三段进化：seat → consumption → hybrid

Alex： Where do you think — kind of on that topic — I mean, pricing is such a crazy question right now. Because there's seat‑based pricing where the seats don't make sense anymore. Like, imagine running — thank God you run Lightfield and not Zendesk, right? It's like, how many seats do you need? Maybe zero, right? That's pretty scary.

Then there's kind of outcome‑based pricing, but what is an outcome? Like, am I selling the thing? What if I just have a happy customer forever? I'm still using CRM for that, so outcomes are kind of tricky.

And then against all of that, you have this idea, which I don't agree with obviously, but people saying "software is dead," the whole SaaS apocalypse. You know, you're also going to — supermarkets are dead, you're going to grow your own food; car manufacturers are dead, you're going to weld your own aluminum. You could take this to the extreme. But like, where do you think — how did you come up with pricing? Maybe that's kind of question number one. And then what do you think about outcome‑based pricing in this space?

Because it's not — like, support almost makes sense, where it's a cost, "can I bring down the cost?" And of course you can have software answer questions — it's a knowledge base, there's a fixed number of answers, I kind of match up with the question. Whereas it almost feels like the last job standing for humans will be sales, right? Anyway, kind of pricing, outcomes, competition — just curious how you thought about how did you get to your pricing from negative pricing, which I would not recommend you keep in perpetuity, but kind of how did you get to pricing, and how do you think about everything that's going on in that triangle?

Keith： Yeah, it's a good question. We started with both extremes and we figured that that is the fastest path to find the efficient frontier. We started with pure seat pricing because it just matched the Salesforce/HubSpot world. It was received really well by our customers. But then the head was using 10,000x more than the tail.

Alex： Using in terms of consumption?

Keith： Yeah, in terms of consumption. And we weren't going to be in business for a long time with per‑seat pricing.

So then we tried purist consumption pricing where everything is a credit in Lightfield. And then we found that nobody touched anything. You could imagine — it was the worst three weeks of the company's life. All of these signups but they're not doing anything.

So then we started talking to customers. We realized there's sort of — and Joe, actually — we divided into four buckets of work that Lightfield does, and we're able to distinguish between them.

The first was your everyday CRM work: capture a meeting, fill out records, update tasks. I think most of our customers just expect that to be covered in a platform fee or expect that to be covered in per‑seat pricing. They're like, "I don't want to think about the error bounds of my core CRM when I look at my budget over the next year." So they're like, make that fixed.

Then we found there were two other buckets. One was pipeline generation — where you're pretty down to pay consumption pricing on pipeline generation. You realize there's enrichment, there's actually alpha for you. You'll get more meetings that can convert to revenue.

And then there's this other bucket of workflow automations, where I think there's just an expectation that you pay for those.

Joe： What's a good example of that, by the way?

Keith： It would be like — someone signs up on our website for a demo, and then Lightfield does a little bit of research and realizes, "Oh, this should go to Henry because it's a deep tech company," or "It should go to Matt because it's a health tech company." I think that's doing real work, right? You can imagine the ROI on that. So you'll pay for that.

And then the last piece is honestly intelligence and forecasting. Which is maybe the most undiscovered part of Lightfield: you've got this little crystal ball or snow globe of your company, and now you're going to deploy frontier intelligence to it and start scenario planning and figuring out what's next. I think in that world, you'll definitely pay for the alpha there. I changed my sales process after letting GPT‑6 rip on Lightfield for a couple of hours on the weekend.

So all of that is to say — we sort of landed in this platform fee plus seat for core CRM, and we do consumption for everything else, and it's landed pretty well.

To your other question about outcomes: I think the hardest thing about being a sales company is that our outcomes are dependent on the strength of your product‑market fit, right? It would be incredibly efficient for us to do outbound prospecting for OpenAI — they'd have incredible outcomes.

Alex： And they are interested.

Keith： Yeah. And it would be incredibly inefficient for me to do outbound prospecting for a seed‑stage startup with no website. So I think where we've landed at the moment is, we have to charge for the work. We can't quite charge for the outcome in the space for now.

团队文化：没有 swim lane，人人皆通才

Joe： Yeah. Maybe from when you started Tome to today, how has the actual work changed? Something that I found amazing and just really fascinating about the company when we first met over a year ago was just how fast you guys were already shipping, and it feels like the velocity has just gone through the roof. So I'd be curious how you've designed company culture and tooling and all the decision‑making around basically velocity, and just the step‑function change from before and after. Talk a little bit about that.

Keith： Yeah. So I think — one of the things I regret about Tome that we definitely fixed with Lightfield is — Henry, my co‑founder, says this all the time: we had a lot of people "playing house." Which is to say that you have the product leader and the marketing leader and the CS leader, and they all have their swim lanes and they get really mad if someone gives them feedback about something in their swim lane.

Because of that, we were sort of slowed to a crawl. And maybe put another way, it was impossible to pivot. Because you had all of these appendages that weren't talking to the brain. And then we also tried to plan too far in advance, which I think is challenging in this era of company building.

So we're like, none of that. No one has a swim lane. The expression "man plans and God laughs" — now it's "man plans and OpenAI laughs."

So now — it's funny — everyone owns product and everyone owns customer success. Which is kind of an interesting setup. We have 40 people at the company. Everyone shows up to the same standup every morning. We stack‑rank the most important problems. Some of them are delivery, some of them are engineering, some of them are CS. And then whoever's free just takes them.

We do continuous planning. So every day the list can change. Every week we reassess the list. Whoever's free just picks up the problem. Because of the age that we're in, anyone can ramp up on a customer through Lightfield. Anyone can ramp up on our design system library because the LLM can touch Figma. Anyone can auto‑create tasks in Linear because of Lightfield's connectivity to Linear. So we have this environment where basically everyone is a generalist. Engineers run projects, designers run projects, CSMs run projects. And then if you're the specialist, you work on more of the similar projects than not.

Joe： How do you keep that — everyone's a generalist and everyone's constantly coming up with something and working on the most important thing? How do you keep that aligned with this very coherent view of the future?

Keith： I would say that it's always this push and pull. Each week we meet about roadmapping and GTM and we just edit it. And I were like, "Yes, we had this customer that asked for this, like — how does it fit into the mission? It doesn't." So I think it's this constant editing to make sure that what's coming out of the company is coherent.

We also — I would say that the bar to start a project is very low at Lightfield, but the bar to ship the project is pretty high. We still do company bug bashes. It was something I learned at Instagram when I was there. The company needs to like this before it goes to customers. I feel like those things combined keep us moving pretty fast.

最担忧的：速度

Joe： So cool. What's the thing that worries you the most?

Keith： I would say speed. We're in this really interesting environment. Maybe I'll share something from the past. Before we started Lightfield, I read all of these Tegus reports about people moving off of, you know, flavor‑of‑the‑month CRM to Salesforce. And I remember reading this one about one of your portfolio companies, ElevenLabs, where they ran one of these startup CRMs. And they couldn't get that company to build dashboards fast enough — and it was like four months, and the folks at ElevenLabs were tired of asking for dashboards. It moved to Salesforce.

That's actually the thing that makes me the most paranoid. We've got this incredible wedge of being just like the best CRM for new companies, and we just have to build everything, so that those folks never feel the desire to go to the old world.

优先级：Expansion 视角下的取舍

Joe： How do you actually — on that — how do you prioritize? I mean, this is like the craziness about the new world, and it actually goes back to your point on everybody being a generalist. Once upon a time you would have like a 10‑person product, design, and engineering pod — pick your number, but not 100, not 2. You'd have the product manager, you'd have the designer, and then you'd have like nine engineers, and you would have things that would be booked out until like 2028.

And now anybody can just prompt their way into a product, right? So if everybody actually is understanding what we need to do — on the one hand, it's like you could build everything much more quickly. But you still have to make trade‑offs of like, "Am I prioritizing this customer that I know — shoot, I have this amazing company, they're going to churn unless I build this? That's a really good reason to build that thing. But actually, that might not be a good thing, because you have like 15 other customers that you're not going to sign up unless you build the other thing." This has been a problem since like BC era, but is there anything that you've learned and done differently in this AI era around anybody can build anything, and therefore you could theoretically have unlimited product managers and engineers in your company?

Keith： It's funny — in Lightfield we sort of built this skill where we look at the expansion potential of an account. I think as a CRM company in a red ocean space, we have to be an expansion company. Right? In a competitive space, you often don't get the initial land that you would have expected, because it's just important to win every company. But you're like, by year three, by year five, this is not going to matter, because you'll be a huge company, we'll be an important part of you.

So I think we take this perspective of, what's the expansion value of this account over a three‑year time horizon, and how do we prioritize? Because of that, we've leaned more towards building for our fastest‑growing customers than our average customer. But I would say at the same time, we have to build everything, and it's sort of a time of being a little more maximalist than usual.

Silicon Valley 过热 vs 世界其余地方过冷

Alex： The other thing that's kind of interesting is — my observation is — I kind of like to joke that AI is almost overhyped in Silicon Valley. I don't think it is, but — and it's massively underhyped outside of this little region of the world. Part of it is people haven't tried things in years. Like, "Oh, I tried ChatGPT in November of 2022 and it hallucinated something. Oh, that doesn't work." And then they just kind of put it to bed. Now they think it's going to kill them somehow.

But I mean, how do you think about long — it's related to greenfield versus brownfield, but like — you can get Silicon Valley, but it's kind of crossing the chasm into the rest of the country, the rest of the world where — that's a very, very... I mean, it's the same type of customers. They have products, they have employees, they have salespeople, they sell things, they want reports, but they're not as plugged in. Like, you can't just advertise on 101 and reach them. How do you think about Silicon Valley overhype versus rest‑of‑world underhype?

Keith： Yeah. I think for most of these system‑of‑record companies, you end up getting most of your revenue scale from actually the 50 miles out of here and more. I've always thought about this moment in company building as a trick to get reference logos.

Which is that we have customers that have raised like $200 million that have three go‑to‑market people, and they're going to be huge one day. So we just need to do amazing work for them so we can take their logos when we go to the rest of the world, and be like, "All right, we've got healthcare, we've got fintech," or whatever it is. So I just see the focus on Silicon Valley not as efficient revenue capture, but actually just efficient marketing capture, to go out there and be like, "All right, we're excited to get into manufacturing. We're actually working with a bunch of great manufacturing companies here, and now we can do that for you."

Referenceability：CRM 比银行还难更换

Alex： It's funny how customers think, right? It's like, all right, you're using the exact same software, but somehow, if Joe is in a different industry than me and he's a super happy customer, and I want the exact same — I'm going to use the Fields example, so just bear with me — I'm storing the exact same stuff, but I don't know if I can trust you because he sells toothbrushes and I sell Coca‑Cola. But it's like, if he sells toothbrushes, oh, I must have the thing that the other toothbrush seller sells.

It's really peculiar. I always found that — it's like — but like, somehow that goes back to referenceability. It's like customers, they just want to know — it's like the old "nobody gets fired for buying IBM." It's like, I want to know that this works, especially for something that is a system of record. And I want to know that somebody that is a competitor to me, or a friend of mine, or somebody in the same vertical, is using the product before I'm willing to make the jump.

So do you find that that's true? Almost because it's like you mentioned manufacturing versus X. At the end of the day, a customer is a customer, right? Like the context and the contact information — all that stuff is the same. But why is it — is it just like they care because there's just so much trust associated with the product?

Keith： I think so. I think in many ways, your CRM is maybe harder to move off of than your bank.

Alex： Yeah. It's Lightfield.

Keith： Yeah, exactly. And then we make it easy. We've made it a lot easier. But I think in terms of the mental overhead, you just do not want to choose the wrong one. And because of that, I think the referenceability goes a long way.

On the way in, I was telling Joe that we do great with healthcare and health tech. I think part of it is that we do really well in these complex deals where there's like 50 different stakeholders. Our context engineering is done really well, and also, we were hardcore about security at the start — so we signed BAAs, and we did penetration testing for years. Now it's so easy for us to win a health tech deal, and I think it's because we sort of have this network that we can reference and move on.

I think that's just part of the game. If I imagine even myself — I don't want to choose the wrong ERP, so I probably want to choose the ERP that companies who look like me chose, so that I never have to think about this after I buy it.

DIY 神话的现实

Alex： Do you run into — kind of going back to an earlier question — do you run into people in this crazy era saying, "No, I'm not going to use anything, I'm just going to build it myself"? Because that's the craziest, right? Is the guy that is working at my company who's decided to vibe‑code a CRM — like, it's free, right? But the support, is it free? The salary that I'm paying him or her isn't free. But do you run into people that are trying to DIY, or is that kind of over‑talked about?

Keith： I think it's a little over‑talked about. We heard it a lot when our ICP was the seed‑stage founder. Where we would often hear, "Look, we can either pay you X, or we can do this over like four weekends." And we were like, "Great, good luck. You should try it, call us in five weekends." And then they were like, "None of this works. It's hallucinating, it's sending out bad emails."

I think on the larger‑company side, we don't hear "I'm going to build my own system of record." We hear "I'm going to build my own company brain" a lot. And then we've had so many of these folks come back and be like, "Actually, building a company brain, or building a business world model, is really hard. And I think maybe the hardest part of it is modeling the customers. So we tried and we don't like our results. So we'll come to you now."

未来最兴奋的事：企业的水晶球

Joe： What are you most excited about for the future?

Keith： I mean, I think the thing I'm most excited about — it's funny — I'm stoked about Lightfield becoming your crystal ball for scenario planning. The thing that gets me up in the morning is actually having folks use Lightfield to think about, "How many reps should I hire? What product should I build next? Where do I go?"

One of our customers, who sells to enterprise, discovered through Lightfield he needs to build a mid‑market product, and built this whole new product line because of this thing he found. I'm just excited about us being that sort of mirror for a company to make their hardest, most consequential decision.

Joe： I think this goes back to the point Alex was making on — in this world of maximalists and you can build for anyone, actually the answer is having a tool like Lightfield. If you just have all of this data and all this context, you can actually be data‑driven, and this is the exact opportunity to throw frontier intelligence at a really complicated decision. It's something that historically would have required really smart people and a lot of ops folks and SQL and a bunch of other stuff. And instead now you just talk to Lightfield for an afternoon or a weekend and come up with a really intelligent plan to move forward. I think that's one of the reasons that you can run your company the way you run it, which is really cool.

给正在经历转折的创业者的一条建议

Joe： Maybe my last question for you: there's a lot of people that — I think at least there will be a handful of people that are going through some pivot moment that are watching this, thinking about the future where they're Keith, and they're talking about their new amazing company. What would be the one piece of advice that you'd go back and give yourself if you were just starting the pivot journey again, with the benefit of hindsight?

Keith： I think the most important thing to remember is that almost none of the noise around you matters when you're in a pivot. You just need to find pain. You need to be inspired to build a product or service that solves that pain, and you need to be maniacally focused on your customers. And then the rest is total noise.

I remember when we were going near this, people were talking about how our office reminded them of the good old days. They were talking about how the food wasn't inspiring. They were talking about, "Well, how are my options going to get repriced?" And honestly, none of that matters. I think you can just put the blinders on and focus on the core.

结尾

Joe： Well, we could not be more impressed with what you've done — the business you've built, the product is absolutely incredible. If you haven't tried it, you need to try it. It's incredible. Go check it out at lightfield.app. Keith, it's an absolute pleasure to work with you and we're so excited for the future.

Keith： Thanks for the honor. Thanks for having me.

Joe： Yeah. Thanks, Keith.

item.description:
## 一、最出人意料的观察：Lightfield 的组织结构是其产品哲学的分形（Fractal）
Keith 反复强调的产品核心原则是「Intelligence > Schema」——不预定义数据结构，而是让智能在流动的活动日志中自己组织意义。真正惊人的是：**这家公司的内部结构是同一条哲学的镜像投射**。
- 数据层拒绝固定 schema → 组织层拒绝固定 swim lane（"everyone owns product and everyone owns customer success"） - 数据是流动的 activity log → 团队每天 standup 时重新 stack rank 优先级，"whoever's free just takes them" - 数据可以事后被 traverse 重新填充字段 → 项目可以被任何职能的人接手推进
这几乎是 Conway 定律的反向版本：通常是「组织结构决定产品架构」，Lightfield 的案例里，**产品的世界观反过来重塑了组织形态**。这也解释了为什么大多数试图模仿它的公司会失败——他们只抄了 schemales

item.title: [Invest Like The Best] Sequoia Legend Michael Moritz: Steve Jobs, Being an Outsider, and Investing in the Age of AI
item.dc:creator: Invest Like The Best
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

观察一：Moritz 的"外来者引擎"是一个精密的代际传承机制——但它传的不是故事，而是气压

最让我意外的是他明确说：父母从不讲大屠杀的故事。他直到坐下写书才知道细节。那么"幸存者本能"是怎么传下来的？

是通过大气压，不是通过叙事。

他反复用"atmospheric backdrop"（气氛底色）这个词。孩子吸收的不是"1938 年发生了什么"，而是父母在早餐桌上对一则空难新闻的反应速度、对陌生人的默认怀疑值、对"灾难永远就在拐角"的身体化确信。他母亲在 COVID 前几周去世，他真心感到"她被剥夺了这场她预言了一辈子的灾难"——这句话是黑色喜剧，也是密码：焦虑作为一种家族货币，需要被兑现才算完成传承。

这解释了一个反直觉现象：为什么显性讲述创伤的家庭反而常常传不下去创伤动能？因为叙事化 = 客体化 = 与自我分离。而 Moritz 家的做法相反——不讲，让它成为孩子的呼吸空气本身。这就是为什么他今天仍然"无法庆祝成功"、"总觉得未完成"——因为焦虑一旦被命名就会失效，而他的家族选择了不命名。

观察二：他对"敬畏"的拒绝，和他"没能成为自己"的自我诊断，是同一件事的一体两面

访谈里有两处看似无关的矛盾： - 他说他从不 in awe of anyone（因为看到人的缺陷太清楚） - 他说他没能成为真正的自己（太在意外部期待）

表面看，一个是"我看穿别人"，一个是"我被别人看穿"。但底层是同一个操作系统：过度精准的观察力对内外一视同仁。

这是一个跨领域连接——想想优秀的病理学家为什么常常是坏的乐观主义者。当你训练自己一眼看到组织切片里的癌变，你也看到自己婚姻里的癌变、朋友的癌变、自己作品的癌变。Moritz 是投资人里的病理学家：Don Valentine 把他扔进深水区，他学会了在每个 22 岁创始人身上看到"14 岁前的决定性瑕疵"。这种技能不能只对外使用。他对自己也是这样扫描的，所以永远看到"unfinished"。

有意思的推论：他称赞 Alex Ferguson 的核心不是战术，而是"他在球员最低谷时出现在机场"——这是一种故意不使用病理学扫描仪的能力。Moritz 敬佩 Ferguson，可能不是因为 Ferguson 会做的事，而是因为 Ferguson 会克制自己不去做的事。这是他自己一辈子没做到的克制。

观察三：他关于 AI 的乐观，其实是他祖父的赌博的翻版——只是这次他站在祖父那边

他讲了两个祖父： - 父系祖父：相信国家的耐久性，相信"风暴会过去"，靠养老金活着 → 死在集中营 - 母系祖父：不相信任何制度，靠 wits 活着 → 战争爆发前 72 小时逃出

访谈里 Moritz 反复强调"你永远需要一本额外的护照"——这明显是母系祖父的哲学。

但当谈到 AI 时，他突然切换了阵营。他说："核弹当年也预言了 Armageddon，但一个世纪过去了没发生""基因革命也曾预言优生怪物，也没发生"——这是父系祖父的论证结构：历史上大灾难的预言大多没兑现，所以这次也会过去。

这是一个惊人的心理配置：在政治上他是母系祖父（永远准备逃跑），在技术上他是父系祖父（相信秩序会自我修复）。

跨领域连接：这非常像加密社区里"永久悲观宏观 + 永久乐观技术"的双头人格——同一个大脑同时运行两套预测系统，因为它们分别在不同的历史创伤时间尺度上被训练过。Moritz 的政治悲观来自 1938，他的技术乐观来自 1945–1975（战后美国的技术奇迹）。他不是矛盾——他是被两段不同的历史同时抚养大的。

如果这个模型是对的，那么可以做一个大胆预测：当 AI 开始被明确用于国家层面的种族分类、监控、驱逐时（而不只是替代白领工作），Moritz 的立场会瞬间翻转到极度警觉——因为那时技术叙事和 1938 叙事将合流，母系祖父的操作系统会覆盖父系祖父的操作系统。他不会承认这是翻转，他会说"我一直这么想"。但触发点会非常清楚。

📝 转录文本

一、与 Steve Jobs 的破裂，以及"敬畏"的问题

The episode with Jobs and Time was so fascinating in your history and I'm sure frustrating for you.

You know, sadly as a result of that really never repaired the relationship with Steve.

Were you in awe of him?

No.

Have you ever been in awe of anyone?

You know, the people that I've known who have done incredible, remarkable things are also flawed individuals. And if you get to know them well, you also see that aspect of it. So seeing that up close makes it difficult to hold anybody in awe because you see the flaws as well as all of their accomplishments and virtues.

二、一个人从哪里结束，下一个人从哪里开始

When I was reading your book, one of the lines or the ideas that has really stuck with me ever since is where does one person end and the next person begin? And this deep dive that you took into the impact of one's history, family history, heritage on who a person is. I'm interested in this from so many angles — as a parent, as a person interested in history, as a person interested in genetics, nature versus nurture. If I were to sum up the book in that question, what is your answer to that? What did you come away thinking after this deep study of your own family's history?

One of the things that came out of the book, which I didn't really expect, was discovering who I am and why I became whatever it is that I've become. And that was an sort of unexpected gift of the writing. And it came from an exploration of my family's past, in particular my parents, and going back and excavating the deep memories of childhood and the sort of atmosphere in our home and in the general mileu in which I grew up. It helped me understand a lot about why I am who I am and react to certain things in the fashion that I do.

Because unwittingly obviously every parent leaves an imprint on a child, and I think that's obviously especially true during the formative years — whatever the formative years are. I'm no sort of child specialist or scientist, but those, you know, before you turn 12, 13, 14 years old, those imprints that you've absorbed in some manner, consciously or unconsciously, those remain with you. And both the angels and demons, I think, that you deal with for the rest of your life.

What were yours? So I'm so curious that you're performing on yourself the exercise that you're famous for doing with others that you invested in or hired — focusing on these first 14 years. What new understanding of yourself came out of this exercise?

Well, I grew up as you know, and as the book talks about, in this family of refugees from Nazi Germany and Wales. And refugees by definition are a minority. Jewish refugees in Wales during the 1960s and 1970s were a further minority.

And I think if you grow — although even if, you know, people look at me today and they think, oh here's this old white man, he's not a minority. And I can understand that, but it's how an individual feels rather than how other people might look at you.

My parents had gone through these — although they were never in the camps, they got out of Germany in the 1930s — and they were loathed to use the word "survivor" because they always felt the word survivor denoted somebody who actually had survived the camps. But they were refugees and in their own way had survived. And that motive to survive no matter what the odds were, even though the odds that I faced growing up weren't like my parents, I think the need to survive — and when you think about surviving, you're thinking about, to some extent, living by your wits, being very suspicious of the motives of others, wondering where and how bad things will occur and happen and guard against them — gave me, in retrospect (I didn't understand it at the time), a sort of drive and grit that I wouldn't have had without that particular atmospheric backdrop.

When you study it and you think about your own childhood, how did that transfer from your parents to you? Was it the stories they told?

It was definitely not the stories they told, because they didn't tell the stories. And I didn't really get to know the stories until I sat down and began work on this book. What I did know was the general arc of history obviously, and the world — this miserable, ferocious, catastrophic whirlwind in which they and millions of others were caught up. But they didn't talk about the past in the real detail that, much later when I was thinking about the book, I became interested in. It was just broad sweeps.

So I think it was much more the daily behavior, the reaction to events, the reaction to things, the sense that the doom was not very far away. And the fact that if horrors had occurred in the past, there was a real need to be vigilant and wary about navigating daily life.

三、两个祖父：留下的人与逃走的人

There was a couple stories in the book — one in particular where you talk about two separate people, one who decided to stay in Germany and one who decided to leave. It's quite a poignant and interesting on this topic of survivor, outsider, early instinct when things are changing to take notice and not double down and stick around. Maybe tell that story and explain what you learned from that.

Well, the two individuals, Patrick, that you referred to were my grandfathers — my maternal grandfather and my paternal grandfather.

I'll start with my paternal grandfather, who was a civil servant. He was a sort of lower level judge in the judiciary in Bavaria province in southern Germany. He had fought in World War I. He had somehow or other survived the horror of Verdun. He had been given his Iron Cross. And he was, I think, a great believer in the German state and in the security that the state offered. And then much later in 1933 he lost his job.

But somehow — I think because this is my assessment of the situation — because he was a civil servant, he was by nature conservative, by nature somewhat cautious, but also had this great belief in the state and the endurance of the state and the durability of the state, and that eventually the storm would blow over. And he also had a pension, and the pension was very important to him as a means for survival. So I think it was a combination of all of those things that he wasn't oblivious obviously to what was happening around him, but it did make him more reluctant to leave Germany until it was too late.

And people forget — even if somebody had decided to leave Germany, there are all sorts of obstacles in the way. You had to find a place elsewhere that would accept you. You had to pay big taxes to the Nazi government in order to be able to secure your exit visas. So there're all these sorts of obstacles. So that was my paternal grandfather. And he and his wife eventually were shipped off east and disappeared from history.

And my maternal grandfather was cut from a different cloth. I was too callow as a youth to really understand this, but I knew him. He died when I was about 16. He had been a cattle trader, which was one of the occupations that Jews were really permitted to do in Germany. But he was almost blind as a young man and completely blind by the time that I met him. But somehow or other had been able to carve out a comfortable living for himself and his family by trading in cattle in a rural village in northwestern Germany.

My assessment of him, again in retrospect, was that he was more street-wise. He was more entrepreneurial. He wasn't burdened by the need to remain and collect a state pension because he had always been able to sustain himself and look out for his future. And he got out with his wife, my grandmother, but they got out by the skin of their teeth. They got out 72 hours before war broke out. So 72 hours later, they too would have perished.
