item.title: [Sequoia Capital] Box's Aaron Levie: On Reinventing Yourself in the AI Age and Enterprise Diffusion
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正的护城河不是模型，而是"权限拓扑学"

Levie 抛出一个看似普通的观察，却隐藏着一个惊人的悖论：当研究员想象"个性化模型"时，他们下意识地假设自己就是用户——一个拥有全域访问权限的人。但真实世界里，一个律师的知识边界是由他今天早上被加入/移除的项目组决定的。

这里有个反直觉的洞察：企业级 AI 的最大瓶颈不是智能，而是"访问控制的动态拓扑"。每一秒钟，组织内数以万计的权限关系在重构——某人被加入一个诉讼、某个文档被移入法律保留、某个客户关系需要"中国墙"隔离。这意味着，未来最有价值的不是"更聪明的模型"，而是"能在毫秒级理解组织权限动态的中间层"。

这也解释了为什么 Levie 说"研究员想让模型跟他们一样"——因为研究员活在一个低摩擦的权限世界里，而企业活在一个权限每秒都在变化的动态图谱里。这种认知落差，就是 Neolab（应用层新贵）的全部机会。

二、"Work Slop" 的真相：这不是内容危机，而是"信任协议"的重写

大家在讨论 AI 生成内容时聚焦"质量"，但 Levie 揭示了一个更深刻的层面——当我们看到别人的 PPT 时，我们其实一直在做一件被 AI 打破的事：把内容当作"这个人能力和思考深度"的代理指标（proxy）。

跨领域连接来了：这与经济学中的"信号理论"（Signaling Theory，Michael Spence 提出）完全同构。Spence 说文凭之所以有价值，不是知识本身，而是"完成文凭"这个行为向雇主发送了"我能坚持"的信号。而 PPT、备忘录、邮件长期以来都是"我思考过、我理解、我投入了时间"的信号。

AI 生成内容摧毁的不是"内容"，而是这套人类花了几个世纪演化出来的隐性信号系统。所以我们不是在讨厌 slop，我们是在哀悼一个刚刚失效的信任协议。未来 3-5 年，社会必须重建一套新的信号系统——可能是"你对 AI 输出的编辑轨迹"、"你的提问深度"、或者干脆是"你的现场反应能力"。

会议里那种"当场被问倒"的尴尬会重新变得神圣。

三、隐藏在对话表面下的分形结构：Levie 的整个策略其实是一个"托尔布思-反托尔布思"博弈

表面上 Levie 在夸赞"Cloudforce"营销，讥笑"toll booth（收费站）"这个词。但如果你把整个访谈作为一个系统看，会发现一个惊人的分形自相似：

  • 模型层：Anthropic/OpenAI 试图向下延伸做应用 = 收费站扩张
  • 应用层（Box）：想抓住模型不愿做的"工作流桥梁" = 反收费站
  • 企业内部：CIO 想要用开源模型摆脱模型商锁定 = 反收费站
  • UI 层：横向 chatbot vs 垂直 agent = 收费站 vs 定制路径
  • 知识工作者：AI 让人试图"直接输出结果"跳过流程 = 但组织权限体系是最终的收费站

每一层都在重复同样的博弈：抽象层的通用性与场景层的特殊性之间的张力。

这与生物学中"红皇后假说"（Van Valen）惊人地相似——所有物种都必须持续演化才能保持相对位置。Levie 真正的战略洞察是：在 AI 时代，"离客户更近"不是一个位置，而是一种永动状态。谁能持续在"通用能力"和"特殊场景"之间找到新缝隙，谁就能吃到 diffusion 带来的红利。

四、一个让人意外的元观察：Twitter 悖论

Levie 提到"关注 20 个账号能让你的职业领先/落后一年"——但真正意外的洞察藏在他说"最遗憾的是脑细胞"那句自嘲背后：

Twitter 现在是全球唯一没有 AI 中介、由原始个体判断构成的实时精英信息网络。所有其他信息渠道（新闻、报告、搜索）都已经被 AI 摘要、聚合、过滤过一遍。这意味着在 AI 时代，最稀缺的资源是"未经算法压平的、活生生的高质量个人判断流"——这恰好是 Twitter 在娱乐化后依然保留的核心资产。

结论反直觉：AI 越发达，Twitter 这种"低算法密度的社交网络"反而越有战略价值。它成了 AI 时代的"人类判断黑市"。

📝 转录文本

开场：Twitter 与信息代际差

I want to send an emergency alert to like everybody who's like a sophomore or junior in college and just be like: follow these 20 accounts on Twitter, and also join Twitter, because like this will just help your career.

You're either like a year ahead or a year behind simply based on your feed, and my feed is like so, so wired in. I'll still talk to 20-year-olds that are like, "Yeah, like you know, I see some articles," and I'm like, "What do you mean? How do you see articles? Like I don't even know what that means. Do you just like get lucky that somebody emailed you an article?"

You just have to be wired in. I enjoy it. It's a lot of fun. I play with everything.

[music]

引入嘉宾

Today I'm excited to welcome Aaron Levie, founder and CEO of Box. Box is building a collaboration platform and content management platform for the enterprise that has now taken on really new life with AI. And I'm excited to chat with you today about Box and AI, about your general thoughts on AI — because you are such a thought leader — and about how founders can reinvent themselves for this AI wave. So, thanks for joining us.

Aaron: Thanks for having me. I'm a big fan of the podcast. I religiously watch every episode, so great work. I am wondering though — I know this is a different podcast — but when do you talk about root canals in this?

Oh my gosh. Is that — have we call in Doug Leone? Have we figured out how to weave that in yet or not?

Aaron: I mean, I'm happy to talk about different kinds of pain and suffering that I've been through.

We should just do this pod with a live root canal. Let's do it and see how it goes. Actually — it would be like Hot Ones, but you get a root canal and you have to talk about your strategy while you're in a dentist chair, and Doug is just on the other end of it.

Aaron: Amazing. Doug is so pleased with himself right now.

Has he seen every tweet?

Aaron: Oh, yeah. Very pleased with himself.

一、Application Companies 就是新一代的 Neolabs 吗？

Okay, let's start with — I'm curious your take on this: application companies are the hottest neolabs. Agree or disagree?

Aaron: Two years ago, I think it would have not made that much sense — like, what does that mean? But very clearly, I think this is what's playing out in the market, and it's all working out mostly because of open source.

What's pretty amazing is right now the whole concept of being an LLM wrapper or model wrapper is actually working out, because what people underappreciated was that in the real world, in the enterprise, what you need is some bridge from the model's capability to the actual workflow that the enterprise has.

And that bridge — basically a trillion dollars has been bet on one of two outcomes: either that bridge is very limited, or that bridge is actually very vast and needs to be able to take on a lot of depth within organizations.

That bet basically looks like: are you only long the model itself and super intelligence, or are you long this application tier — you know, maybe previously would have been just pure neolab? But it's very clearly playing out that there's a lot of gap between the model and the workflow. And as you bridge that gap over time, you get to a point where you realize, "Oh, I should also do the model" — and then you have enough data, enough domain expertise, where that becomes its own flywheel.

So I'm very bullish on this idea. And what's cool is it's opening up multiple layers of opportunity for startups. You could either be the actual applied company itself — i.e., the neolab — or you could be the infrastructure provider to the neolab. You have multiple layers of going and attacking that space. A huge update for the market and everybody's view of it.

Box Labs

Box Labs — let's go.

Aaron: We already have it. It's a little bit secret, but we pay very close attention right now. The main focus is: let's make the agent really, really good on any model. But over time, obviously, you would peel off certain use cases either on a per-customer basis or across the whole data set.

Yeah, it seems like there's two forces happening. One is: people don't want the fox to be guarding the hen house. They don't want the seller of the token to be the one that is also metering and gating what is the best token for each use case. And then the second is, there's actually a lot of work to do on that bridge to cross, and there's real research involved in it. And it's pretty bespoke to the exact workflow and the exact end customer that you have.

Aaron: What I tend to see happen in the Valley — for very good reason, and it's actually why these companies have been so successful — is that everybody is so research-pilled. Which is totally awesome, big fan, it leads to all these breakthroughs. But the sense that "okay, the model and the intelligence in the model is the only form factor that matters" — then you go to the real world and see how intelligence actually gets rolled out in people's workflows, and the model could be the most intelligent super intelligence in the world, but that workflow still requires you to connect up to other data systems, still requires these moments where there's a human-in-the-loop interaction, there's delays in the workflow so the agent has to sit idle, there's change management of the actual business process, there's legacy systems that haven't been modernized.

So you kind of go through these five or ten things that are way more operational, much more blocking and tackling than just the pure super intelligence of the model. And the last thing that a classic research organization wants to go do is go attack every single one of those things.

历史类比：AWS → Snowflake / Databricks

This is not a one-off in history. We've always had this relationship between infrastructure and application. Obviously AWS or GCP or Azure have created trillions of dollars in market cap of infrastructure — but guess what, there's also trillions of dollars of value in software that only exists because of that infrastructure.

If you were to go back 10 years ago and look at what early versions of GCP or AWS were building, I guarantee you would not have predicted Snowflake or Databricks existing. You would have been like, "The infrastructure already does that — why would you pay another $10 billion of revenue to all these other products that are just making it so you can work with your data?"

The same thing is going to be true for intelligence: the models will be insanely valuable, but the application of bringing those models into real workflows in banking and life sciences and healthcare and government — that's just going to be a lot of software.

Now the challenge for the next two to five years is: how much do the model providers need to move up that stack and try and compete at that layer, or do they either leave open — intentionally or accidentally — that entire space for the application ecosystem? To some extent this is a big strategic question for them: on one hand, you want to be closer to the customer; on the other hand, you also want to have an ecosystem so people trust you. So that's going to be a really interesting tension over the coming years.

二、模型层与应用层之间的博弈

How do you think that'll play out? I feel like that's the question we spend every day wrestling with.

Aaron: I don't want to speak for Sequoia, but you can sense some of the existential dread of a VC right now — like, should I just put another billion dollars into Anthropic, or should I attempt to see what at the applied layer is going to play out?

Nobody's that envious of your guys' position having to figure that out. But obviously, it's even harder for the entrepreneur.

I'm pretty long, obviously, the application layer. I'm also equally very biased — I have a very concentrated bet with very limited diversification on it working out that you still want to buy technology that understands your workflow and can get to the core enterprise data.

But I just don't see a different event happening than all of history. We only have like 50 or 60 years of computer software history. But basically, when you go to that law firm, to that pharma company, to that bank, they need something that bridges the core technology to their workflow and their business process. And AI has not meaningfully changed the need or the shape of what that looks like.

Chatbot vs. Agentic Workflow

The best manifestation of this is this chatbot versus agentic workflow demarcation. The chatbot can be totally universal and totally horizontal, but all of a sudden you look at that and say, "Well, my workflow needs something to ping me at the right time in the process, or it needs access to a certain kind of data that the chatbot can't natively get access to. So somebody has to go into that organization, get it set up, and provide domain expertise to this model so it really understands our particular business process."

Unless you really just underwrite the big labs at — honestly, I'm not exaggerating — like 100,000 employees, if you don't underwrite that, then the diffusion economy is going to be massive. Because every single one of those companies, whether that's a 50-person firm or certainly a multi-thousand person firm, is going to need an army of people to go in and help them with that transformation, that change management. Whether it's the FTE phenomenon or just understanding that domain expertise — that's going to be a very big deal.

Fox Guarding the Hen House

Then you alluded to this point — "fox guarding the hen house." That might actually be singularly the biggest reason this has to happen. Even under complete benevolence, nobody's actually doing something in any sneaky way — it just stands to reason that if I'm going to give a task to an agentic system, I just want that task to be cost-optimized, with accuracy holding constant.

And so, who can do that? It's the company that doesn't care among 10 different models which model is performing that task. Definitionally, you would want that to be the company that does not have a preference.

补贴的经济学

And then the force you have going against that is that the model companies can subsidize their models or offer them at different rates.

Aaron: I don't know how long that lasts, though. When these companies become public, I think they'll be held to basically the same laws of capitalism that everybody else is. So the subsidization is working very well up to a certain threshold of spend, and we might have exceeded that spend when you're at tens of billions of dollars of capital. In fact, if anything, it might even be worse — because eventually you have to go in and pay for your training runs as well. The subsidization of tokens has to be a temporary phenomenon.

You mean from a gross margin perspective, or from like an antitrust perspective?

Aaron: Entirely gross margin.

But they have such high gross margins on inference right now.

Aaron: But then, what are they subsidizing? Then they're charging actually decent rates.

Yeah, but they can afford to price the API higher than their own first-party products, right?

Aaron: So that part — totally fair. There's an interesting dimension: if API is the high-margin thing that is paying for the subsidization, but you've moved all your customers over to the applied product and there's no API revenue — there is an equilibrium you have to strike with this.

Totally.

Aaron: And all the while, if you have some sort of either non-economic actors or people just with a totally different game theory in this — Meta being one, maybe SpaceX being one, China certainly being a giant one, even Nvidia being one — that changes the calculus. Those four cohorts don't necessarily need to make money on inference at the same margin structure that Anthropic or OpenAI needs. They might be fine to bring down inference to 10% margin because they just want to pay for massive compute clusters.

As long as that happens, and as long as there's not insane proprietary closely-held secrets, then no matter what you're going to have cost per token go down on a for-like basis. All of which means more value accrues to the application layer.

Which is a very long-winded way of saying: I think there's just value in kind of everybody in the stack. I just don't know that one or two labs get 95% of the value creation. I think it's going to be a much more dynamic environment. And honestly, if I were one of the two or three biggest labs, I'd prefer this outcome too — because back to your antitrust point, at some point you'll just be nationalized if you're the only thing that exists as intelligence. So you want a little bit of healthy competition in this ecosystem anyway.

Yep. Totally.

三、Box 的历史与 AI 转型

Let's transition to talking about Box. I'm going to come back to talking about tokens and Jevons paradox and China and all this stuff, but let's talk about Box for a second.

Aaron: I love that topic too.

Give folks — I'm guessing a lot of people that listen to this podcast use Box — but give people a brief explanation of the history of Box and how you're reinventing yourself with AI.

Aaron: We started the company as a way to be able to securely store and share data in the cloud. It was a very simple idea, but we cracked a nut or struck a nerve. For Doug out there — we were able to scale up quickly. We pivoted rapidly in the enterprise.

The idea was: enterprises would be moving from on-premises systems to the cloud, and they would need a better way to store, share, collaborate, and manage all of this unstructured data — their corporate documents, financial documents, marketing assets, research materials — in the cloud securely.

第一次 AI 冬天 (2015–2018)

We had been flirting with AI products and experiences really since 2015. If you remember, the first rise of — at least in modern times — the AI winter happened in like the 2015 to 2018 period. Which is like, we think it's going to happen now, and then it didn't.

That was a period where these very early AI models were showing us signs: okay, if you looked at an image and you could classify the image, well, that's pretty useful if you're in an enterprise — because now maybe you take all of your image data and label it, or maybe you'd OCR something and pull out the text. That's enormously helpful.

The problem was: insanely expensive, and you had to have a model for every single use case — required a hyper-trained model for each workflow. So we shelved it.

ChatGPT 时刻

Few years later, started paying attention to the GPTs. We had some hackathons where people were like, "Oh, we could do type-ahead in one of our note-taking products." Those were early versions. We did some early work in text detection and classification which helped with security use cases.

Then obviously ChatGPT moment hits, and that was the big head-exploding moment. If for no other reason than they figured out a form factor that opened up everybody's mind to: oh, these could be interactive systems that you just ask a question, get an answer back, of increasing complexity and length.

We looked at that very quickly, jumped all in. We did the whole company pivot — like everything was exactly academically what you should do. We had a team carved out, we put the best people on the team, we met every day, looked at the updates, and slowly but surely built out what today is our AI stack and basically the Box Agent.

Box 的核心用例

For us, the use case is very straightforward. We sit on hundreds of billions of files. Every single one of those files contains critical information for an enterprise — contracts, research files, marketing assets, loan documents.

The problem is they rarely know what's actually inside of it. Unless you literally look at the document and search and find it, you just don't know what's inside.

So now agents can go and basically be farmed out to answer questions about that data. They can pre-process it and extract metadata from those documents and turn it into structured data. You can use agents to automate steps and workflows. So we've built a platform that basically lets you deploy agents against all of that unstructured data.

内容生成

Are you using agents to create new content?

Aaron: We are. There's a couple modalities where that shows up. One is we have an online collaborative product that an agent can just generate any amount of content in. We've done most of the exciting work with OpenAI and Anthropic on advanced document creation, PowerPoint creation. We've decided that their tech at this point can always be frontier — so we have an agent that goes and interacts with those systems to produce a high-quality PowerPoint, etc.

四、"Unleash Your Content" — Hero Use Cases

Your tagline: "Your business lives in content, unleash it with AI." What are the hero home run use cases for how people are unleashing it today? And if you had to fast forward a few years, what do you think people will be doing with AI in your products?

Aaron: Probably the easiest hero for a traditional enterprise: you have a million contracts — why don't you find out what's inside them? Or you have a million research documents — be able to pull out all of the critical structured data, put that into a database, and then query, analyze, automate workflows around that.

That's the thing that just knocks it out of the park every single time, because it's been a long-standing problem that people have never been able to apply human labor to — it's just too expensive to read every contract, every research document. Maybe you could do it if you had a loan document process, but most other data just never gets read at that scale.

长时间运行的 Agent 工作流

The stuff we're probably as much if not more excited by is the equivalent of what we see with coding agents or other complex agents — where you have long-running agents that are just executing your entire workflow or process.

This would be in the form of: you go to a bank, you're onboarding at a bank, and they've basically automated every step that is possible to automate, and then jumps out to a person in the steps in the process for extra review or verification. But instead of that one or two week back-and-forth, it just happens in like an hour.

That's the dream state of most of these enterprise workflows: What if we could onboard a client faster? What if we could discover critical data inside of our research much more quickly? What if we could alert to a security event much more quickly?

To do that, you need these background agents or workflows that are pre-established for those processes.

Totally. It's the year of the long-running agent.

Aaron: It is. Yeah.

五、代码 vs. 内容：为什么 AI 在编程被接受，在写作却被抵制？

I'm curious — you made the analogy to Claude Code. It seems to me that in the coding domain, using AI is not only accepted, it's embraced. In the content domain — which is where a lot of the content in Box sits — using AI to produce content, there's almost this allergic reaction to it. All the pangram stuff on Twitter, this concept of "work slop." I'm curious what you think about work slop, and will this still be a thing in a few years?

Aaron: I'm going to separate the Box corporate hat and just riff as a consumer of — gosh, I wish there was a better term — but "work slop," as you know, inside of an enterprise context.

I get board decks that are entirely written by AI these days, and it kills me.

Aaron: Here's the difference on the acceptability. There's probably more symbolism to this topic than just the slop element. The diffusion of AI in general almost ties to this: code — other than the top engineers we hang out with that have deep taste in the code, where the judgment is incredible and it is as much an art as a science — take that group aside. For most of the world, code is a utility. It's just trying to accomplish something, automate something, put an interface up so somebody presses a button and moves to the next step.

For most of the world, the value creation of code has been to automate things and have it as a utility. So at the end of the day, we'll probably still use the term "slop" for a while, because there's taste in front-end design and in systems, and you don't want vulnerabilities in your code. But if you can tell an agent, "Please go and generate my entire back-end system or my front-end system" — it's not only acceptable, it's preferable. That was the thing that was blocking us from moving forward.

内容作为"信号"

At least the way society functions and the way our brains work at the moment — maybe this changes — when you get a presentation from somebody, there's still this association: I'm trying to decide if I can trust that person to execute on that thing, deliver that result, or understand that topic.

When you see work slop, you're like, "I'm losing my ability to know for a fact how much of the thought process was them versus how much was the AI. How much should I even care about that, because I myself am doing the same thing?"

So we have this weird collective issue: I'm doing work slop for some of my brainstorms and decisions, but when I get it from somebody else, I'm like, "Hmm, should I trust you?"

I don't know — it might be a thing that as a society we have to keep cranking through over the next three to five years and end up at the other side. Obviously, you don't care when you see somebody's financial model — "Yeah, that was generated clearly by a macro, you did not personally compute all of that, but you're showing it to me and we're talking about it." So why can't the same exist for a strategy deck?

Right now we're going through this evolution: What is the person's role? What is the content a proxy for? Is it a proxy for how much that person knows? Is it a proxy for what we think they can execute on? We're in this very messy period.

六、Harnesses（工具编排层）

Let's talk about harnesses. How does the Box —

Aaron: Great transition to harnesses.

Speaking of calculators, let's talk about harnesses.

Aaron: This is back to the neolab / applied layer. There's a bunch of things we know about our file system, permission structures, our search engine that — by all means, we would love all the labs to train on our understanding of this because it would only make external agents as good as possible. We always talk to labs, "Hey, we'll give you as much data as you want about how the system works."

But let's just say that aside — we have a lot of depth of understanding of: what do people do in Box? How do they search Box? How do they decide, when they look through 10 files, which is the one to pick? What is their internal calculus or heuristic on figuring out the most relevant document to look at?

We know all of that, and we've built an agentic harness that attempts to understand that set of domain understanding about our system. It has access to our search system, our file system, a bunch of mechanisms for pulling out just the text of a document, just pulling out chunks, doing embeddings on the fly.

Effectively, it's a harness for asking questions of a large data set. In my Box account I have — I don't even know the latest number — but on the order of tens of millions of files. It's like everything that has ever accumulated over 20 years. But I can now ask any question of all that data set using the Box Agent. It does multiple searches in one, re-ranks it, quickly pulls out the most relevant information, and in some cases reads the full document.

We compare that against: well, what if we just gave Claude our API, or gave OpenAI our API? And we see meaningfully better results on accuracy and latency, because we know exactly how to tune it for our workflows.

Evals

What evals matter the most to you?

Aaron: I have a couple funny personal ones I keep track of, of my own use cases. But we have hundreds of different tests we do on every single model. We actually have two evals at the moment:

  1. Complex Work Eval — a set of domain-specific work in life sciences, financial services, public sector, tech, etc. Given these five documents and this set of problems, what would your answers be? We test every single model against those with our agent.

  2. Holdback Eval — our Box instance and how Box employees use their data. Then we eval every model again on that.

We keep track of all incremental progress — we see when things move by half a point in terms of model improvement. Then we roll out default models based on different cost and accuracy thresholds. And we let customers choose any model they want from effectively our model garden.

模型比赛：Race Perspective

What's your current view of the race — where all the horses are in terms of model performance on your use case?

Aaron: They more or less closely correlate to code, with one exception: in some of our use cases, Gemini is disproportionately better than what you'd see from coding. It might be better tool use — given the Gemini ecosystem and what they need to build for. It solves a strong set of general knowledge work use cases as well.

But mostly correlating to code. So Fable 5.1 was clearly state-of-the-art and the best model we've seen. There's obviously rumors about other models, so we'll see how the race continues. When you look at GDPval, Mercor has their APEX eval — these will all generally follow the coding models. It's neck-and-neck on Grok, Muse, the Fable class, GPT-5.6, whatever they're building next. It's a total race right now.

客户选择

Do your customers typically express a preference on which model, or do they just use your default?

Aaron: By volume they use our default, because it's easy and works extremely well. But by volume of tokens, most goes through our workflow agents or data extraction. That's where customers actually do evals — saying, "Okay, I want to really make sure that at this cost profile I can get 98% accuracy on data extraction." That's a place where we have an FTE that goes in and helps understand your data environment, tests against five different models, and then you're basically at the mercy of the eval.

七、开源模型的采用

What are you seeing in terms of the adoption of open-weight models in your customer base?

Aaron: Higher than people think, lower than what enterprises actually want, and much, much, much, much lower than what it'll be in five years. Some mix of that would be the message.

Is it primarily cost driving that decision?

Aaron: I have to probably attribute 30-plus percent to just the sexiness of "I want to try GLM."

Yeah, I've heard CIOs of Fortune 500 companies say, "We're playing with open source here" — and I look at that and I'm like, well, Gemini or Muse would have been just fine at that particular cost profile you're trying to do. Or probably even 5.6 Luna, or Terra, or whichever had the crazy discounting they just did — it probably would have been totally fine. But you want to be able to be like, "Okay, I'm a little hedged." It's cool — we're at that phase still.

Over time, it stands to reason you'll see meaningful different costs, because you'll be able to peel off workloads that only make sense at grinding down to the cost of inference — in which case open weights will have the economic advantage.

Right now there's this challenge — sometimes it's more token-inefficient, sometimes randomly (I've heard stories) it'll just speak Chinese mid-chain, so you're like, "Okay, well, that'll be weird for a bank." So funny. We need to work on some of those things. But long-term, you're going to peel off those workloads.

Decagon 的悖论

One of the more interesting posts on this that I totally subscribe to is Jesse at Decagon. Did you read that post about this paradox — we're going to see closed just continue to go exponential, but what's going to happen is each use case that matures you can peel off to open source. Once you have stability in that use case, it starts to make sense to veer it toward an open-weights model, assuming one of two things is true: (1) it's actually literally cheaper, or (2) having some post-training gets you X% more performance.

You will be in a reality where — this is going to be very confusing probably for the press more than people in the Valley — the revenue of Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. are off the charts, but somehow open weights is also growing exponentially. You're like, "How is Open Router so fast? The pie is growing so fast."

There's an interesting duality — not even just "rising tide lifts all boats." It's: no, we either use Fable or 5.6 for orchestration and then farm out all these long-tail tasks to a cheaper model. Or the opposite: you have an orchestration agent that by default does the cheaper stuff, but occasionally sees something too hard and pops it out to one of these heavier models. You might have blended 50% spend on each, but 10 times the amount of tokens on the open-weights model. Everybody's winning, but there's an interplay between why they're winning.

If I listen to my friends at the labs, like continual learning — this idea that the model's weights should adapt as it gets to know you.

We had Engram on the podcast. I don't know if you know Dan —

Aaron: I just got introduced to him. I listened to the podcast. I would have loved to have been the fourth person in the room.

They're working with customers to help bake in some of the context into the weights themselves. What direction do you think this is going to go?

Aaron: You're catching me at a time right before I'm actually doing my call with Dan, so I wish I could have talked to him first and then I'd have a way more eloquent answer.

I'm extremely fascinated by the approach. I have no reason for not wanting it to work and exist. We live in a world at Box where we see the high degree of complexity on permissions and access controls and data that tends to be the rub on a lot of these types of approaches.

权限的复杂性

I'm going to put Engram aside — I'm sure they've thought this through — so I'll talk more generic philosophically.

Sometimes you talk to a researcher who imagines the world working the way they work: "I'm a researcher, I have access to everything, and if I had a model that was trained just on my world, this would be amazing."

And then you're like, "Let me introduce you to a lawyer." The lawyer has this tiny little access point of just the five projects they're working on, because somebody one door over is working on the competitive project to another company in the space that they can't have any overlap with. There can't be a single document that passes between those two walls — they have to be hard barriers.

Sure, you could still train a model just for that one user, but what happens if every single day they get added or removed from something that adds important context to what they need to understand?

I think there will probably be breakthroughs in continual learning that resolve this. This is why previously it was just — there was no way you could pull this off 5 years ago because it would be insanely expensive, impossible to wrap your head around how those access controls are supposed to work. But obviously, as the cost curve goes down, as open weights get cheaper, smaller, faster, better, this becomes super interesting.

什么进 Context vs. 什么进 Weights？

You have to be a little thoughtful about where the massive performance gain by baking in the weights is. There's probably some incredible calculation of when the rate of change of the data is not so fast, but the upside of the weights dramatically changes the accuracy of the model — you'd have to land on some rubric like that.

If you could wave a magic wand, it almost seems like — I think Karpathy has said this in some prior interviews — if you could almost remove all the memorized information from the models and just have it encapsulate the specific reasoning capabilities, like the ethos of how we do things at Sequoia, and then you have all the actual content in a lookup system. That almost feels like, if you could wave a magic wand, what the system would look like.

Aaron: That's super interesting. The question will be: how much are enterprises different at that level, versus is it actually their literal IP that is what makes them different? How many different types of styles of execution are there in the world, versus, "No, it's just the depth of knowledge about that particular legal case and how I apply it to this other project I'm working on" — that's where so much of the value sits.

Wait till my Zoom call with Dan, and then I'll really know the answer. But I'm a fan — because no matter what, at a firm level, there's probably ways to take this approach.

I'm a big fan of what Trajectory or Applied Compute doing, or Prime Intellect — because there's no question that if you're Eli Lilly, you want a model for how you do drug discovery, and that probably does need to go farther, deeper, or more specific than what you're getting off the shelf. There's not a lot of church-and-state problems for drug discovery workflows — they probably want as much information available to as many people as possible.

九、Box Labs 的研究领域

You hinted at the beginning that there's a Box Labs. What type of work is Box Labs doing?

Aaron: It's the equivalent of Box Labs — I don't know if we've used capital L yet — but basically it's our applied AI team.

What research areas are most interesting to your team right now?

Aaron: The biggest areas — of the continuum of engineers, there's some cluster that's more on the research bent. Of that cluster, the things we spend time on are still at the applied layer, but a lot around: how do you take agents and make them another 10 points of accuracy improvement given X problem? How do you build a map of the problem set with a given set of data to best execute on that task?

We spend a lot of time on that style of work. We have a team working on how you do effectively, at the agent level, at the harness level, some form of auto-research on hill-climbing on accuracy of answering questions or sets of problems given a set of client data.

If you're a bank, you have a bunch of loan documents coming in — these are 100-page documents — whether you're getting 70% accuracy with an off-the-shelf model or 97% is obviously a world of difference in whether you can actually automate that process. Somehow you have to hill-climb from the base model to the 97%, and there's a lot of work going into the system to pull that off.

两件必须做的事

If you're in our contemporary group — you built a SaaS platform and have some set of data and workflow your customers operate in — there's effectively two things you just have to do. Anybody attempting to do one over the other is going to lose:

1. Build an agent that is insanely great at your product. That agent has to be provably 10 or 20 points better than an off-the-shelf agent at using your system — not because it's hobbled the other side, but you're so eval-maxed and tuned to your particular workflow that you can improve your system.

You probably, because you understand your domain (unless you're totally asleep at the wheel), have use cases that no one has thought to build products around, because you talk to customers every day and see what they run into. You're like, "Oh, we could just have our agent go do that for you."

I've had at least a dozen — I probably talk to a couple hundred customers a year in variety capacities — at least two dozen times where the customer has a use case that is a breakthrough moment for me.

Example?

Aaron: Unfortunately, since you put me on the spot, I don't know if my example will pay off the level of excitement I just had. But — a customer had this idea of wanting an agent in the background trying to figure out when documents met their governance policies. Like, does something need to go into some archive, or into some legal hold?

Oh, cool.

Aaron: See — exactly, that was exactly the voice I was worried about. No, no — I meant cool sincerely.

Aaron: Okay, I believe you. Listen, you do enterprise, so I think it was at least half-serious.

Imagine you're an enterprise. You have a head of compliance and head of governance. They can only be overseeing the whole enterprise — they've never been able to be everywhere at once. Now imagine they could sit next to the employee and basically say, "Oh, you're about to go do something that breaks our governance policy." What if there was an ongoing agent that automatically was just like, "Nah, that's going to break your governance policy"? Instead of the user having to predict or understand this stuff.

If you have an agent within your product, you're going to identify sooner and better than the rest of the market — and do things that maybe would be impossible to do off-platform.

2. Go headless. You literally have to make sure your APIs are exposed to Claude, ChatGPT, and all the different platforms. Either a direct way into deterministic APIs so those agents can use your APIs to make calls via MCP or whatever, or at least make your agent be headless and be exposed in those systems.

The only reason maybe this is a hard debate is you have to make sure as a system of record that you can find a way where commercially it makes sense on the other side and is valuable and interesting.

为什么很多人错了

The reason a lot of people got that wrong, that weren't in these companies, was underestimating the amount of new use cases that are total upside — complete whitespace opportunities for these systems of record.

If you're solving real problems for customers, it'll just make money. This is so cheesy, but I've told LinkedIn product managers I'd probably pay 10x more for LinkedIn if I could just MCP into it. 十一、产品 UI 的未来

Super interesting. Maybe related — let's talk about product UI. Big generic chatbot / chat box agent — is that going to be the dominant UI for how people are using AI in the future, especially at the application layer?

Aaron: This is why I think the applied layer has so much room to run. The universal chat system that you ask a question, get an answer back, or it does work in the background — obviously that's going to be a mainstay. That UI will always exist. The horizontal products will have it, the vertical products will have it, everybody will have it. Just like your product has a search box — obviously it does.

That's always going to be here for one-off asks of an agent, or go find this thing, or answer this question, or produce something for me on demand.

But most of the enterprise is made up of processes and workflows that are just happening behind the scenes. Sometimes with computers running things, sometimes with other people, sometimes they should be happening with people but you could never afford to have them happen with people so they just didn't happen.

That's a slightly different metaphor than a chatbot. I want agents in the background to do things for me — read every contract, look at every log, triage every security incident. Instead of me chatting, maybe I'll chat as a means of doing catch-up. I want a dashboard. I want a workflow. I want a queue. I want a task list.

横向 vs. 垂直

The challenge becomes: does the horizontal product take on every one of those components and manifest every one of those experiences? In which case, you'll start to be like, "Man, that thing is really heavy — this is no longer this simple, easy, delightful thing anymore."

Then the vertical players actually understand the process and can manifest all the right buttons and tabs and the names of the things for that particular workflow.

As you have agents doing more work in the background, more async work, that leans more toward the applied companies that can understand those workflows and processes.

You'll have these in every field. Certainly, we already know how they're going to look in legal with Harvey, Lor, etc. We're seeing them start to emerge in security. We've seen them emerge in the long-running coding agents with Cognition and Factory.

Ultimately, in five years from now, I would bet 90% of all tokens in the enterprise are things that a user never kicked off, and they just see a result. They see a task show up and they have to review it — it's just happening.

十二、AI Diffusion 与代码之外的世界

Let's talk about AI diffusion. Coding agents — it was like, boom, January 1st 2026 happened, and the fastest diffusion of anything into the economy we've ever seen has happened. The diffusion of the rest of the AI magic into the rest of our jobs seems like it's been a lot slower. What are your thoughts, and where do you think we're going to see faster diffusion?

Aaron: You always have to compare and contrast coding versus everything else to really understand the dissimilarity.

为什么编程如此适合 AI

In coding — and this is back to the utility point on slop — the utility of code is almost 100% represented by the amount of text you can generate. Obviously an insane amount of value went into the text — knowledge, expertise, meetings, everything — but ultimately the text is the thing that produces the program that is actually the thing you're trying to do.

If you had the world's greatest programmer, and they never had to sleep, never had to eat, they could intuit what to build and just sit on a computer all day long — your value creation would be 100% correlated with how many hours they could sit at that computer and type code. Lines of code — ideally, good code — is the thing most correlated to whether you produced software that people wanted.

So it's all text. The models are hyper-trained on these. Everybody in AI labs treats coding as a competitive benchmark to constantly try and exceed. They get to do their own evals on it every single day because they are the ones coding the models themselves.

It's the most technical audience of all time. When they deploy an agentic system and run into a bug or a problem — like some MCP server comes back with "connection invalid" — they fix it. They know how to triage the problem. They don't call IT. They just, "Oh yeah, no, I didn't open up that port. Sorry, I'll go fix it."

So that's like five things. And maybe the sixth — it's a very high-paying vertical. It's automatically valuable if you could get 10% or 20% productivity gain, let alone 5x productivity gain.

与其他领域对比：法律 vs. 销售

Take those five or six things that coding has as beneficial properties to automation, then compare that to every other form of knowledge work. You'd probably have a histogram — I don't know if anybody's published this, maybe you can — of similarity to coding, and what are the domains that start to look less and less like coding as you scale out.

Legal is kind of interesting, because there's a lot of value creation to somebody sitting at a computer reviewing legal documents, writing legal documents, processing large amounts of information. Okay, so that's blowing up.

Then you go down the list. Let's take something like a sales rep. So much farther down the list in terms of likeness. The sales rep's value creation is basically convincing an external customer to buy software or technology, or a Caterpillar truck, from them.

Let's say we brought the world's best automation to them. First of all, they'd have to figure out how to technically wire it up. They'd have to make sure they give it all their data. But no matter what, they're rate-limited and constrained by: Did the customer respond to them? Do they want to meet? Can they meet next Tuesday, or can they meet today? Does the customer have budget?

That's maybe the entire continuum right there — of knowledge work (this isn't even touching working with Adam). One end: somebody rate-limited by so many external factors. The other end: somebody who could sit at a computer all day long and just type text. That's your ability to basically automate things.

GitHub 与数据可访问性

For the real world, we have to bring intelligence to these workflows in ways that somewhat feel like the shape of their workflow, somewhat feel like the shape of their work, and then find a way to deliver the change management, deliver the implementation, get data into a format and environment that actually works with these systems.

Asterisk: one of the other big things is if you go to most engineers in 2026 — maybe like minus two months ago, given the latest phenomenon — but the code's in GitHub. You just connect to GitHub. Remember, there's this period when you launched a coding agent, there was no sign up or register — it was just, "Give us your GitHub."

That doesn't exist in knowledge work. There's no "give us your GitHub" for knowledge work. There's like, "Give us your Box"—

Well, Box customers have a much easier time with all this. Unfortunately, we're only $1.3 billion in revenue run rate — that means there's a lot of people not using Box. What are they using? Their data is in on-premises systems, legacy file shares, legacy infrastructure, enterprise environments that don't talk to agents particularly well.

Think about that distinction between implementing coding agents versus everything else.

访问控制的差异

Even something you'll fall asleep about — access controls in the enterprise are totally different. In coding, you get access to basically most of the stuff ever relevant for your job. In knowledge work, you're like, "Hey Sally, can you open up that file share for me? Can you open up that project because I didn't get access to it?" How do you make sure the agent has access to those sets of things?

All of that work has to get done. Two things to prepare for:

  1. Silicon Valley has to prepare for diffusion taking a lot longer than they think — or than I'll say we — but really they, because I know how long it'll take.

  2. The good news is this is all correlated to the applied layer value creation. The companies that will have the patience, the full domain expertise, and just the sheer work ethic — because it's not like the floodgates open, you have to go pound pavement and get out there — that will be the applied layer.

This represents a trillion dollars of applied-layer AI value: how do you go get the technology to the lawyer, or to the sales rep, or to the life sciences researcher, or to the person who runs the customer support team? That's all opportunity right now that exists.

That's amazing — because it is the global town square for AI.

Aaron: It is. And I want to send an emergency alert to everybody who's a sophomore or junior in college and just be like, "Follow these 20 accounts on Twitter, and also join Twitter, because this will just help your career. You're either a year ahead or a year behind simply based on your feed. And my feed is so wired in."

This is the number one advice I give people when they ask how to get current on AI. Follow these 100 accounts.

Aaron: Virtually first step: join Twitter. I'll still talk to 20-year-olds that are like, "Yeah, I see some articles." I'm like, "What do you mean? How do you see articles? Do you just get lucky that somebody emailed you an article? Just join Twitter, like what are you talking about?"

You just have to be wired in. I enjoy it — it's a lot of fun. I play with everything.

最喜欢的新 AI 产品

What's your favorite new AI product? Please say Instinct.

Aaron: Full disclaimer, I have not done the Instinct invite code yet, simply because I have a backlog of like three other personal assistant products.

You gotta try Instinct.

Aaron: I know, I know, everybody's raved — I'm very excited.

I'm not an investor, so —

Aaron: Oh, you're not? Okay, so this is totally genuine. I 100% will have — I don't know when this is going to run — but I'm sure I will have played with it by the time it runs. I'm in pre-release in a couple right now that I'm spending some time with.

The personal assistant stuff is super exciting. In some of my use cases, it's still showing some of the limits of browser use as an example. We still have some work to do there. Probably the entire internet needs a CLI for their product. So we still have some blocking and tackling at the infrastructure level for these things to be totally awesome.

I look like your average AI-pilled knowledge worker — every day I'm asking one of five different AI systems 20 to 30 questions on research, looking for talent, looking for what a competitor is doing, what's happening in this market, how to expand there.

十四、公司建设建议：如何让企业适配 AI

What about on the company-building side? You have a 20-year-old company at this point. What's your advice for other people trying to reinvent their companies to make sure they have max adoption of AI, not just at the individual level but also at the company level? How do you make your business legible for AI?

Aaron: Some of this we have as a byproduct of how we've always thought about information systems in the company. To no exaggeration, if you have a question you want to ask about the business that has ever been documented in a form of unstructured data — a meeting note, project plan, roadmap, presentation, financial document, financial planning session — it's 100% in Box.

We benefit from a data architecture that's already insanely tuned, because this is how we run the company. We didn't let anybody use anything else. The data is very easy for us to work with at scale. And of course we have Salesforce and all the other core canonical systems. We've been able to have pretty good data hygiene, so agents running on top of that make it a little easier to be AI-first in how we operate.

最佳实践

A couple best practices:

  • Figure out where the highest-leverage impact workflows are going to be and target those. Our CIO is very AI-pilled. We have a little bit of a center of excellence on AI. We've hired some internal AI FTEs to help with these processes.

Do you have leaderboards?

Aaron: We don't token-max. We actually have a list of people by number of tokens, but usually to inspect: okay, do we think that's useful, or is there a learning we should take back to some other function? Probably our top three AI users at Box — one of them is wasting half the tokens, and two of them are like, "Oh, whatever they're doing, we need to go do an internal training session for everybody else."

We had this thing two weeks ago where I was like, "Can you just get everybody in a room on this particular team and show them how this one person is using AI?" Six hours later they were in a room and the guy was doing a full demo. Shout out to Mick.

That's the kind of stuff we're trying to do — how do we show everybody what it looks like to work in this way.

不断变化的元游戏

For as fast as we're moving — and we are shipping at some parts of the stack two or three times more actual customer-facing products (I don't care about how much code, but did we actually deliver more functionality the customer's asking for) — you'll go talk to a friend at Anthropic and you're like, "Oh my god, we still have ways to go."

The particular meta constantly changes. Two years ago you'd be like, "You're just using a plugin in your IDE." "Man, that's — we're not going to be that, we're not ready to fully be AI-first." Then you're like, "Okay, everybody roll out Cursor." Then everybody rolls out Cursor. Then you're walking around like, "You're not only working from Slack, just @-mentioning bots doing your code? What are you doing?"

We're constantly changing what the workflow paradigms are on this.

Slack Agents

Do you guys have like a Slack co-worker agent, for lack of a better term?

Aaron: We have a few that have that shape. I'm pretty excited about Cloud Tag as a form factor. You still have to get the team construct right and the data right. We have a variety of ways people work with agents in Slack. I don't know if it's as Slack-pilled as Benioff would like us to be, or as Anthropic or OpenAI — but we're heading in that direction.

十五、AI 时代创业的新艺术

I think history books will be written about the art of business in this time. I would love to read the new Art of War with everything that's happening. What do you think it takes to win in AI vs. pre-AI? What does it feel like to be a founder right now versus when you started Box?

Aaron: I am both jealous of and also not jealous of the young founders you meet. You're like, "Oh, to be young again — the whole world is your oyster, you can go in any direction, and the leverage you have..."

You'll meet with them, and you're like — I saw a product a week and a half ago, they did a demo, and I was like, "Absolutely, this would have been a 40-person project five years ago." Especially when we were starting out, easily 40-person. And it was two people. And you're like, "How do you have so many tabs that work, and they all seem to have stuff behind the tabs that seems very functional? This is not fake."

I'm very jealous of that. It's incredible — you can start your company from scratch with that as the design principle.

Now we will get there because we're just going to muscle through it. There's a couple things we can't do — we're very uncomfortable at the idea of removing the code review and some of these things that get talked about. Because our customers can't possibly entrust us with their data security and compliance if we don't take that seriously. So we're always going to have a little bit of a discount on the productivity because of where we are in the stack and what we do as a business.

Jealous of being able to be fresh in that.

另一面：竞争的密度

On the other hand — for every great idea, it's instantly five competitors. We didn't have that problem. We had a good couple years where we could just grind on our product and experience. It wasn't like every three days you were like, "Oh, Sequoia funded this thing, Benchmark funded this thing." We weren't going nuts with that.

Now we had our own version of that — so at the time I probably was going nuts, but in retrospect it wasn't worthy of going nuts. Now it's like, "Oh man, this is a real race in every one of these markets."

Totally.

决胜的关键

I'm probably pretty consensus on this: in a world where AI builds things so much faster, then probably the shift moves to whoever can actually get it to the customer is in the best position.

It's fun talking to founders that are pilled on that. Scott or Matan — they get the mandate. They're just like, "This thing is going to be an enterprise diffusion play. So you have to get it to the enterprise."

Anybody who mistakes the mandate right now — you're just going to lose. It's game over. Sorry. There's quite literally trillions to trillions up for grabs at the applied layer, and the companies that know how to build the teams and get to the enterprise will be the ones that win. Obviously guaranteed.

Well said, Aaron. This is a very fun conversation. Thank you so much for joining.

Aaron: Thanks for having me.

[music]

## 一、真正的护城河不是模型，而是"权限拓扑学"
Levie 抛出一个看似普通的观察，却隐藏着一个惊人的悖论：**当研究员想象"个性化模型"时，他们下意识地假设自己就是用户——一个拥有全域访问权限的人**。但真实世界里，一个律师的知识边界是由他今天早上被加入/移除的项目组决定的。
这里有个反直觉的洞察：**企业级 AI 的最大瓶颈不是智能，而是"访问控制的动态拓扑"**。每一秒钟，组织内数以万计的权限关系在重构——某人被加入一个诉讼、某个文档被移入法律保留、某个客户关系需要"中国墙"隔离。这意味着，**未来最有价值的不是"更聪明的模型"，而是"能在毫秒级理解组织权限动态的中间层"**。
这也解释了为什么 Levie 说"研究员想让模型跟他们一样"——因为研究员活在一个**低摩擦的权限世界**里，而企业活在一个**权限每秒都在变化的动态图谱**里。这种认知落差，就是 Neolab（应用层新贵）的全部机会。
