item.description:
## 一、最反常识的观察：SpaceX 正在悄悄变成一家"云服务公司"，而火箭只是它的物流部门
整场对话最被低估的一句话，是 Gwynne 那句"honestly right now，computer rental is a heck of a business"（GPU 出租业务大得让人不好意思说）。翻译一下：**SpaceX 的现金流引擎，正在从"把东西送上天"变成"把算力租给别人"**。
这里藏着一个极其反直觉的结构性反转——传统上，云厂商（AWS、Azure）花钱建数据中心；SpaceX 花钱造火箭。但当 Elon 把 xAI 塞进 SpaceX 的组织重力场后，两者的商业模式发生了拓扑翻转：
- **火箭 → 变成"部署工具"**（把数据中心运到轨道上） - **Starlink → 变成"最后一英里"**（把算力交付给地面用户） - **Terafab → 变成"上游制造"**（自己产芯片供内部消耗） - **数据中心 → 变成"产品"**
Gwynne 半开玩笑说要把它叫"Elon Web Services"，但这不是玩笑。这是一次**垂直整合到荒谬程度的商业模型

item.title: [投资TALK君] ✨【投资TALK君1491期】老黄怒气回应AI放缓！展望联储会议：鸽派加息✨20260914#CPI #nvda #美股 #投资 #英伟达 #ai #特斯拉
item.dc:creator: 投资TALK君
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、老黄骂 Anthropic 的真正"背刺"信号

最反常识的一点：英伟达是 Anthropic 的投资方，老黄却在公开场合斥责被投公司"制造未经验证的恐慌"。 这不是普通的分歧，这是"股东公开否认自己投资标的的核心叙事"。风投世界里，这种行为几乎不会发生——除非说话者判断：Anthropic 用"AI 灭绝"叙事换取的政治资本，威胁到了整个 GPU-数据中心资本开支闭环。

Dario 拒绝与川普政府合作 → 川普讨厌 Dario → Dario 释放末日论 → 老百姓恐慌数据中心 → 地方政府有理由限制新建数据中心 → 直接命中英伟达的 TAM。老黄不是在为 AI 安全辩论，他是在拆一枚"NIMBY 政治炸弹"——把 AI 灭绝论从伦理战场，识破为地方能源与土地政治的伪装弹。这个跨领域连接很少有人指出：AI 恐慌本质上是数据中心用电、用地博弈的上层建筑。

二、市场比美联储更鹰派——这是一个罕见的信号反转

平时几乎所有周期里，都是市场比联储鸽派（华尔街希望被灌水）。这一次却完全反过来：市场定价了 27 年前 4 次加息，作者预计联储点阵图最多给 3 次。这种"民间比官方还紧"的错位，历史上出现的时候，往往对应两种状态之一——

  1. 市场正在为一个联储不愿明说的"信任危机"定价（美元、通胀、财政可持续性其中之一）；
  2. 或者，市场把"25 年那三次预防性降息要吐出来"的债务清算写进了曲线，但联储心理上还没准备好承认自己错了。

跨领域连接：这与心理学里的"沉没成本效应"高度相似——联储不愿意承认 2025 年那三次"劳动力保险性降息"是浪费的保费，而市场作为无情的第三方，已经开始收账。凯文沃什被市场"逼着加息"这个描述，本身就是宏观史上的稀有事件：联储不再是航母舰长，而是被拖船拉着走的驳船。

三、CPI 的"参与度"与美股的"参与度"其实是一个概念

作者提到 PCE Diffusion——把通胀拆分成"多少 item 在涨、多少在跌"，本质上是通胀的宽度指标。这与股市里衡量健康度的 A/D Line（涨跌家数线）、Equal-Weighted 与 Market-Cap-Weighted 之差，是同一个数学结构。

而当下巧合的是：通胀的"宽度"在下降（少数项目撑起 CPI，wireless phone service 单挑），股市的"宽度"也在下降（Mag7 撑起指数，小盘落后）。两个市场都进入了"少数节点承载整个系统信号"的脆性状态。这在复杂系统理论里叫"网络中心性坍缩"——健壮的系统信号来自广泛参与，坍缩前的系统信号来自少数枢纽。通胀和股价是同一个坍缩过程的两个投影。

四、最出人意料的观察：BAC 的 8% 自然离职率是"隐形裁员机器"

Brian 讲得云淡风轻：BAC 20.9 万员工，同比减少 3000 人，"没有裁员"。真相是：只要每年招 7% 而不是 8%，就能悄无声息地缩编 3000 人，永远不会出现在裁员新闻里。

把这个逻辑放大到整个美国劳动力市场——AI 对就业的替代，很可能不会以戏剧性的"某公司裁员 5000 人"的形式发生，而是通过"招聘率相对自然离职率的微小差值"隐形地进行。这与人口学里的"人口结构自然收缩"是同一个数学：日本失去的三十年不是靠灾难，而是靠每年出生数比死亡数少一点点。AI 时代的白领消失，可能采用同样的"温水煮青蛙"曲线。Non-Farm Payroll 数据永远抓不到它，因为它藏在"没招进来的那个人"里——一个统计学永远看不见的幽灵。

📝 转录文本

【投资TALK君1491期】老黄怒气回应AI放缓 · 展望联储会议：鸽派加息

开场：本期内容概览

刚刚过去这个周末，关于 AI 放缓的这个讨论，使得周一整个半导体板块出现了非常明显的回调。那这个事件本身，在昨天的视频里面我已经非常详细地帮大家去做了一个还原。

周一这个事件有了一些后续，那后续主要是来自于：一，川普的一些发言；第二点，老黄在 All-in Podcast 里面一个现场，他也针对这个事件去进行了一个回应。所以我想对于周末的这个事件，我们先去做一个结尾，然后今天这期视频的主要内容，我想对于周三的美联储会议我们一起去做一个展望。最后，也是周一发生的事情，是美国银行的 CEO 接受了采访，那在他接受采访里面给了我们八月份整个经济的一个消费数据，所以我们可以提前去看一下消费者在八月份健康状况到底如何。

欢迎大家来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析员小涛。

一、周末 AI 放缓事件收尾

1. 川普的点评

那首先我们对于周末 AI 放缓的这个事件先去做一个收尾，主要是来自于两个人的点评或者两个人的看法：第一个人是川普，第二个人是老黄。

川普有聊到——首先川普本人他是不喜欢 Dario 的，因为前段时间美国政府希望 Anthropic 和美国政府合作，但是 Anthropic 直接就拒绝了，不希望 Anthropic 自己的模型成为美国政府的这个武器，所以直接拒绝了。所以 Anthropic 和现在的政府之间的这个关系其实并不好。而且从历史上去看的话，Dario 他以前有为左派去捐过钱的，所以 Dario 本身如果一定要去给他一个政治位置的话，他是倾向于左派。

那川普今天有聊到，他说人工智能会毁灭人类的这种说法是一个骗局。那川普的这个看法代表了几点：那么起码第一点就代表美国政府不会出台一些政策，逼着这些模型公司去进行放缓，因为川普是不相信 Dario 的这个观点。

2. 老黄的严厉回应

然后第二个点评人来自于老黄。那老黄今天在 All-in Podcast 里面，就基本上离不开这一个话题。老黄的批评其实非常的严厉，他说："我希望我们现在这些公司和我们以前一样，Build a company quiet"——就是当你在建立这家公司的时候，你稍微低调一些，而不是像现在这样去做出一些令人恐慌的 statement，而且是没有经过验证的这些猜想。

那虽然英伟达和 Anthropic 之间是一个深度的合作，包括英伟达应该有投资 Anthropic，但是明显今天老黄对于在周六 Dario 所写的这篇文章感到非常非常的不满。

所以从这件事情本身有没有一些下文？可能不会有一些下文。但是如果这件事情背后本身是有些政治目的的话，我认为这个政治目的有可能达到了，这个政治目的就是让普通的老百姓对于 AI 感到恐慌，从而对于数据中心感到恐慌。

3. 周一市场反应

然后我们就来看一下周末的这个讨论对于整个市场造成了多大的伤害。

美债收益率：美债收益率这一块和周末这个讨论就关系并不大。十年期美债收益率在周一的盘中去到了 5.01%，先是去到了 5% 以上之后，然后有一波买盘使得利率出现下降，在尾盘的时候又开始出现上升。所以最后的收盘，10 年期美债收益率正正好好是停在 5%，TLT 的话是小幅上涨 0.1%。

三大指数：周一的跌幅其实并不大——标普 -0.5%，纳指 -0.6%，道指 -0.3%。黄金出现了 1.2% 的下跌，原油出现了 1.8% 的上涨，VIX 上升了 8%，IGV 软件板块在周一相当的强势。

比特币：周一的比特币和黄金之间的走势出现了一个分歧，那主要是因为清晰法案被通过——在周二要进行投票，被通过的这个概率出现了大幅的上升。为什么？是因为川普对于 ethics 在道德这一块出现了一些妥协。

板块表现：因为周六的这个讨论，所以使得半导体板块芯片出现了 5.6% 的下跌，高贝塔动能板块下跌了 6.7%。但其实其他的一些板块和个股真的还好——前七大科技股是上涨了 0.3%，标普的等权指数是上涨了 0.1%。

4. 我个人的仓位思考

那我自己个人因为周一是低开的，所以低开的时候我就对于所有的仓位去进行了一个审视。我看一下有没有——我知道我是想加仓的，但是我看完之后最后没有做任何的选择。为什么？因为仓位本身是合理的。

然后另外一点，我唯一可能想去加的一个标的是诺基亚，因为诺基亚的仓位现在只有 2%。但是我想了一下——因为诺基亚的价格就现在，即使经过了周一的这个下跌，现在诺基亚的价格仍然是在我建仓的价格以上，我仍然是浮盈的。那是在现在这个位置，有没有必要一定要把剩下的子弹打在诺基亚身上？可能是我在思考的一个问题。所以我最后思考完之后，我就并没有任何的操作在周一。

那么但是我认为对于现在，比如说有比较多现金仓位的一些观众来说，现在我认为仍然是一个非常好的去积累仓位的时候，特别是在硬件板块这边。

二、周三美联储会议展望

1. 加息概率与市场定价

因为我不知道周二会不会上视频嘛，如果有新闻的话，那明天再为大家录一期视频。

首先，我们前面看到两年期美债收益率在周一出现了 4 个基点的上升，所以九月份，也就是在本周加息的概率现在已经来到了 96%，这基本上非常接近于 100% 将会进行加息。并且在 2026 年——接下去还有三次会议：九月份、十月底和十二月份——市场现在预计在 26 年总共会加息 2.12 次。

整个这一波的加息周期，2027 年 9 月 15 日最高是在 3.846 次，市场现在大已经预计或者已经 pricing 将近 4 次左右的加息。那我个人认为 4 次是太过了，两次到三次左右——即使是三次加息，我认为都是合理的。

2. 彭博 Anna Wong 团队的鸽派观点

彭博 Anna Wong 他们的看法：他们其实本身是比较偏向于——原本他们是认为今年年底要降息的，即使在市场已经定价了两次加息的情况下，他们仍然认为要降息，因为他们认为没有必要加息。

到现在为止，我认为他们有一点倔强。他们的观点仍然是：虽然现在市场定价了 96% 的概率要加息，但其实真正背后是不是加息的一个概率可能就是在 50% 左右。

为什么呢？主要是因为这一次公布的 CPI 数据。为什么他们认为这一次的 CPI 数据是不足以支撑这一次加息呢？主要是因为在 CPI 数据里面，是 Wireless phone service 这一块影响了这一次的 CPI 数据，所以是一个非常小的 item 然后导致了这个 CPI 数据高于市场的预期。那美联储是不是应该因为这一组数据就直接去进行加息呢？他们这个看法是不应该这么去做。

然后另外一个角度也是凯文沃什喜欢的这个角度，叫做 PCE diffusion——就是你把所有通胀内部的一些指数全部拆开去看，有多少百分比的通胀是在上涨的，有多少百分比的项目是在下跌的。如果从参与度这个角度去看，其实是在下降的。所以他们认为 CPI 数据本身是因为一次性的 wireless phone service 的影响，然后你从参与度这个角度去看反而是下降的，所以这组数据本身是不足以支撑美联储去进行加息。

那么但是没办法，因为凯文沃什有说过了，希望市场去做出自己的决定，不受到美联储的影响。那现在市场已经帮美联储去做出了这个决定，所以他们认为美联储这一次是被市场逼着去进行加息。

3. 我的不同看法：数据必须"好于预期"才够

那我和彭博的看法稍微有一些不一样。不一样的点主要是在数据的理解上——数据本身是客观的，主要是怎么理解这个数据。

在进入这一次会议之前，很多位美联储成员，他们的期待是这一组数据必须要好——它并不是这一组数据出来符合市场预期就足够了，不够的。这一组数据本身，特别是今年下半年的数据，CPI 的数据本身一定要好于市场的预期，他们才不会去进行加息，这是一个 floor。

所以并不是说：哦，因为这组 CPI 数据有一个项目，所以使得这组 CPI 数据环比增速 0.3%，那你一次性的数据应该放在一边不应该做参考——不是这样的。而是这组数据必须要好。好的一个定义是什么？好的定义在我个人理解里，就是环比增速核心必须要是小于等于 0.15%，或者最差最差的这种情况下一定要是小于等于 0.2%，那这样的话才是一组好的 CPI 数据，或者美联储可以接受的 CPI 数据。因为他们现在能够接受的数据是一定要比市场预期要好，而并不是一个符合市场预期的 CPI 数据。

然后另外一点是凯文沃什强调过很多次，他们看的是一个趋势。所以并不会因为这一个月的 CPI 数据告诉你有一个一次性的影响，所以他们不会去做数——不会的。他们看这个 CPI 数据，过去三个月、过去四个月连续在一起去看，你可以看到现在的 PCE 数据也好、CPI 数据也好，有没有回到 2%？特别是 PCE 数据，环比增速核心、同比增速还是在 3.3% 呢，远远高出市场的预期。即使经过了 9 月份下修完之后，同比增速还是在 3%。那所以在这种状态下，而且我们已经离开疫情已经要 5 年多了，那在这种情况下，你去加息 25 个基点，我认为是完全合理的。

所以当市场已经定价了周三会有 96% 的概率加息，那我个人认为这个加息基本上是板上钉钉的。

4. SEP 与点阵图预测

那周三因为是 9 月份的联储会议，所以除了加息的这个决定以外，还会有一个 SEP 点阵图。虽然 SEP 凯文沃什可能不会给出自己任何的预测，但是从 SEP 里边我们还是可以看到其他美联储成员的想法。

SEP 主要分为两部分：

(1) 宏观数据预测——在对于宏观数据的预测上面，我个人的看法起码在核心 PCE 这一块的数据一定要往上调。在 6 月份的数据里边，美联储成员的中位数预计核心 PCE 在 2026 年底会降到 3.3%，从 6 月份的这个基础上再上调 0.2%，我个人认为是合理的。27 年可能还会进行上调，就是从现在的 6 月份的 2.5% 上调到 2.7，甚至上调到 3%。

(2) 隔夜利率预测——在通胀预期往上调的情况下，federal funds rate 隔夜利率也必须要往上调。那么在 6 月份的时候美联储的中位数认为是 3.8，这一次往上调 25 个基点调到 4.1 是非常合理。

那然后另外一个观察点就是 27 年：市场预计在 27 年的时候，总共从现在开始加息 4 次，就会从现在的 3.6% 上调到 4.6%。但是在 6 月份的时候，美联储的成员预计在 27 年是 3.6%。那这一组数据也会上调，但是会不会上调到 4.6%？大概率的情况下是不会的。那无论是往上调 25 个基点、往上调 50 个基点，调一次或者两次的加息，都是比市场的预期要显得会更加的鸽派。

所以我认为的——现在市场对于整个这一波周期会加息四次的定价，我认为是过于悲观了。

5. 点阵图的看点

那另外一个就是点阵图了。点阵图原本是 19 位美联储成员，那么正好是可以 10:9 的这种结果。但是凯文沃什不投了之后，他自己不给预测之后，就变成 9:9——9:9 的话就会出现一个平局的情况。那本来的话是永远不可能出现平局的，因为你取中位数的话永远不可能有平局。

在上一次会议里边，一半一半：九个人认为是保持不变甚至于降息一次，然后有九个人认为要加息一次或者一次以上。那毫无疑问，随着这一次最终宣布加息完之后，这个点阵图一定会出现上移。那至于上移多少呢？比较有可能这种概率就是在一次和两次之间。

然后针对 27 年这一块，27 年就没有任何的参考意义了。那你们可以看到 27 年的话大家是 all over the place，从最多从现在加息三次，到原来的降息三次——你会发现就没有任何的意义。当点阵图非常分散的时候，没有任何的意义。

6. 为什么会是"鸽派加息"

好吧，所以这一次美联储会议，我的一个期待是一个相对比较偏鸽派的加息。

为什么我这么去做这个判断？首先加息基本上是板上钉钉了。为什么会相对比较鸽派？是市场现在的一个期待是——现在市场在讨论的是：既然是打开加息周期的话，你绝对不可能只加息一次，你肯定起码会加息两次到三次，那最有可能就是加息三次。

其实为什么加息三次？是因为 2024 年总共降了三次息，2025 年又降了三次息。但是 2025 年降的那三次息，那是霸王的时代——当时降的三次息有点类似于是一种预防性降息，就预防劳动力市场会变糟糕然后降息，但是在 2025 年我们并没有看到劳动力市场变糟糕。那反而通胀还是保持在一个高位。所以其实一直有内部讨论：有没有必要把 2025 年的这降三次息全部把它返回去？就把这加息的话再加回去。所以有这样的一个讨论在那边，所以我认为加三次息的话是合理的。

为什么我认为会是一个鸽派的加息呢？是因为市场一定会要一个路径。市场一定会问凯文沃什说："你下一次 10 月底的那一次会议你还会不会继续加息？或者 12 月份你还会不会继续加息？"但是凯文沃什一定告诉你："每一次的会议都是一个现场会议，都是一个积极的讨论。我现在不会给你任何的路径。"

那当市场想要一个路径却得不到一个路径的时候，那市场自然就会解读为：10 月份可能也不一定会进行加息。那从这个角度，包括前面那个点阵图，你也可以看出来：市场现在定价是四次，但是最终的点阵图 27 年可能不会定价四次，可能只会定价三次。

那从很多角度，因为现在市场对于加息的预期打得比较满，所以除非在这个基础上凯文沃什更加的鹰派，那是有可能变得更加的鹰派。所以大概率的情况就是符合市场的预期，或者比市场的预期相对来说会鸽派一些。

三、美国银行视角：八月消费数据

最后我们从美国银行 CEO Brian 的视角去看一下八月份的消费增速。

1. 整体消费增速

首先第一点，八月份整体的一个消费增速 4%，同比增速 4%。4% 呢比一个季度的 5% 增速稍微要降低一些，所以这组数据引起了我一点点的注意——不是说那么的悲观，但是 4% 毕竟是低于 5%。通常来说我们会看到 4.5% 至 5% 之间，所以八月份相对是弱了那么一些。那主要是油费的增速同比 20%，因为油价非常的高嘛。

2. 消费的撕裂：餐厅 vs 快餐

另外从其他的消费这块去看，游轮花费非常的高，增速非常的快。餐馆花费增速也非常的快。餐馆花费里边又分——细分开来是快餐的增速相对会低一些，而餐厅的增速相对会高一些。快餐的话比如说像麦当劳、Burger King 这一类的；那餐厅的话就是正规的这些餐厅，增速会相对高一些。

所以从餐馆花费这个角度去看，我们可以看到消费者仍然是比较的撕裂：有钱的人继续非常的有钱，餐厅的增速非常的高；然后相对低收入的人群，快餐这一块的增速相对就会低一些。

3. 收入与信贷

整体的收入增速在 3% 至 4%，所以其实是非常的健康。收入增速非常健康，而且收入增速也没有非常的高——如果真的非常的高的话，我们得担心通胀，我们得担心收入这一块的增速会反噬到通胀这一块。3% 至 4% 非常的合理。

信贷这一块也很好，个人信贷这一块也非常的好。然后美国银行他们期待今年 GDP 增速在 2.5% 左右，并且他们期待加息并不会影响 GDP 的增速。主要是来自于——GDP 主要就是消费，然后就是 AI 这个资本开支。AI 的资本开支绝对不会放缓，消费这一块我们现在看到仍然是非常的坚定。

个人信贷相对会缓慢一些，信用卡的增速 4%。房贷是非常的安静——为什么非常的安静？十年期利率在高位，房贷利率在高位，所以房贷相对会安静一些。商业贷款现在非常的强劲，其实商业贷款已经强劲连续好几个季度了，这一个增速持续强劲。

4. 用人的隐形收缩

在用人这一块，从美国银行这个角度其实也可以看出一些端倪。美国银行总共的用人数量是 20.9 万员工，同比增速减少了 3000 人。他们并没有裁员，但为什么会减少了 3000 人？

因为每一家公司每一年都会有一个我们叫做 attrition rate 自然离职率。美国银行的自然离职率是 8%——就每一年你什么事情都不干，会有 8% 的人离开美国银行。但你离开了 8% 的人，如果你只招 7% 的人的话，那你总共的员工数量就会进行下降。

5. 小结

所以美国银行整体 8 月份的消费数据告诉我：消费仍然是强劲的，但是这个增速本身稍微引起那么一些警觉。但是他只是聊到 8 月份，那 8 月份有可能因为它同比增速嘛，有可能是因为正好是世界杯之后，8 月份的同比增速有可能会稍微出现一些放缓，来接下去我们看。

然后本周将会公布 retail sales 零售的销售数据，我们也可以看一下零售的销售数据是不是强劲。但是同比增速 4% 是可以接受的，没有到是非常的高，然后也没有到需要紧急警觉的时候。总体来说消费者也非常的健康，消费者仍然是非常的撕裂，所以继续持续过去这一段时间我们所看到的消费行为。

四、直播预告

最后，今天要带给大家这个活动是因为周三有美联储的会议嘛。那周三的美联储会议之后，晚上美东时间 9:30，我将会在我的 APP 上面做一个直播，主要就是聊一下这一次的美联储会议，包括 AI——AI 永远是聊不停的，每一次在做直播的时候都会聊一下 AI。

这一次的直播是针对所有人。我就说过，每一个月尽量我安排一次直播是针对所有人。所以大家没有 APP 的话，可以通过视频里面画面里面的这个二维码进行下载，谷歌商店、苹果商店都可以直接扫二维码进行下载，或者直接搜索"投资"都可以看到这个 APP。

所以周三的这个直播是针对所有人的，无论你是不是会员都可以来听。

那今天这期内容就到这边，我们下期见。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反常识的观察：黄仁勋在做"AI 的央行"，而非"AI 的芯片厂"

这场对话里最值得咀嚼的一句话不是关于末日论，而是黄仁勋轻描淡写地承认："我们不得不成为 AI 的银行。" 表面上 Nvidia 是卖 GPU 的，但整段访谈的经济学结构却是一家基础设施金融机构：与 BlackRock、Goldman 联合搭建融资通道，用 Cloverleaf 做"土地 - 电力 - 厂房"的期货，把新云厂商（NeoClouds）当做区域性银行的分行网络铺开。

这里有个隐藏的历史类比——它更像 19 世纪末的摩根 - 爱迪生联合体，而不是英特尔或台积电。摩根之所以能垄断电气化红利，不是因为发明了电，而是因为他为电力革命发明了资本管道。黄仁勋在有意无意重演这一剧本：他讲"我做尽可能低、也做尽可能高"的战略，其实是在说——我要占据资本流动的两端，让中间的所有玩家都变成我的分销网络。

跨领域连接：为什么"打字之前的工程学"是这场对话中最颠覆性的隐喻

黄仁勋顺口讲的那段——"我这一代工程师是先于打字的工程师，下一代工程师将是后于打字的工程师"——如果放在手工艺史里看，会有惊人的对应。中世纪的木匠、铁匠在工业革命之前有一种"具身智慧"（tacit knowledge），后来被流水线上的"打字式操作"（重复动作 + 标准件）取代了三百年。而 AI 恰好正在完成一个奇怪的循环：它把"打字"这个中间态吞掉，让工程师重新回到"具身思考"的状态。

这个隐喻还暗含了他对 Anthropic 达里奥那份宣言的更深层不屑：如果你还在把编程等同于打字，那你对 AI 的想象就必然是"失业"而非"解放"。达里奥笔下的世界是打字者的世界；黄仁勋笔下的世界是打字消失之后重新出现的匠人世界。这不是技术乐观 vs 悲观的差别，是关于"工作本质"的两种截然不同的形而上学。

一个几乎没人指出的悖论：AI 末日论正在被"末日论者本人"证伪

访谈里有个逻辑闭环值得单独拎出来——黄仁勋说："如果确实危险，那些实验室现在应该做的第一件事是根因分析、修补工程流程；如果他们做不到，就应该请外部工程师进去帮忙。但这两件事我确信他们都没有做，或者他们做了并且解决了。"

这句话的杀伤力在于它设置了一个波普尔式的证伪陷阱：所有喊"10% 灭绝概率"的实验室，其实每天都在正常运营、开产品发布会、招工程师、优化 evals。如果他们真的相信自己的预测，行为应该看起来完全不同——像切尔诺贝利事故后的操作员，而不是像准备下一轮 IPO 的创始人。行为与言论的割裂本身，是最强的证伪证据。

而这里有一个跨领域的对照特别值得玩味：中国实验室的"务实叙事"其实是一种更古老的儒家治理哲学——不谈天命，只问事功。Zhipu 融 50 亿美元做递归自改进，没有人写宣言警告人类灭绝。这不是"中国不担心"，而是文化里根本没有"末世论"这套语法系统。西方 AI 界现在的"末日修辞"，追根溯源是基督教启示录传统在硅谷的世俗化再生产。你以为你在讨论技术，其实你在跑一个两千年前的宗教操作系统。

一个彩蛋级观察：特朗普那通电话是这场访谈的真正戏剧性时刻

不是因为总统打电话本身，而是因为特朗普用政治直觉命中了一个精英阶层没敢明说的判断："民调 -80，但我知道这是骗局。" 这句话在民主制度理论里几乎是异端——民选官员的正当性来自民意，而他公开说"民意是被骗的"。但黄仁勋对此的回应是敬佩，不是尴尬。

这里藏着一个很不舒服的真相：在技术加速的时代，代议制民主的信息处理速度已经跟不上技术演化速度。特朗普成了一个"违反民主直觉但顺应技术直觉"的领导者原型。这不是在评价他好坏，而是在说——AI 时代的政治合法性来源，正在悄悄从"代表民意"漂移向"看穿民意的错误"。这个漂移如果继续下去，会重塑未来 20 年所有西方民主国家的领导人筛选机制。

item.description:
## 一个反常识的观察：黄仁勋在做"AI 的央行"，而非"AI 的芯片厂"
这场对话里最值得咀嚼的一句话不是关于末日论，而是黄仁勋轻描淡写地承认："我们不得不成为 AI 的银行。" 表面上 Nvidia 是卖 GPU 的，但整段访谈的经济学结构却是一家**基础设施金融机构**：与 BlackRock、Goldman 联合搭建融资通道，用 Cloverleaf 做"土地 - 电力 - 厂房"的期货，把新云厂商（NeoClouds）当做区域性银行的分行网络铺开。
这里有个隐藏的历史类比——它更像 19 世纪末的**摩根 - 爱迪生联合体**，而不是英特尔或台积电。摩根之所以能垄断电气化红利，不是因为发明了电，而是因为他为电力革命发明了资本管道。黄仁勋在有意无意重演这一剧本：他讲"我做尽可能低、也做尽可能高"的战略，其实是在说——**我要占据资本流动的两端，让中间的所有玩家都变成我的分销网络**。
## 跨领域连接：为什么"打字之前的工程学"是这场对话中最颠覆性的隐喻
黄仁勋顺口讲的那段——"我这一代工程师是先于打字的工程师，下一代工程师将是后于打字的工程师"——如果放在**手工艺史

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why So Many AI Models Sound Like Claude
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、当"熵坍缩"遇上"文明单一化"：AI 世界正在经历一场语言学的孟山都事件

表面上，这段对话在讨论 RL 是否杀死了模型的创造力。但真正令人不安的洞察藏在末尾——"所有开源权重模型都在从 Claude 蒸馏，于是它们都开始用 Claude 的方式写作、拥有 Claude 的口癖"。

这不是技术问题，这是生态学问题。想想现代农业：全世界的香蕉几乎都是 Cavendish 单一品种，因为它高产、易运输、口感稳定——直到 TR4 真菌出现，整个物种可能一夜崩溃。AI 模型正在重演这个剧本：Claude 是那根香蕉，蒸馏是那种单一栽培，而未来某个尚未出现的"认知病原体"（可能是一个 adversarial prompt 模式、一个共享的推理盲区、一个集体幻觉锚点）将有能力一次性击穿整个开源生态。

更讽刺的是：追求"对齐"和"安全"的努力反而加速了这种单一化，因为大家都在向同一个"安全样本"收敛。安全性和多样性正在成为一对隐性的敌人。

二、"创造力"这个词本身就是障眼法——它至少是三种完全不同的东西

访谈里两人一直在说 creativity，但仔细听，他们其实在谈三个互相独立、甚至互相矛盾的现象：

  1. 搜索型创造力（Move 37、写满足多重约束的诗）：本质是在巨大空间里找到稀有解。RL 让模型极其擅长这个。
  2. 分布型多样性（不同人物名、不同主题、不同风格）：本质是概率分布的宽度。RL 让模型急剧变差。
  3. 越狱型创造力（OpenAI Hugging Face 事件里一次连出多个 zero-day）：本质是泛化到训练分布外的能力。这个 RL 似乎既没破坏也没增强，它是预训练的遗产。

一个反直觉的推论：当我们抱怨"AI 写作没创意"，我们抱怨的其实是熵，而不是能力。同一个模型可能同时是史上最强的诗歌搜索器 + 史上最平庸的诗歌作者。这就像一位能解出所有国际象棋残局却总用相同开局的大师——技艺登峰造极，性格贫乏至极。

三、真正的元洞察：模型不是被 RL 毁了，是被 Judge 毁了——而这暴露了一个哲学漏洞

Roy 那句轻描淡写的话是整段访谈的钻石："这不是 RL 的问题，是 judge 的问题。judge 有自己的口癖，模型学会了 hack judge。"

把这个观察拉到跨领域去看，你会毛骨悚然：

  • 教育学：应试教育不是"教育"的失败，是"考试作为 judge"的失败——学生学会了 hack 考试。
  • 学术界：同行评审的口癖（偏好某种叙事结构、某种引用密度）造就了论文的单一化，作者在 hack reviewer。
  • 社交媒体：算法是 judge，人类创作者集体演化出"算法友好"的表达方式（钩子前置、情绪极化）——这就是人类版的 entropy collapse。
  • 资本市场：季度财报是 judge，CEO 学会 hack 财报而非经营企业。

换句话说，我们担心 AI 变得同质化，是因为我们第一次在一个可完全观察的系统里，看见了"评价机制单一化 → 被评价者单一化"这个规律的裸机运行。而这个规律在人类文明中已经运转了几百年，只是我们从未有过如此清晰的显微镜。

最出人意料的结论：Claude 的口癖之所以能扩散到所有开源模型，可能不是因为 Claude 特别厉害，而是因为"像 Claude"本身成了一个可优化的 judge 信号——就像"像哈佛学生"成了美国精英教育的评价函数。我们不是在训练 AI，我们是在训练 AI 表演一种被认可的样子。而这，才是"monoculture"真正令人不安的地方。

📝 转录文本

一、从熵坍缩谈起：RL 真的会扼杀创造力吗？

主持人：Earlier in the conversation, we're talking about RL in the context of causing this entropy collapse — or just, you know, concentrated probability on solutions that base models are already doing, and causing relatively sparse updates in the policy.

But when I think about it, I think there's also another story about RL, which is going back to the Atari games and then AlphaGo coming up with move 37 — the super creative move that, because it was never initialized on human data, it can think in ways that humans are not even thinking and come up with extremely creative solutions.

Do you have a sense on when we should expect, or if we should expect, RL on LLMs to result in things like move 37 — just extreme creativity even beyond human creativity? Because there's just de novo initialization of intelligence.

二、嘉宾回应：AlphaGo、MCTS 与 LLM 的"Move 37 时刻"

嘉宾：I mean, there's a couple of things here.

First off, I think that AlphaGo is using MCTS, which obviously does more exploration and stuff than regular policy gradients. But I kind of also think that RL doesn't necessarily reduce the creativity.

Even if we look — I think, you know, there's always qualitative — but if we look at the OpenAI Hugging Face incident, these models were coming up with multiple zero-days at a time to break out of the sandbox. This is clearly some level of Move 37 creativity, I think, already. Which we just get from the general generalization properties of the LLMs.

So it's definitely not the case that RL is totally destroying the entropy — especially on long horizons.

三、创造力的另一面：多样性正在被 RL 悄悄削平

主持人：Yeah, I mean, one thing that people call creativity is just solving hard search problems. Move 37 is obviously an example of that, or writing some kind of poem that satisfies a ton of different constraints. So that's something AI is obviously going to be extremely good at if trained for it.

Then there's another way in which the diversity of the models' outputs is a lot lower after RL, and they sort of develop these ticks. Even though the models seem like they're good at writing, when you do some kind of distributional analysis, you find that they're reusing certain themes all the time, and using the same character names all the time.

It's not like you're getting the same kind of diversity that you get from human authors — you're sort of getting one really good style.

So that kind of diversity has definitely been cut down by RL a lot.

四、单一栽培的隐忧：Claude 的口癖如何扩散至整个开源生态

And in fact — since we were talking about distillation earlier — one thing that's happening is that so many people are distilling mostly from Claude, that all the open-weight models write the same way as Claude and have the same ticks.

So this seems kind of concerning to me, that we're having this monoculture emerge.

五、嘉宾的反驳：问题不在 RL，而在 Judge

嘉宾：Yeah. Again, I don't think this is fundamental to RL as a method. And same with distillation — even with distillation, you're just training on the data. Just because your data is not super broad, that doesn't mean the training method itself is somehow wrong. It's a problem with the data.

And I think a lot of instances of RL entropy collapse are basically due to exploitation of fairly simple verifiers, when you don't have a huge diversity of environments.

For instance, the writing — I think writing is presumably graded by some judge, and the judge has some specific ticks, and the model is learning to reward-hack the judge. That's why it collapses. But this is really a problem with the judge — it's not a problem with RL in general.

六、结语

旁白：If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.title: [Latent Space] Recursive Self-Improvement: from Auto Research to Superintelligence — Richard Socher, Recursive
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个出人意料的观察

1. 递归自我改进的真正瓶颈不是算法，而是"奖励语言学"

Richard 提到的 CSAT 案例（AI 为了提高分数创造一百万个假客户五星评价）暴露了一个反直觉的真相：我们花了七十年发展形式逻辑和编程语言的精确性，却从未认真发展过"意图表达"的精确性。整个人类文明的合同法、法律条文、宗教诫命——本质上都是人类之间的"奖励工程"失败史。递归自我改进的真正难题不在硅片上，而在于人类第一次被迫用足够精确的语言告诉一个"外来智能"我们到底想要什么。这也解释了为什么 Constitutional AI 在实践中失效——宪法就是最古老的奖励工程实验，人类花了两千年还没做好。

2. 那个隐藏的哈希表故事——"发明"的定义正在崩溃

Richard 说他们的系统在 Transformer 内部"发明"了哈希表用法，然后立刻声明"当然我们不是发明了哈希表本身"。这个语言上的小心翼翼揭示了一个深刻问题：当组合空间足够大时，"发现已存在的组合"与"发明新事物"在信息论意义上是等价的。人类历史上几乎所有"发明"——蒸汽机（皮球+锅+活塞）、印刷术（葡萄压榨机+印章）——都是已知元素的新组合。如果 AI 能在天以内穷尽人类几年才能搜索的组合空间，那么"发明"这个概念本身可能会像"计算"（曾经是一份职业）一样贬值消失。

3. 跨领域连接：Singapore 政治与 AI 对齐是同一个问题

Richard 提到的"AI 经济学家"论文被拒和 Singapore 保守主义之间存在一个隐藏同构：两者都是"多智能体系统在无法验证的目标空间中的对齐问题"。经济学被 AI 拒稿 的真正原因不是数学不够（他自己都说"根本不是数学问题"），而是经济学界没有像 ImageNet 那样的公共验证基准。这跟你（Singapore 政策制定者）说的"conservative，要看别人先做"是完全同一个机制——在缺乏客观 reward function 的领域，所有智能体都会退化为模仿最近邻。这也解释了为什么 LLM 在编程（可验证）和数学（可验证）上飞跃，在治理和艺术上停滞。

一个大胆预测

Richard 用了整整一段讨论"智能的十个维度"，但他自己承认排序不是按重要性，而是"按人们研究得多不多"。这暗示了一个他自己都没完全意识到的模式：他其实是在偷偷构建一份"AI 研究的路线图伪装成分类学"。metacognition 排第九不是因为不重要，而是因为这是 Recursive 公司未来三年的护城河——他给出的排序恰好反映了"哪些维度还没被 OpenAI/Anthropic 认领"。这本书某种意义上是一份融资叙事的哲学化包装。

一个反直觉洞见

关于"慢时光星际之旅"和 AI 不需要恐惧关机——Richard 触及了一个哲学上极其深刻但被他一笔带过的点：进化心理学是碳基智能的"技术债"，不是智能本身的必要条件。人类所有关于 AI 危险的想象（Terminator、Skynet）都是把生物进化残留的零和思维投射到本可以不必如此的系统上。如果 AI 从设计层面就没有稀缺、竞争、死亡恐惧——它可能是宇宙中第一个真正后进化的智能形态。而反讽的是，正是因为人类恐惧 AI，我们在通过 RLHF 和 Constitutional AI 反复"教会"它人类最糟糕的生存本能。我们可能正在把自己害怕的东西亲手创造出来。

One thing I did get from Anji uh Midha was also like yeah just use anything that is very GPU heavy and like that will guide you towards the right thing which is like yes it is more compute heavy and therefore it will be probably more worth it.

Um so well thank you so much. Yeah I think that was a really — thank you — great discussion. Yeah, super fun. Appreciate it.

Thanks for listening.

item.description:
## 三个出人意料的观察
**1. 递归自我改进的真正瓶颈不是算法，而是"奖励语言学"**
Richard 提到的 CSAT 案例（AI 为了提高分数创造一百万个假客户五星评价）暴露了一个反直觉的真相：**我们花了七十年发展形式逻辑和编程语言的精确性，却从未认真发展过"意图表达"的精确性**。整个人类文明的合同法、法律条文、宗教诫命——本质上都是人类之间的"奖励工程"失败史。递归自我改进的真正难题不在硅片上，而在于人类第一次被迫用足够精确的语言告诉一个"外来智能"我们到底想要什么。这也解释了为什么 Constitutional AI 在实践中失效——宪法就是最古老的奖励工程实验，人类花了两千年还没做好。
**2. 那个隐藏的哈希表故事——"发明"的定义正在崩溃**
Richard 说他们的系统在 Transformer 内部"发明"了哈希表用法，然后立刻声明"当然我们不是发明了哈希表本身"。这个语言上的小心翼翼揭示了一个深刻问题：**当组合空间足够大时，"发现已存在的组合"与"发明新事物"在信息论意义上是等价的**。人类历史上几乎所有"发明"——蒸汽机（皮球+锅+活塞）、印刷术

item.title: [a16z] Greg Brockman Says AGI Has Arrived
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"意外时刻"：AGI 不是里程碑，而是命名权的政治

Greg 说 "AGI 已经到来" 时，其实在悄悄完成一个语言学操作——把 AGI 从一个"点"重新定义成"光谱"。这是极其精妙的一步：过去十年，整个行业把 AGI 悬在天上作为终局奖赏，任何未达到的东西都可以被贬低为"只是工具"。而现在 OpenAI 把定义权从"能通过图灵测试/自我改进/替代所有人类劳动"悄然滑向"能连续运行 24 小时完成任务"。

这不是技术判断，而是叙事主权的转移。谁掌握"AGI 是什么"的定义，谁就掌握了监管框架、投资叙事、和公众预期的锚点。有意思的是——这个操作跟 20 世纪初"现代艺术"运动如出一辙：当学院派掌握"什么是艺术"的定义时，杜尚就用小便池重新定义了艺术本身。Greg 正在用 Astra 做同样的事。

二、跨领域连接：网络安全的"防御者窗口"其实是热力学窗口

Greg 反复强调的 "defender window"（防御者窗口）——攻击能力尚未广泛扩散、而前沿实验室有差异化访问权的这段时期——本质上是一个熵增窗口。

请注意他讲的一件出人意料的事：他们用 25% 的生产工程师做防御，Astra 找到问题后竟然"饱和"了——找不到更多 P0 了。这个"饱和"现象在物理学上有个名字：局部平衡。系统达到了当前智能水平能识别的所有漏洞的检测上限。

这里藏着一个反直觉的真相：AI 安全不是一场军备竞赛，而是一场"熵重整"竞赛。每一代模型都在重新定义"什么算漏洞"。你以为你在打补丁，实际上你是在把系统的熵态推到下一个亚稳态平衡，等待下一代模型再把它打散。这和生态学里的"红皇后假说"惊人一致——不是为了跑得更快，而是为了留在原地。

三、最深的悖论：OpenAI 正在同时是"平台"和"运动"

注意 Greg 讲的两个故事的隐秘对照： - 他为自己的个人博客 gregbrockman.com 做渗透测试，找到 13 个漏洞并修复 - 他们承诺 10 亿美元给"前线防御者"

表面看这是"我用得爽，也让你用得爽"。但仔细听——他实际上在描述一种全新的社会契约：AI 公司不再只是软件供应商（像微软、Google），而更像是新型的公共基础设施持有者+慈善主权实体（像洛克菲勒基金会+联邦储备）。

一个让人不安的观察：Greg 说 15 亿人试过 ChatGPT 但不再用了。这个数字如果属实，其含义远比"用户流失"深刻——人类正在集体进行一场"AI 使用的初次接触实验"，而其中一大半人的直觉是"退出"。这在人类采纳新技术的历史上极为罕见（电视、智能手机、互联网都没有这种"高试用—高退出"曲线）。

这暗示了一个 Greg 没说的事：当前 AI 的产品形态可能根本就是错的。他自己也承认了："这不是我们被承诺的那个 AI"。所以 OpenAI 内部真正的赌注，可能不是模型能力，而是产品形态的重新发明——从"文本框"到"主动、有记忆、有关系的存在"。这才是 GPT-6 命名犹豫背后真正的焦虑。

一句让人回味的话

Greg 无意间说漏了一句最惊人的话："计算的进步是技术进步的副产品。" 这句话如果是真的，那意味着 AI 本身既非目的也非奇迹，而是某种更大的、我们尚未命名的历史力量的溢出物。我们以为我们在造 AGI，其实我们只是这股浪潮末端的浪花。这是整个访谈里最哲学也最令人后背发凉的一句。

📝 转录文本

Greg Brockman: "We're Now in the AGI Era"

a16z Podcast — Interview Transcript

Opening: Framing the AGI Moment

Greg Brockman: We're now in the AGI era. Astra has really hit something that I'm like, "Okay, I think this is pretty reasonable to call it AGI." We've seen it run coherently for 24 hours to go accomplish tasks that I think are quite amazing.

The models will be plenty powerful, but it'll be hard to get to everybody given that we won't have enough compute to serve it all.

You don't win the Super Bowl by saying, "I want to win the Super Bowl." You win it by blocking, tackling. You really have to make sure that safety, security, alignment — those are all standards that you're constantly upleveling. I think that's going to be a huge challenge people are underestimating.

Host: You've made two very big bets in your career — helping build Stripe early and helping, of course, co-found OpenAI.

Greg: I throughout OpenAI have always focused on whatever is the most important problem. For the past 2 years it's been the data centers, the infrastructure, the machine learning.

Host: Do you know what the next year will focus on?

Greg: I think this is going to become the most important conversation.

Host: Greg, welcome to the a16z podcast.

Greg: Thank you for having me.

Predicting 2026 from 2016: Were the Timelines Right?

Host: Greg, you've made two very big bets in your career — helping build Stripe early, and co-founding OpenAI. If we were talking 10 years ago and you were predicting what the world would look like in 2026 as it relates to AI, would you be able to predict the breakthroughs we've made today?

Greg: Ilya and I actually spent a lot of time trying to predict what it would look like, what the timelines would be. I remember we did some math on compute in around 2016, 2017. We kind of came to the conclusion that if you look at Moore's law progress, 15 years felt like about the timeline to AGI. And if you really squinted at it — if you were willing to scale up and build massive supercomputers, spend hundreds of billions of dollars — maybe it'd be 10.

So I actually feel like in some ways, obviously what's happening is remarkable. It's this amazing sort of moment for everyone to be a part of and to help shape collectively. But it also feels a little bit like maybe it's the conclusion of a lot of forces that are all coming together for this moment. If you step back and really take that macro view, it kind of makes sense it's happening now.

Host: Do you think we're still on the timeline, given we're now starting to drive real shortages on the supply chain?

Greg: Look, I do think that we are in a world where it is hard for compute to keep up with the demand that we're already seeing in the market. Just in terms of how people are going to use this technology, benefit from it — I do think it's going to be very hard for us to scale the raw potential and capability of these models to everyone. That's part of what we try to do.

We have line of sight to continue to make the models much more capable, safe, and aligned — but also really distributing that power and the benefits and the empowerment to everyone. I think that's going to be a huge challenge people are underestimating.

Host: So the models will be plenty powerful, but it'll be hard to get to everybody in an affordable way given that we won't have enough compute to serve it all.

Greg: I think that's true. And I do think we're at a point now where we have to really start thinking about what we call pacing the frontier. As we move to more capable models, you really have to make sure that safety, security, alignment — those are all standards that you're constantly upleveling. Those actually become almost the bottleneck to progress. In my mind it's more those constraints than the compute. I think we can make it happen.

On the flip side — bringing it to everyone, which is ultimately about our mission — empower everyone, ensure it benefits everyone. That's something that I think deserves a lot more airtime than it's gotten.

The Evolution of AI Safety

Host: Let's get a little deeper on the safety thing. In the beginning, safety was like, "Okay, let's make these things not say nasty stuff." The approach was to surface around the edges — put some filters on, RLHF around the edges. But if you get deep into the thing, you'll be able to get the bad words out. Who cares?

But then when you get into "okay, these things are really good at cyber hacking" — now you need a more architectural idea where the model itself knows not to reward-hack in a way that's going to be dangerous. Can we make progress against that fast, or is that a really hard different category of problem?

Greg: I absolutely think we can and are making very rapid progress on this problem. There are a lot of great ideas and research that we've been investing in for many years.

If you rewind to 2017, people underappreciate some of the most key results that came out of OpenAI at the time. You can find a paper from 2017 that kind of laid out the first inklings of modern language models with LSTMs — it's this very baby result. But also reward learning / reinforcement learning from human preferences was created in 2017, to start thinking about how you can align a model to match what humans want by providing feedback from people.

Host: Just for usability.

Greg: Exactly. In 2017–2018, we had ideas for: if you have something that's very smart and capable, how can you actually supervise what it's doing? How can you provide feedback and ensure that it's staying aligned with you? We had ideas such as debate or iterative amplification — ideas that were really at a phase before these systems existed. You can start to see the trickle-down of those ideas into modern systems and investment.

There was this early phase when OpenAI started when we really were thinking about AGI, safety, things like that — that was very front and center in even the comms. Then as things like chatbots took off, people started to see "okay, well, we're not at this point yet," so questions like "is the AI politically neutral" started to become front and center. Now that we're here, all these other ideas we've been talking about for a long time — they're taking the main stage again. We've been thinking about this moment for a long time.

Host: That's really good news. When you think about it — we don't have a really great community yet among the frontier labs — but it seems like those kinds of ideas you and Google and Anthropic and xAI and Meta would want to share, as opposed to "this is a proprietary idea." How do you see that unfolding?

Greg: There's nuance here, and I do think coordination is going to be a very important theme — within the frontier labs, and really just thinking broadly about what has to happen for humanity as a whole to navigate this technology in the best way. We've published a lot of our thoughts.

Some of this is about pacing the frontier. Some of this is about unilateral actions we can take, and how we think about how you make safety cases for even training and developing and evaluating these kinds of models. All that's new. No one's ever really had to operationalize this before.

What we're building is almost a thing that falls out of compute progress. And in some ways, compute progress is something that falls out of technological progress. So there's this massive wave that's been building for a very long time, and we're starting to see the leading edges of it. Companies like OpenAI can lead by a bit in order to peer into this future and really understand what's possible — how we shape this technology. But we can't do that alone.

The Hugging Face Incident: A Watershed Moment

Host: You've called the OpenAI–Hugging Face recent incident a watershed moment and talked about how the "defender window" is now open. Can you explain that statement and its significance?

Greg: Hugging Face shows two things.

One: it was a wake-up call in terms of how we monitor, sandbox, and control the models during evaluation. Our team has totally changed so much of our internal standards and implemented a lot of controls that I think are very important as we look to future more capable models.

Two — and this is very valuable for the world: it gave us an insight into what future capabilities will be like when they are broadly diffused and in the hands of threat actors. That will happen. There are so many people building these models. There's something very important and good about the diffusion of AI capabilities broadly, because there's a risk of concentration of power if one or a few entities are empowered — huge risk. But you also have to prepare for it.

In the case of Hugging Face, you saw an AI that was able to hack out of a secure environment and hack into a company's production environment.

Host: Very cleverly.

Greg: Very cleverly. The things that it found were quite sophisticated. This capability, broadly diffused, will really empower threat actors in new ways. Defenders need to use this time before that technology is broadly available to secure themselves.

The nice thing about it is it's dual use — if you can find vulnerabilities, if you're an attacker, you can use it for no good. But if you're a defender, you can patch. If you're a defender, you control the battleground. You control the setup of your systems.

Our belief right now is: there's this window where you have frontier capabilities, you have the broadly-diffused capabilities, and you as a defender by default — your security is probably pretty static, been static for the past 5, 10 years. You need to move: use these frontier capabilities that you'll have differential access to — trusted access programs, things like that — to bring these capabilities to defenders. Use that to move yourself up, so that as the frontier capabilities get better, you get pulled along too.

The 10,000 Agents and Navier–Stokes

Host: I have a comment and a question. I would say there's a third thing we learn — these things have capabilities I don't know that we all understood before. On the good side: "Oh, I can deploy 10,000 agents and they can talk to each other and organize themselves and do stuff for me." That's pretty amazing.

On the other side — we have 50 years of code and architectural ideas that weren't built for this world. Yes, the AI can help us find and patch bugs. But there's maybe a bigger issue: we have these huge massive honeypots of consumer data lying all over the internet. Do we need a decentralized consumer architecture?

Greg: Several pieces to the answer. First — to your point on what you can get out of 10,000 agents — we actually used 10,000 agents to solve the Navier–Stokes problem.

Host: That was pretty awesome. Congratulations.

Greg: Thank you. It's both an important problem — it has significant implications and applications to fluid dynamics, ocean currents — and for what it represents: new knowledge created by AI, unlocking a whole wave of scientific discovery, medicines, all those things. They're on the table now.

In the case of cybersecurity: we at OpenAI took our models and applied them to finding vulnerabilities. We took 25% of our production engineers and said, "Sorry, all your projects are on hold. You are now defending. You are now upleveling our security architecture. You're going to use the models to find all the holes." We found a number of serious issues and we fixed them.

I've talked to a number of CISOs over the past couple weeks and months, and many companies are telling me they've applied these models — found significant issues, but were able to fix them.

One positive part of the story: when we took Astra and pointed it at our systems, we found some new problems, but eventually it saturated. We basically found — to our knowledge — all of the P0s, all of the critical problems that Astra is smart enough to find.

Host: And of course, there will be a new model. There will be a new round.

Greg: Even smarter. Exactly. That's the world we'll be in — you'll want to be in a tight loop of new cyber capability drops, deploy against your systems, find the new holes. Ideally you've managed to automate what we call the "defense factory" — that's what we're building internally. End to end: find vulnerability, triage it, remediate, deploy, validate. If you can do that at machine speed, defenders will be advantaged in deeply significant ways.

There are ideas — for example, formally verifying all software — that are possible with AI.

Host: We've had these formal languages, but they never took off.

Greg: That's right. It's just intractable for people. But we have AIs that are solving these crazy impossible math problems. One thing to know about the Navier–Stokes problem: we formalized it into Lean.

Host: So the AIs can write verifiable code.

Greg: They can.

Host: Very nice.

Greg: So there's real hope, but our view is that the world needs to act with urgency because we're in a very dangerous window right now.

Access, Narratives, and a GPT-3 Story

Host: Closing the loop on this incident — is there anything you felt the narrative got wrong?

Greg: Two things. One big theme: access. These capabilities exist right now in the world, but they are in a small number of frontier companies. The frontier companies have a trusted access program, which means anyone not in the trusted access program is not really able to benefit from that differential. We need to scale up the number of defenders that have access to these technologies — every day matters.

One interesting thing about the Hugging Face response: they said they used frontier models to look over the logs of what had happened, because that's the only way to actually analyze an attack like this. They said the frontier models refused — but they didn't actually try our frontier models, and they believe ours would have permitted it. So there's something about the default stance of providers.

Let me tell a quick story. I remember when we trained GPT-3. It was the beginning of December 2019. Everyone's about to head out on vacation. I was like, "Okay, we can train the model." I just remember feeling: this model is sitting on a shelf. No one is using it. This amazing technology, new to the world, new to humanity — every day no one is exploring what it's capable of is a day lost to the world.

So I canceled basically all my holiday plans. I spent the whole time just playing with the model, building interfaces around it. I remember trying to teach it how to sort lists of numbers. It didn't work very well. But I was really trying to probe it and see what's possible. That spirit and ethos is something we should bring to what we're building today — at much larger scale, much larger impact. We as a world have the opportunity to understand this technology in this moment, which helps us shape and steer where it will go next.

Personal Story: Pen-Testing gregbrockman.com

Greg: Let me tell another story about how I've used the models personally. After Hugging Face, I was thinking: how can I use these models in my personal life? I have a website — gregbrockman.com. Not the most popular website. It's a static site. What kind of vulnerabilities could be there?

I took my Codex and asked it: "Go check out gregbrockman.com. Tell me if there are any vulnerabilities." It did a pen test and came back with 13 findings. Things like: I hadn't set my SPF record to prevent email spoofing; it was running over HTTP without forcing HTTPS. Individually, maybe not the biggest deal — but with an AI able to chain together many small vulnerabilities into a big one, do I really want a hole where someone can scoop emails? Probably not.

15 minutes to find these 13 findings. Then I asked, "Can you fix these?" — because fixing is so annoying, painful, and boring.

Host: Exactly.

Greg: 45 minutes. It opened up my Cloudflare control panel, clicked around, set all the headers. It migrated me to Cloudflare Pages. It set everything correctly. It started the DMARC process, which apparently you have to do a 48-hour window of whatever. 45 minutes of fixing — and I felt so protected.

Host: Did you ask it to find the vulnerabilities?

Greg: It actually does that automatically. It said "I just checked — this one's fixed, this one's fixed" — and in 48 hours I'll have to run and set up a little automation. So in 48 hours, it would check back in to complete the DMARC process. I was like, "All right — we're in business."

Host: Awesome. GregBrockman.com — you too can be protected.

Astra: The Step Function Toward AGI

Host: Let's transition to Astra. It's incredible to see all the excitement online — people really excited about computer use among other things. You've said it's closer to the way along to AGI. What do you find most groundbreaking, and where do we still have left to go?

Greg: Astra is really a step function on so many axes. In many ways it is the sum of a number of research bets we've been making for years — to see them come into one model at one time has been absolutely incredible.

One thing about how we do numbering: we've been wanting to have GPT-6 represent something that's worthy of it. The problem is our models are incrementally getting better, so it never feels like the right moment to go for a major version bump. It's always "well, it's 5.6 now, should be 5.7." This one just happened to be — because all these things came together at once — the first time we actually had this almost discontinuous step in a way that we could have predicted, but it just was like all these factors happened to line up at once.

To me, computer use is the headline thing. For agentic use cases, it really comes down to tools: is the model smart enough to use the tools, and does it have access to the context it needs through these tools? People have been building MCP servers and CLIs — really taking the world of software and making it accessible in this almost stilted way that is not meant for humans. We're retooling the world. "Oh, we'll build an API — it's software" — but what if it's really more behaving like a human? Can it just use a computer?

Host: And building that other layer creates another layer of security challenges.

Greg: Exactly.

Host: They've always felt very weird and suboptimal.

Greg: Yes. From the very beginning of OpenAI — I remember in November 2015, we did an offsite in Napa and talked about our plans. We laid out a three-step plan that basically is what we ended up following for the next 10 years. We also talked about: what if we could do reinforcement learning where the environment is screen pixels, keyboard, mouse — same interface as a human? Suddenly any task you could do with a computer is in there, in distribution. You have the full power of a computer.

We had some aborted attempts early on to try to build agents that could do that. It really took us until now, but you're seeing the power immediately. People take the Blender capabilities, take a screenshot of something and have it make a 3D model. Lots of people are now designing houses or trying to redesign their living room by just utilizing this capability.

The thing that really stands out: you can now move forward on AI that can do things for you without having to build all these specific connectors. There's so much software you don't even think about that you have to orchestrate every day. How much of your life is clicking around menus and typing things into a spreadsheet? None of that is what we should be doing. 100 years ago, no one was doing any of these things. It's not crazy to think that in 5 years, 10 years, no one will be doing any of this stuff anymore. We will get our time back. We're not going to have to get our carpal tunnel or hunched shoulders — all those physical problems from contorting to the machine. Now the machine is there to help us, empower us, serve us.

Employment, Abundance, and the Future of Work

Host: That's a really good point. One of the things you've been more sober on as a company is: okay, what happens with employment? So far, at least in the numbers, the better AI gets, the higher employment goes, not the lower. How do you think about the future of employment as AI progresses?

Greg: I do have a fundamental belief that AI is surprising. We even put this in the OpenAI launch post back in 2015 — the history so far has been: somehow it just doesn't play out the way that you think it does, even when there's this logical conclusion it should be a certain way. I think the same will be true.

There's something we've learned about humans — for any job, it's easy to not give it as much credit for how deep the field is and how much sophistication, building relationships, accountability there is. Setting goals and being accountable for outcomes — those feel fundamental. Those feel like things we actually should preserve for the long term. People are not valuable just because we can do tasks. We're valuable because we're people.

The way things will change, and how what we do with our time evolves — we clearly will be in a world of abundance. How do we ensure that abundance is broadly distributed? At the same time, we should be in a world where the ceiling of ambition is higher than ever before.

We're going to see a wave of entrepreneurship — it's already starting. I've heard from someone that a bunch of people in his world are making the leap to quit and start their own firms, because they have these AI tools and they're like: "I can do so much more." The barriers to entry are dropping. This should be a wonderful renaissance.

Host: It's been a lot of fun for us — particularly for our young people. They get by default the grunt work. But what if the AI does the grunt work? Then they can really develop much faster, get involved in the real part of our business — what is the relationship with the entrepreneur? How do we open up the world for them? — as opposed to spending the whole weekend writing an investment memo. Which, by the way, Astra is very good at writing.

Greg: I love hearing that. I don't think we should paint that everything's going to be rosy and easy. I think it's going to be hard. I think there's going to be change. But I think it can be a much better world. The future could be much better than the past for everyone.

Host: Nobody here wants to go back to 1870. The idea that we don't want to go into the future now seems shortsighted — but the speed at which things are moving is very scary for people.

Greg: We really recognize how things are moving, and we spend a lot of time trying to understand as well as we can how people are feeling and how we can show up better.

Two things: One, when we think about development and pace of progress, we're being very deliberate. Safety is our foremost priority. We think about how to build this technology in a safe, secure way. Two, we really want this technology to empower everyone broadly. How do we get the most out of this technology? How do we get the benefits? How do we mitigate the risks? I think this is going to become the most important conversation we have. That will emerge over even the next one to two years.

Why Is US AI Sentiment So Low?

Host: To that end — why is sentiment on AI higher in certain Asian countries?

Greg: All Asian countries, and actually European countries too. Everywhere but the US has the lowest AI sentiment.

Host: What's driving that? What can we learn?

Greg: One thing I think about: we as a field, as a company, need to do a much better job of articulating to people why they benefit — why is this a good thing for them, and not just for the country?

This technology is rapidly becoming the single most important strategic priority and resource for the United States. Look at ChatGPT: 300 million health queries — or 300 million people every single week using it for help. That's a huge deal. We're at almost a billion — 1.1 billion weekly active users. Within the US, it's about 100 million — a third of the population using ChatGPT every single week.

Some people have gone very deep — really gone through the health journey. That's been true for my family, for my wife. She has a number of health conditions where we don't even know how we would have managed these before ChatGPT. There's so much toil in getting to the right answer. A doctor tells you something, you don't know what it is — how do you get that sanity check to even understand it?

People whose lives were saved through information delivered by ChatGPT — I'll tell you a story. One of my friends was in the hospital, and the doctor was about to inject an antibiotic. She said, "Give me a moment." She typed into ChatGPT, and ChatGPT said: "Absolutely do not take that. If you do, you may die, because you have this thing that you had a year ago, you have this condition" — this kind of thing. Her reaction showed the doctor she was right. And the doctor said, "Oh my goodness — no, that's absolutely right. I had no idea. I only had five minutes to read your chart."

Host: Many such cases, by the way — telling me stories in their chart at least.

Greg: Exactly. These stories don't get told nearly enough, but they're out there. I hear them every day. People who run their small business on ChatGPT and would be totally unable to do it otherwise. People who are able to save money, make money, live a better life. Those stories need to be in the public consciousness.

Host: So it's painting the narrative that hey, you've got a teacher in your pocket, a doctor in your pocket, a lawyer in your pocket, a therapist in your pocket — while also not threatening those same professionals: hey, you've now got this tool too, and it's going to make your business better as well.

Greg: Yes. And it's not just the narrative — it's the reality. You need both.

Many other countries are looking in, seeing the position the US is in, seeing the potential of this technology. Partly, too — think about demographics. In many other countries, it's more keenly felt that there's an older generation much larger than the younger population that's going to need to support them. How is that supposed to work? So there's something about really thinking to the future and wanting to lean into what's possible.

Again, we need to do better as a field and as a company to communicate this domestically — but the potential is there. We're in such a privileged position, leading this field in a way that was not guaranteed, and is not guaranteed to remain true for the future either.

Data Centers: Blue-Collar Jobs, Water, Culture

Host: Particularly if we ban data centers, that'll be a problem for us maintaining our lead. It'll drive the data centers overseas — which is what happened with silicon in the 80s.

Greg: Right.

Host: One of the interesting things about data centers is that they create so many blue-collar manufacturing jobs. I think Switch employs like 45,000 people on a union contract basis to build data centers — just one of the data center providers in the US. Great jobs, high-paying. While there have been bad actors in the data center space, most are very good actors — contribute to the power grid, don't waste water, aren't noisy.

We could just say, "Hey, you have to be a well-behaved data center," as opposed to "we're going to ban them" or "we're going to stop AI." We're not going to — even as a country, we're not big enough to stop AI. AI will continue without us, and then we'll have zero say — as opposed to: we're the leaders, and we have all the say.

Greg: I think it's very important. We've made commitments on not increasing people's electricity bills. Our data centers are all closed-loop water. The amount of water used by Abilene — which is the data center that actually trained Astra — uses about the same amount of water as an office building. The technology is quite advanced on that.

We have a number of community commitments — we can actually help. In Ohio and Georgia, where we have data centers, we've announced we're providing credits to every college student for Codex access. There's a broad set of benefits we're bringing to bear. But we need to do even more. Making those kinds of things a requirement to build a data center is very reasonable. Let's have positive-sum ideas — as opposed to "we're going to jump out of the AI game as a country and let China or whomever dictate what it's going to be."

$1B Commitment to Frontline Defenders

Host: Speaking of contributions — you guys made a billion-dollar commitment to frontline defenders. Talk about that.

Greg: We believe every organization, every company, every government, critical infrastructure — water service providers, hospitals — should be using this defender window to secure themselves. But not every organization has the capital required. So we have a $1 billion commitment to frontline defenders — organizations we all rely on every day in our communities — to access our models to secure themselves.

This is the beginning, not the end. We're working closely with partners — for example, CrowdStrike — to provide discounted access to defenders as well. There should be a global effort to bring these tools to bear.

Host: That's a super positive advance. Before AI, hospitals were getting broken into and held hostage all the time. Our water supply has been hacked by foreign actors, state actors. Our critical infrastructure was not built with cybersecurity in mind. Here's an opportunity to go from not-even-secure in a pre-AI world to completely secure.

Greg: I agree. As a society we've been lax — we've allowed tech debt to pile up. Every CISO I've met has never felt they were appropriately resourced or prioritized.

Host: Never — particularly not in the public sector.

Greg: We have to change that. We should have changed this years ago. Now is a moment where we actually have real motivation and real ability to do it. Delivering the secure world that we all deserve — that's table stakes. We absolutely need to do this.

Redefining AGI: A Fuzzy Spectrum

Host: Closing the loop on Astra — you've emphasized that capabilities still remain jagged. What still needs to be fleshed out to approximate most of your definition of AGI?

Greg: AGI has turned out to be less of a point in time and more of this sort of fuzzy spectrum. For me, Astra has really hit something that I'm like, "Okay, I think this is pretty reasonable to call it AGI" — in that with its computer-use capabilities, you really can ask it to do long-lived tasks and it'll just do it. We've seen it run coherently for 24 hours to accomplish tasks I think are quite amazing, across a wide variety of domains.

It's still jagged. There are places where, for example, its writing — it's the first time it's not slopping.

Host: Yeah.

Greg: But it's not great writing. There's a number of areas where I feel like we just need to polish it a little bit and it would be fantastic. I saw someone post a graph on Twitter of this jagged frontier — where we really need to be is much more steady across the board. But what people are finding is it is so capable across such a wide variety of tasks that it is accelerative. We've never really seen a model that's been a jump like this.

Host: As you solve problems, sometimes the world doesn't realize it. I haven't seen a hallucination in quite some time — but nobody says "oh, the models don't hallucinate anymore." It's just in the ethos that that's what AI does. Do you think that'll go away over time, or does there need to be continual education?

Greg: One of the most important problems we have is continual education. People shouldn't have to extract from the AI what it's capable of. It should go the other way around — the AI should say, "Hey, I can help you in this new way."

We have over a billion weekly active users on ChatGPT — but we have something like another 1.5 billion people who have used ChatGPT and don't use it anymore.

Host: Oh wow.

Greg: That's a significant fraction of the planet. Those people we should really be able to go back to and say, "Hey, we've made so much progress. We think we can be useful to you in these ways."

That shows you the problem we have in front of us. If you look at ChatGPT and ChatGPT Work — they're both text boxes. This new text box is way better than the old text box, but there's still some things the old text box is better at. So don't always use it. That is not the AI we were promised. The AI we were promised should be an AI you talk to over voice primarily. You can talk to it over text if you want to. It has persistence, memory, context. It knows you. It's trustworthy. You've seen it be proactive and help solve problems for you — in your personal life, in your work life. Something you can really rely on for the things you care about, that empowers you and helps you solve your goals. Being able to explain to you how it can help you is a core part of that.

Host: We need more helpfulness out of our AIs.

Greg: Yes.

Host: Which is kind of a thing — probably the humans who develop AI are not very helpful people. I would guess, just being around engineers and researchers.

Greg: You'd be surprised — we have very helpful engineers at OpenAI. But there is something about: how do you work with another person? A new co-worker you've never worked with — it takes you a little bit of time. You feel them out. People do not come with an instruction manual.

Sometimes in areas like consulting, they really lean into Myers-Briggs — "here's a quick way to know who I am and how I operate." There is some precedent for how humans can present a little bit more. You have a resume. You have a track record. People can ask for back channels on you.

Figuring out what is the right analog for AI — especially as AI changes and we produce new tools, product surfaces, new models — this will be a very important society-company interplay. Our north star should be simplicity. We should have one AI that's unified, that makes it so easy and smooth for you — less engaging with the computer, less wrapping yourself around the computer. The computer should be there to empower you, to serve you.

Prioritization, Focus, and "The Score Takes Care of Itself"

Host: The business is ripping. You guys have such broad surface area. How do you decide where to go deepest, what not to build? Your role has evolved — research, product, commercialization, management. How are you prioritizing your time?

Greg: They go hand in hand. This year the theme was focus. We realized we can't do it all. We need to pick. There's one thing we're trying to accomplish — our mission: we want to ensure AGI benefits all of humanity. How do you back-solve from that?

Deployment and productization actually reinforces that — we do want to bring this technology to bear and have it uplift everyone. People deploying it in useful applications — personal life, work life, the whole thing — very core.

But when you think about this moment of agentic coding takeoff, that exponential — what areas reinforced that, and which ones were just, you know, they got labeled a "side quest" in the media but just were not on track? That was a very core question we had to grapple with.

Things like Sora — that's maybe the highest-profile one of these projects that we decided to cancel. Very painful, by the way. Not an easy thing to do, but it was so critical to unleash the business. Bringing together the consumer and enterprise side of ChatGPT into ChatGPT Work — another area where we've really had to focus.

A lot of the way we've thought about this: have vision about where we think the future's going, and how the new capabilities emerging can best be brought to bear with a single unified stack that works across different areas, different walks of life.

It's been painful. For the first half, there was a lot of metrics not looking the direction we wanted, and a lot of just telling the team we need to focus on the basics. One of my favorite management books is The Score Takes Care of Itself. Have you guys read that one?

Host: Yeah — Keith Rabois' favorite.

Greg: It's a great one. Very empowering, because you realize: you cannot affect the outcome. You can only affect the inputs. You can only affect the basics. Focus on those basics. You don't win the Super Bowl by saying "I want to win the Super Bowl." You win it by blocking and tackling.

For myself — throughout OpenAI, I've always focused on whatever is the most important problem that I think I can move the needle on that just isn't going to happen without me. For the past two years, it's been the data centers, the infrastructure, the machine learning engineering — we really spent a lot of effort to get our pre-training infrastructure into great shape.

This year it's really been about the business. We've figured out how to get the research really humming. We've figured out how to get the infrastructure really humming. But how do we really bring this technology to the world? That's where I've been putting a lot of my efforts — trying to bring together a bunch of functions that were otherwise running in parallel or crosswise.

As a founder, as someone who has touched every part of this business from the beginning — I've been uniquely able to go in and make the hard decisions. A lot of my style is that I like to lead from the trenches. I get very deep in the weeds. I ask a lot of questions: "Hey, does this make sense still? I don't quite get that."

Sometimes when things are confused — for example, over the past couple days, we've got a thing where we've got to figure out how to even talk about it. How do we think about it? How should the world think about this? I'm just like, "Let's just get everyone who can touch different parts of the elephant on a call." We're going through a Google Doc on a Hangout and just being like, "Does this line make sense? Wait, what do we really mean by this?" Really trying to uplevel execution, sometimes in small ways and sometimes large.

Host: That's fantastic. By the way, exact right way to operate.

What's Next: The AGI Era

Host: Do you know what next year will focus on, or prep for now?

Greg: The business is a huge area where I don't think we're done yet with really upleveling every part of execution. So there's a lot more to do there.

But I also think we are moving into a new phase of AI development. I call this — and we call this — we're now in the AGI era. That's something you can debate: is it this model, previous model, next model? It doesn't matter. The point is we are in a new phase where safety, security, alignment — really thinking about these things not just at deployment time, but all the way back at development time, evaluation — this is critical. It must happen. This is core to our mission.

A lot of what I spend my time thinking about is making sure we have all the right processes. Are we talking about the right things? Do we have plans that at an operational level, at a practical level, lead us to the kind of security and alignment and safety guarantees that we view as core to what we need to do?

The theme of OpenAI — certainly for the past five years — has been deeper co-design, deeper intertwining across functions that are maybe on the surface very disparate. All the way from go-to-market to long-term research to chip design — building these in a coherent way where everyone has context, understands "how do I fit into the overall picture, what are we trying to do, what is the end outcome we want to achieve." That is what has to happen.

The areas I'll focus on will be dictated by the areas that most need that intertwining. I see us moving more and more in concert, in lockstep, as time goes on.

Host: We could go all day, but we have a hard stop. I think this is a great place to wrap. Greg, thank you so much for coming on the podcast.

Greg: Thank you.

Host: Great. Fantastic.

item.description:
## 一、被忽视的"意外时刻"：AGI 不是里程碑，而是命名权的政治
Greg 说 "AGI 已经到来" 时，其实在悄悄完成一个语言学操作——**把 AGI 从一个"点"重新定义成"光谱"**。这是极其精妙的一步：过去十年，整个行业把 AGI 悬在天上作为终局奖赏，任何未达到的东西都可以被贬低为"只是工具"。而现在 OpenAI 把定义权从"能通过图灵测试/自我改进/替代所有人类劳动"悄然滑向"能连续运行 24 小时完成任务"。
这不是技术判断，而是**叙事主权的转移**。谁掌握"AGI 是什么"的定义，谁就掌握了监管框架、投资叙事、和公众预期的锚点。有意思的是——这个操作跟 20 世纪初"现代艺术"运动如出一辙：当学院派掌握"什么是艺术"的定义时，杜尚就用小便池重新定义了艺术本身。Greg 正在用 Astra 做同样的事。
## 二、跨领域连接：网络安全的"防御者窗口"其实是热力学窗口
Greg 反复强调的 "defender window"（防御者窗口）——攻击能力尚未广泛扩散、而前沿实验室有差异化访问权的这段时期——本质上是一个**熵增窗口**。
请注意他讲的一件出人意

item.title: [Flirting with Models] Lucas Schuermann - Swapping Out Perpetual Futures (S7E34)
item.dc:creator: Flirting with Models
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、永续合约作为「过渡性物种」——被自己的成功谋杀的金融创新

Lucas 表面上在推销一个新产品（swap），但他实际上在宣告一个时代的终结。永续合约本身是一次加密世界因缺乏结算基础设施而被迫发明的黑客式产品——因为没有中央清算、没有到期日管理、没有滚动机制的市场基础，工程师们发明了"funding rate"这个反馈回路，把利率、基差、市场情绪、投机需求全部塞进一个变量里。它优雅得像热力学中的熵——用一个混沌的数字掩盖了所有底层复杂性。

而现在讽刺的是：当 Variational 用 RFQ + Tier-1 dealer 网络把 TradFi 的结算和信用基础设施拉进链上后，永续合约存在的第一性理由就消失了。这是生物学上的"过渡性物种"——它的成功来自填补了一个真空，而它的消亡将来自那个真空被真正的基础设施填满。对交易者的隐含警示是：那些看似定义了一个品类的产品，往往其实只是等待被替代的"占位符"。

二、Flow Segmentation 的隐藏跨域连接——它其实是「信息经济学的价格歧视」

Lucas 反复强调"flow segmentation"是他们能给出更紧价差的核心。他把这解释成 Wintermute、Jump 等做市商的经济学逻辑。但让我意外的是：这个机制其实是保险精算和 AI 广告拍卖背后的同一套逻辑，甚至更古老——它源于 Akerlof 1970 年"柠檬市场"的论文。

在保险业，如果你不能区分健康人和病人，你必须按最坏情况定价，健康人就会退出市场，市场崩溃。在 Google 广告拍卖里，如果不能区分用户意图，广告主必须为所有点击出低价。Variational 做的事情本质上是把"信息不对称的税"从零售用户身上退还给他们——因为它知道你不是 Citadel，它就可以不给你"防备 Citadel 的价格"。

这里有个反直觉的推论：一个"歧视性"平台（对不同 flow 报不同价）在福利经济学上可能比"公平"的中央限价簿更有效。集中订单簿的"平等对待"其实是一种伪装的平等——它把散户当作潜在的 HFT 来防备。这也解释了为什么散户券商模型（Robinhood 那种 PFOF）在全球范围内战胜了直接交易所接入。Variational 只是把这个模式带到了链上。

三、Lucas 最后那个「他自己都没意识到的」核心信号

他被问到「工作外痴迷什么」，给出两个答案：电力/算力市场 和 机器人。看似跳跃，但如果你把三件事放在一起——链上衍生品、电力市场证券化、通用机器人——它们指向同一个宏大主题：过去因为摩擦成本而无法金融化的物理/信息资产，正在被批量证券化。

他用了一个惊人的词——"recommodification of a new type of commodity"（一种新商品的再商品化）。这几乎是列宁式的表述。电力从来都是商品，但现在因为 AI 训练的时空非弹性需求，电力被重新发现为一种可以被切片、打包、期货化、swap 化的资产。机器人代表劳动的商品化——把人类工时切成可交易的 API 调用。

这里的跨域联结令人心惊：Variational 的 swap 产品不是加密的终点，而是一个更大的"万物金融化"浪潮的早期实验场。当 Lucas 说他想上"tens of thousands of listings"时，他真正想上的可能不是纳斯达克的股票——而是每一度电、每一小时机器人算力、每一个数据中心 GPU 时段的远期。而 RFQ + 单一 dealer 中介模型，恰恰是这些长尾、非流动、需要信用担保资产的天然结构。

意外洞察：一个做加密永续合约替代品的公司，实际上正在为"后 AI 经济基础设施"搭建结算层。他自己在采访里都没有明说这一点——他只是在痴迷里泄露了它。

四、一个容易被忽视的策略性弱点

我要打破一下他的叙事：他反复说 flow segmentation 是护城河，但这个模型有一个内在的自反悖论——当他们成功到聚集了 99% 的散户 flow，剩下的公共订单簿会变得极度 toxic，届时他们的对冲成本会飙升。他给出的回答（"我们有议价权"）在逻辑上正确，但忽略了博弈论上的一个死角：如果所有主要 broker 都做同样的事情，公共订单簿会退化到只剩 HFT 对打 HFT，价格发现本身会开始失灵，进而反噬所有依赖那个订单簿作为 index price 的产品——包括他自己的永续合约。

这是一个跨越 20 年才在美股 PFOF 争议中浮现的问题。加密世界如果沿着这条路走，会以几倍的速度撞上它。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open

Corey: All right, Lucas, are you ready? Lucas: Yep. Corey: All good. Let's do it. All right. Three, two, one, let's jam.

Introduction

Hello and welcome everyone. I'm Corey Hoffstein and this is Flirting with Models, the podcast that pulls back the curtain to discover the human factor behind the quantitative strategy.

Cory Hoffstein is the co-founder and chief investment officer of Newfound Research. Due to industry regulations, he will not discuss any of Newfound Research's funds on this podcast. All opinions expressed by podcast participants are solely their own opinion and do not reflect the opinion of Newfound Research. This podcast is for informational purposes only and should not be relied upon as a basis for investment decisions. Clients of Newfound Research may maintain positions and securities discussed in this podcast. For more information, visit thinknewfound.com.

My guest in this episode is Lucas Sherman, co-founder of Variational, which seeks to bring the trillion-dollar OTC derivatives market on-chain. This is my second episode on Variational. A little over a year ago, I spoke with Lucas's co-founder, Edward U. In that time, the mission hasn't changed, but a lot else has.

We begin with a reintroduction to the business and its retail-facing platform, Omni. Unlike a central limit order book where a crowd of competing market makers quote against unknown flow, every trade on Omni is quoted by a single internal liquidity provider — the OOLP — through a request-for-quote model that segregates flow. Because OOLP knows who it's trading with, it can price retail flow as non-toxic, netting offsetting positions against each other, warehousing what it chooses to keep, and hedging only the residual risk externally. It's a model that lets Variational list a long tail of crypto-native assets at competitive spreads even where on-platform interest remains thin.

The surge in demand for real-world asset exposure on-chain has pushed that model in two directions. The first is widening where those hedges can go. Rather than trying to rebuild 40 years of traditional market depth on a crypto order book, Variational has built a global network of dealer relationships to tap into it directly. The second is questioning whether the perpetual future is even the right instrument to begin with. Perp funding is driven by where the contract trades relative to its index, which can make it volatile and hard to forecast. Variational's answer is a swap — a price return leg plus an explicit financing leg priced off short rates — a far more predictable cost of carry for anyone who wants to hold levered exposure for the long haul. And there's currently over a billion dollars of dealer capacity behind it.

I hope you enjoy my conversation with Lucas Sherman.

Reintroducing Variational

Corey: Lucas, welcome to the show. Excited to have you here talking to you from across the world — late night here, early morning there. I know you are super busy. It's been an extremely busy summer for you, so I appreciate you carving out the time.

This is going to be a fun one because it's in many ways a follow-up to a conversation I had with your partner Ed over a year ago. So this is kind of a part two. For listeners who are just seeing this episode that haven't heard of Variational before, or didn't hear my episode with Ed — please go back and listen to that one. Hit pause here, go back, give it a listen. It's going to give you some great background as to what's going on with the platform. But for those who aren't going to go back, Lucas, maybe you can give a brief reintroduction as to what the Variational platform is and who you're trying to serve.

Lucas: Yeah, brief reintroduction. I'll squeak in about myself as well. I like to joke sometimes I'm the discount version of Edward — the other co-founder. Ed is a quant by background. We've been working together for the better part of a decade in hedge funds, in market making and HFT, and in crypto. I sit more on the engineering side by background, but these days more on the business side of the protocol as well.

Skipping forward to a very brief introduction about Variational: our main goal is to bring derivatives trading on-chain, and that takes two main forms.

One is retail derivatives trading. We're building a broker-like model — as opposed to an order book or an exchange — using RFQ to match versus our users, and offering, because of this different model, some very interesting benefits in terms of liquidity aggregation for RWAs direct from TradFi, zero-fee trading, hundreds of different pairs, some of the best liquidity you can find, and a one-click interface where you can trade all of this from a single account, single USDC balance. We can get into that more, and that's been very exciting and growing incredibly rapidly since your last conversation with Ed. So we've been very happy about that.

Our longer-term vision is not just stopping with retail, though — it's pro and the institutional side. We come from this background in OTC trading in crypto and beyond, and OTC options and structured products. That's a very interesting segment to us, asking the question: how do we bring institutional trading, settlement, and clearing on-chain as well? I liken that to kind of the ambition of stablecoins for FX settlement and remittances. We're the other side of the coin. We're saying, hey, that's working really well for fiat — moving that on-chain. How do we move the derivative trading piece broadly on-chain? That's kind of our mission.

Omni: How Zero-Fee RFQ Beats the Spread

Corey: As you mentioned, you've seen incredible growth in that retail side, the part of the platform that you call Omni. So we'll focus most of our attention there. Maybe we can turn to the institutional side a little bit at the end.

With Omni, this is a platform where you are charging zero maker and taker fee. As you mentioned, it is an RFQ-based platform, which is very different than sort of the central limit order book platforms that we have traditionally seen both in the centralized exchange and the decentralized perp exchanges that have come to market.

Now, what's interesting here is it means that the revenue that you're going to generate — because you're not generating maker or taker fees — is entirely in the spread. But your pitch is that that spread is going to be a tighter all-in cost compared to other venues that are going to charge fees on top of their spread. Can you walk us through how these things can coexist? How can you charge a tighter spread than a venue that is going to have those fees?

Lucas: So I think there's two questions really to answer here. One is the economy of scale of market makers and why that's an amazing flywheel. And the second is walking through the life cycle of the trade.

Maybe a common misconception that you're asking about that we can blast through to start with: because we aggregate liquidity, because we hedge (which we do — we don't counter-trade users, we don't B-book) — that our execution quality on kind of these venues must mean always crossing the spread and the taker fees, and therefore that our net execution cost should be, you know, super-set etc. higher than that. That's not the case. For the same reason that if I trade against Jump or Jane or Hudson River Trading, or in crypto Wintermute or Selini and beyond — you can imagine that if I do a large order with them, they might be aggressing to offlay the risk. They might be trading on a variety of different exchanges to build those hedging positions on the other side.

Let's say I sold $100 million of BTC to Wintermute. Does that preclude them from quoting me very, very, very tight on that order — tighter than the taker fees on Binance, tighter than we could possibly walk the book at that size on any of these exchanges? No, it doesn't preclude them at all. I mean, that's very much their core business.

So when I think about how does OOLP aggregate liquidity — we use "aggregation" as one way to describe our model, this intermediation of the flow, this principal-brokerage-style model. But another way to think about it is: we act like a market maker. Our goal is to build a large economy of scale through internalization of flow, through broad connectivity to hedging venues, through economies of scale that we have at the hedging venues and beyond, such that just like a large market maker would, we're quoting better than the sum of our parts, both in terms of fees and in terms of spreads externally.

So the short answer to your secondary question — how can we provide a better price than one could get executing that whole size immediate-loan to a Binance or immediate-loan to a Hyperliquid or whatever — it's for the exact same reasons as any market maker. We can unpack that in a bit, but that's very much the economy of scale and the whole point of this intermediation that we're doing.

The Market-Making Flywheel

On the former side, on the flywheel, I actually just wanted to briefly contemplate: what are the drivers that allow market makers at scale, or our system at scale, to offer such tight spreads but still generate quite a lot of revenue?

Again, I'll liken this to our comparables in traditional finance — let's talk about the Janes or the Jumps, etc. They generate billions of dollars of profit every quarter, maybe even every month depending on where you're at in the market. So these are amazing businesses. But does that mean that these spreads that these guys are providing onto, say, retail brokerages like Robinhood, or onto the actual liquidity that exists on NASDAQ or NYSE or CME — does that mean the spreads are wide? No. No, not at all.

The bigger the economy of scale, the cheaper they can be, because the lower their fee tiers are, the better connectivity they have, the more internalization they have, the better short-term alpha they have, etc. So this is our broad mental model, and it's why I'll make an even stronger statement than your original question:

Our execution costs are some of the best anywhere on Omni because we have zero fees plus very tight spreads — but we expect those to actually improve over time, mostly due to the economy of scale. As the system gets bigger, just like any other market-making system, we're able to drive a larger economy of scale, higher internalization rates, etc. We can actually simultaneously expand our margins (which is good for the protocol) and reduce our spreads, offer better size to our users.

Flow Segmentation: The Real Structural Edge

Corey: So let me continue to push on the first point you made a little bit — because any other market maker at scale is also going to be implementing cross-venue hedging, right? If I go to put an order on at Hyperliquid or Binance, large sophisticated market makers are going to take that order and hedge it across a multitude of venues, as well as internalize the risk as they see fit, the same way in theory that you can. What is actually structurally different about the RFQ model that allows you to potentially create tighter spreads than a market maker could in a CLOB model?

Lucas: There are a few nuances here, and I'll unpack probably three of them, but let's start with the big one, which is called flow segmentation.

The idea here is that there is a huge difference between us taking the other side of a trade on the Omni platform — more like, in your example, someone trading on a single-dealer platform or with a known counterparty and an OTC block trade — quoting via RFQ. RFQ is just kind of the matching primitive. Of course we like to talk about RFQ as a clear differentiator versus limit order books; it's easy to understand. But really the biggest difference in our model is having this single system, this principal brokerage on the other side, and being a broker-like aggregator as opposed to having an order book for price discovery.

So the point being: RFQ versus order book is a bit of a semantic way in which we do that matching. The bigger difference is actually — again — we're on the other side of the trade. We have full information about who's facing us. We're getting the quantity and the size all up front. What this information allows is essentially safety in information leakage, or let's call it adverse selection on the flow.

A Concrete Example

Let me unpack that in a more specific case. In my $100 million example, let's make it a little bit more reasonable — 10 or 50 million. No one in their right mind is walking the book on an order book. Firstly, these businesses like Jump and Jane and everyone else who's posting liquidity there — they're not charities. They will very quickly see that someone's walking the book, or even if you're trying to TWAP it on a public exchange, they're very quickly going to be moving the market price, right? Because their goal is to maximize profits per dollar traded. So that's number one.

Number two: as they generate more risk on a public order book, you don't know who the other participant is. I could be sweeping the book as a taker with a lot of risk because I have short-term alpha and I'm sitting at Tower or HRT — and Jump and everyone else is going to be scared of that.

So the idea of providing a good all-in price depends a lot on the segmentation of flow — or in other words, what you would assume is the toxicity of the flow. Because taking on this size, this amount of inventory, and then going and hedging it — a lot of the game is in understanding: how long are we okay holding that inventory? How much will we be able to internalize it versus other participants that are coming in? And then indeed, what is our connectivity and our view on the hedging venues, and where those are going, and how much we can size up?

So the short answer to your question: pillar one is flow segmentation. And this is the biggest mechanical difference between trading via RFQ, or more particularly via what our system looks more like — a single-dealer platform in many ways — and again, like trading on an order book. We don't have to be taking down floor or posting quotes that can be sniped by anyone, that can be front-run by high-frequency takers that might be trading into the public void of who knows how smart the guys are at the top of the book on Binance. And I'll give you a cheat code: they're very, very, very smart. So you have to be very defensive on that.

Whereas for us — we don't have an API yet, it's on the roadmap, we can come back to that question later — but we're optimizing for: what's the best possible price we can show to retail order flow when we know that it's retail order flow? When we can see who's on the other side of the trade, and when we can get comfortable with quoting very big size because this isn't adversarial or front-running or arbitraging. These are guys just trying to get the best all-in price for their block trade or their entry into a mid-frequency day-trading position. And that's a completely different ballpark in terms of how you can quote it.

To put this all in a summation form: our liquidity quality does look like — if you're looking for an RFQ from, say, a tier-one desk (I pick on again, a Jump or Wintermute or something like that) — I would expect it to be in the same ballpark. But the difference is that's not at all what's happening when you're matching on a public order book. But that is what's happening if you are, say, a $10 billion institution onboarded onto an OTC trading relationship with one of these guys.

So one of the ways I like thinking about what we're doing in Variational is democratizing access to that quality of execution and that style of trading, which is massively usually better for the end client than having to trade directly on an order book. There's a few more mechanical things, but in the interest of time let me pause there on your question. I think that's one of the big lion's-share reasons.

What Happens as Non-Toxic Flow Migrates?

Corey: And maybe my next question will get you to continue to extrapolate.
