What I find is that between 2001 and 2011, farm sizes on average declined by 12.45%, and that implies a 3.2 percentage point increase in agricultural employment share. Which is roughly, if I look at the baseline employment share, that's about 5.5% decline relative to the baseline. Which is, I think given this big share of people that are employed in agriculture, it is precious is what my understanding was.

And similarly, for manufacturing, I find that it's a 2.2 percentage point decline due to this average decline in farm size, and which is about 18% relative to the baseline employment share in 2001. So these are pretty sizable, as what my takeaway was from the structural transformation analysis.

性别效应问题

Shruti： Are you able to figure out and separate in any way, the employment share difference between men and women? Because, you know, that is also impacted by the inheritance law, right? I mean, in part of that is, you know, it changes how women view themselves, their pool of assets, you know, how much one can educate a woman if she gets married earlier or later depending on what the pool of assets are, what she will inherit, and so on and so forth.

Aishwarya： Right, no, that's absolutely right. So, that's one of the biggest concerns with using this instrument. Because there is literature—this reform was, by the way, this reform was passed in five states in India during the 70s and the 90s. So there's a ton of literature by Heath and Tan, by Calvi and Roy, which shows that as a result of this reform, they find that educational attainment of women increased, their labor force participation, and they have greater autonomy within the household. So, all of these effects basically point towards this concern that there can be a direct impact of this reform which do not go through land fragmentation. And they can be driven through the supply-side changes in female labor force participation.

稳健性检验

So to address these concerns, what I do is—one thing is that I first restrict this sample to just male. So these are the results that I have been telling you—comes from just a male sample, where these direct effects are less likely to be prevalent. And there can still be some concerns, some residual concerns, that if women have higher bargaining power within the household, through some intrahousehold bargaining there might be some second-order effects on even male labor supply decisions.

Right? Yeah. So to address that, what I do is that the IHDS survey has this very nice questionnaire on gender relations where it asks women questions about their autonomy within the household when it comes to taking decisions for the household, their financial attainment, autonomy, their physical mobility. And so I follow Heath's paper and I use these three questions to actually construct a district-level measure of female autonomy, and how it changes in the IHDS way from round one to round two, and then control for that to see that if I control for that, does this result still survive. And what I find is that the results magnitudes are almost the same even after controlling for this. So this indirect channel might be less prevalent when we are thinking about structural transformation in the male sample.

Shruti： Yeah. And you know, the female labor force participation in India first of all tends to be low, and a lot of it tends to be in exactly what you would expect—driving the big part of the result, which is, you know, supporting the family farm and things like that, right? So now the story just hangs together very cohesively in some sense based on everything we understand in the Indian context.

对制造业的直接影响

Shruti： So now, ah, you also have a couple of other results, right? And this is between 2005 and 2013—how the decline in farm size changes manufacturing employment, the number of firms, and the decline in average firm size. Now this is the part which is both quite surprising to me and very very large. So, can you walk us through how you went about measuring and finding that result?

Aishwarya： Right. So, for this result, this was essentially my attempt of trying to test for one of those mechanisms that we were discussing through which structural transformation can be affected.

And so I use the Economic Census of India, which records at the establishment level. It gives me information on how much labor is employed, industry of the establishment. It's not very detailed, but it gives me the important things that I would require for this analysis. So, I aggregate this establishment-level data at the district level. And what I see is that the three measures that I track, as you said, is the total employment in the manufacturing sector in a district, the number of firms which is basically establishments in the manufacturing sector, and the average firm size which is the number of employees.

Yeah. And I run this through the same empirical strategy with two periods and the inheritance reform. And what I actually find—and even I was surprised to see how large these effects turned out to be. Like, I was expecting them because of the presence of other literature on India that there should be some friction to the manufacturing sector. But I was surprised to see that land is really a big constraint, that it translates into almost like a 20% decline in the number of firms, and like a 30% decline in employment, and on average firms becoming smaller.

土地密集型行业的异质性检验

And then just to like tie this all together in terms of, is it still picking up something else? Like, why are these effects so large, are these picking up some other effect? I did this heterogeneity exercise where I divide my establishments based on their industry affiliation as more land-intensive versus less land-intensive. So basically depending on the median—the above-median land-reliant industries vs. small. And I again aggregate my sample to the district level, and what I see is that this negative effect is larger for the high-land-intensive industry. So that kind of reaffirms this mechanism that it is operating through the land-related friction somehow.

土地碎片化并非"意外后果"

Shruti： Well, I mean, not somehow—you have told us how. Or, land fragmentation is not exactly an unintended consequence in India, right? It was the intended consequence. Right after the Zamindari experience, for 50-plus years we've tried our very best to make land holding smaller and cheaper. Sometimes land holding got smaller because the governments were successful, and sometimes land holding size got smaller because of population growth and not having primogeniture and having the Hindu Undivided Family setup, and so on and so forth. But it's not like this is a surprising, weird, unintended consequence of a weird regulation. This was very much intended government policy, and now we see the terrible effects of what that kind of, you know, policy does. And it's a little bit hard to now undo time and expect that everything will consolidate, you know, overnight.

一般均衡模型

Shruti： And so in some sense, the reason comes from—do you tell us exactly how this is happening?

So now to step away from the empirical results you find, then you develop a general equilibrium model, because now you're finding these sort of really large effects. And the large effects are both about the share of agriculture vs. manufacturing in the economy, but also about the wedges, right—the difference in wedges between agricultural wages and manufacturing wages, agricultural profitability, and overall welfare effects.

So first, can you walk us through: how does someone model something like this? For true, a complex topic. And then what sort of welfare effects do you find when you look at both transmission mechanisms?

模型框架

Aishwarya： Right. So, I tried to get to the welfare results using this two-sector general equilibrium model. And I omit services from my model because I don't find significant effects there. And then I try to see—this model is essentially based on models by Farrokhi and Pellegrina in the trade literature and also by Hibbich and Redding. So these people recently, like they have these papers in the trade literature which looks at structural change, and their models are based on land allocation. So that's where I got my idea because I'm probably trying to study this, this might be a good framework to begin with.

模型运作机制

So what is happening in this model is that within every district, there is a fixed supply of land, and this land is held by some N number of landowners in fixed parcel sizes. And specification in the model do not account for any transactions of land between landholders because, VC that is not very prevalent in India, that's not very easy for landowners to transact between among each other. So I can treat this parcel of land that's an endowment to a landlord as an exogenous endowment.

Yeah. And what I do with this is that essentially, the whole point of structural transformation in this model comes from the land allocation decision of the landlords. So each landlord has this land parcel which has a distinct suitability for agriculture. So you can think about it as differences in soil quality, fertility, which makes some parcels better suited for agriculture as compared to others. But each plot is equally productive in manufacturing.

So from a landlord's perspective, the landlord first observes the suitability of their land plot, and then they decide what they want to do—put it to agriculture, or they want to lease their land plot to a manufacturing firm. Because I model there this one representative manufacturing firm in each district which wants to take land from landlords for manufacturing production. So basically there is this land allocation decision that landlords need to navigate.

模型的简化设置

In the model, it's a very simplified framework because I wanted to get to its larger implications for structural transformation. So it is—I just have two factors of production in this model, it's just land and labor for now. And in this model, I essentially don't treat separately agricultural versus manufacturing wages, but it's more of like—land, the labor in this model is willing to supply its labor inelastically to whichever sector has demand. Right? There is going to set one common wage in the district in their equilibrium.

碎片化如何进入模型

And so this is how land fragmentation enters the model—there is a fixed stock of supply. So you think about any hobbies and even like the general process of land fragmentation, what it is going to do is that it is going to increase the number of landlords. And given the fixed supply of land, it just basically changes the land endowment of each landlord. So on average, the land fragmentation shock just decreases the size of the land owned by a landlord.

And then it alters the land allocation decision through precisely the two channels that we have been discussing so far—that in the agriculture sector, as that land size becomes smaller, it changes the per acre profits from that particular land plot. So it alters the rents or the profits that a landlord can get from putting his own land into cultivation.

In the manufacturing sector, because of small farm sizes, this land acquisition costs are going to increase, which are going to reduce firm profits, as a result of which the rents that landlords can receive from firms are going to decline. So this friction comes basically model like this—reduced form wedge on the rental rate that firms can offer to landlords. And this wedge is modeled as a function of the district farm size, such that when the average farm size declines, this wedge increases and it reduces the rent that landlords can get from the manufacturing sector.

So in a very reduced form way, I'm trying to capture this entire story into the land allocation decision. So as the shock hits, what it does is—through both these sectors, it basically alters the relative rent a landlord can get from putting the land in manufacturing versus agriculture. And that shapes and that drives the land allocation process, and consequently it shapes the labor allocation as well. Depending on which sector expands, there is more labor in that sector, and that drives structural transformation as well in the model. So, that's like a big picture overview of just how the model is working in the set.

弹性估计

And so, one of the central exercises in this paper was essentially to estimate the elasticity with which as farm sizes change, how these two frictions in the manufacturing and agriculture sector shape.

So, what I did in this paper was that for the manufacturing sector, I actually used like firm-level data from the Annual Survey of Industries. And what's good about this data is that it actually reports what is the value of new land purchase made by a firm. Using that data, I am able to estimate the elasticity with which the land acquisition cost change as district farm sizes change. And what I find is that between 2001 and 2011, on average, this land assembly friction that is there in my model increases by about 35%. So it is a very large increase.

And similarly, than using micro data from farms from IHDS, which reports in detail the output and input expenditure at the farm level, using the panel structure of that data, I am able to estimate that within the sample of households by land size changes due to inheritance—so it's like more of an exogenous change in the farm size—in this sub-sample, I find that the profits per acre increase as farm size are smaller. But this profitability advantage in my sample is—it's roughly like on average, it increases by 1.1%, this is what I find.

令人震惊的福利结果

Aishwarya： So then when I took these are like elasticities, I use them to actually quantify the model. And what I still find is that so when it comes to welfare, all master, the model does a good job of replicating the structural transformation results that I find in the empirics, which was really assuring—that it is very closely able to match the empirical estimates. So, it does show that structural transformation is hindered.

But then when you look at welfare, which is the total real income in a district which is the income of workers and landlords together, that actually goes up. And there is substantial variation—there are some districts that even lose. In fact, 50% of the districts in my sample experience welfare loss, but 50% also gain. So the variation is from -0.8% to about 1.85%. So it's a huge variation. But overall, the relationship is negative—that districts that experience more fragmentation are experiencing overall welfare gains.

分配效应的分解

So, I was overall a bit puzzled to like basically, like, think about okay, what's going on here. And so, I basically then look at the distributional implications. And what I find is that the two components that make up welfare is wages and land rents.

And what I find is that real wages are actually falling by about 1.92% on average, and all of these gains are coming from land rents increasing, which increase by almost 5%.

So even whatever we're seeing as a positive effect is actually not overall should be concluded as a good thing, because we are creating a very large distributional gap. The workers who are in the models are landless are essentially the ones who are bearing the cost of this land fragmentation, because manufacturing frictions prevent the expansion of manufacturing activity. And it's a fact that manufacturing is related to be more labor-intensive than agriculture. So when the more labor-intensive sectors shrink, it reduces the aggregate labor demand, it reduces the wages in the model. So that was like the key takeaway for me from this model—that yes, we do find some positive effects, but there are these like very sharp distributional implications that we should be careful about.

常识层面的解读

Shruti： And you know, just common sense tells us, right, even without taking sides, there are more workers than there are landowners. Right? Just simply put. So, what you are now trying to pass through where it is going, it's a small number of people who see these huge gains, and there is a large number of people who are actually trying to exit agriculture and move into slightly more productive sectors of the employment, who simply can't find employment in those sectors.

Ah, which also tells you why there are so many people kind of vaguely hanging around agriculture, you know, underemployed sort of in there but don't end up finding manufacturing jobs and moving into anything more productive.

So, overall, again, the story hangs together, and I think it's just a coincidence tell the way you walked us through the model and these distribution effects, that we should not look at headline results, and we should really parse through what's happening. So overall, I find that, you know, your structural transformation story hangs together both empirically and in the model.

政策含义

Shruti： And now what does this mean for policy reforms? At least the most immediately, you know, policy reforms that you can think of when it comes to land.

反事实：消除制造业土地摩擦

Aishwarya： Right, so I think to get to that, like one exercise that I do in the model is that I start by switching off all land manufacturing and assembly frictions in manufacturing in the model. So this is like the benchmark case where there are just no frictions for assembling land for manufacturing.

And when I do that, what I find is that these welfare gains that were coming from agriculture due to land fragmentation, they almost increase by 50%. So the average effect on the welfare increases by 50%. And which is the better result—that even the distributional gap closes, because now what is happening is that you allow manufacturing sector to relatively not contract by as much as it was in the baseline. So it does not shrink as much, which means that the demand for labor and the wages are also not going to fall by as much.

So now in this counterfactual where there are no land manufacturing/land assembly frictions, real wages just declined by about 0.17% on average, which was 1.9 in the baseline. And even the real rents don't go up by as much. So basically we are kind of closing the gap between the owners of labor and the owners of land.

So that was a very interesting finding. And that's when I would like to circle back the discussion to even your policy paper on the ease of converting agricultural land to non-agricultural use. It kind of points towards working in that direction—that if we are, I am not saying that we completely eliminate fragmentation because that's a big political economy issues to deal with, you can't so easily change.

Shruti： Yeah, but you're hinting towards what we need to do: reduce frictions. And some of those frictions come from changing land use, some of those frictions come from assembling parcels, some of those frictions come from inability to sell to a farmer or a non-farmer and so on and so forth. So, then all your policy recommendations would be targeted towards reducing frictions in converting land use, either by changing the user or the use.

Aishwarya： Correct, correct. So exactly, like as you said, that if—as your paper mentions—there are like six to eight policy hurdles on average to convert your land to non-agricultural use. So just a very utopian world where it's a one-stop destination to converting your land, then even if I—however much a firm I am suppose to do that process with 10 landholders—it will significantly reduce the cost of doing that rather than doing this process 10 times with like 10 landowners.

Right? So that was like my first policy takeaway from this paper—that any efforts that can reduce this land assembly frictions are very important in this context, both distributionary as well as when we think about just the aggregate district-level welfare.

土地市场功能失调

Shruti： That sounds simple but that's actually pretty big, right? Because we don't have well-functioning land markets. Ah, part of that is the friction, a consequence of that is also the friction. So, the big takeaway: we need to systematically move towards just better-functioning land markets, because then consolidation can happen through the market with greater ease. And we don't need to rely on eminent domain and political brokers and, you know, all these other—like, we are basically pointing a gun at people and forcing them to consolidate their land. And so a lot of that can be avoided. So I think we're on the same page when it comes to some of the policy recommendation.

小农盈利优势的警示性解读

Aishwarya： Right, exactly. And like another thing that I wanted to pinpoint is that there is this discussion on what really the small farm profitability advantage means. And there is a lot of like discussion in the literature that it could also just like reflect some of this size-dependent distortions in markets which enable small farms to have larger profits per acre. And so if this is some result of some market distortions, that also points us towards how carefully and how consciously you should interpret the welfare results.

Because what we essentially talking about is that in my model, when I shut down this profitability advantage, I see the results flip completely—like the with greater land fragmentation, welfare actually goes down. So basically what this exercise shows is that this profitability advantage is an important counter-weighing force against this very large manufacturing section. So to the extent to which this profitability advantage is a real resource gain and is it just reflective of some distortions in the input markets, we again need to be conscious about promoting small things in a lifetime policy.

So, although my paper is not taking a stand on decomposing this and whether this is a resource gain or whether these are distortions, but something that should be interpreted with caution is definitely something I would.

结语：破除小农浪漫化神话

Shruti： And also interpreted with common sense, wouldn't you say? Now there is the story across the world that things get more productive as fewer people work in agriculture, and there is more mechanization and there is larger holding size. I see no reason to think of India as some kind of, like, you know, sort of unique outlier in this story. Like I have literally no reason to believe that. It may be true for very specific things, you know, particular kind of organic farms that produce a particular kind of mango or something like that. But largely when we are talking about like regular agriculture, scale effects are everything. Ambedkar was saying this 120 years ago, people are still saying this now. But we do have a very romantic notion attached to the small farmer and this small sort of land holding, a sort of family farm. And I think some of this comes from the colonial experience and otherwise. But I'm pretty glad that you're helping us, you know, overall dispel these crazy myths.

Thank you so much for doing this. This is truly a pleasure. The paper is fantastic. It's really really rigorous and very important, because we just see what a big barrier land has become to India's structural transformation—which is really the only ladder we have towards greater economic growth and development in India. So, thank you so much for doing this.

Aishwarya： And a very long ladder too, but yes.

Shruti： Yeah, for a very large number of people, right. So, thank you so much. It was really fun engaging with you on the job market paper.

Aishwarya： And even I learned a lot from this conversation.

## 一、被误读的"小农优势"：一场统计幻觉的胜利
Aishwarya 论文中最耐人寻味的悖论在于——**小农场每英亩利润更高**这个看似"温情"的结论，可能根本不是"小的更美"，而是市场扭曲的统计残影。当她在模型中关闭"小农盈利优势"这一渠道时，整个福利结论**符号翻转**：土地碎片化变成了纯粹的净损失。
这暗示了一个令人不安的可能性：**印度过去 70 年被歌颂为"社会正义"的土地再分配政策，其经济正当性可能建立在一个测量伪影之上**。那些用来为小农辩护的"每英亩产出更高"的经验证据，或许只是投入品市场（信贷、劳动力监督、家庭劳动力的机会成本被系统性低估）扭曲的镜像。换言之，我们看到的不是小农的效率，而是大农被更严厉的税收和监管所惩罚的负片。
## 二、跨领域连接：土地碎片化 = 印度版的"专利丛林"（Patent Thicket）
